119-hjres-42.one_liner: Cancel a Department of Energy rule on appliance energy efficiency requirements
provisions: Cancels a Department of Energy rule from October 2024 about energy efficiency standards for appliances
Removes updated requirements for companies to certify that washing machines, dishwashers, and other appliances meet energy standards
Removes updated labeling requirements that tell consumers about appliance energy efficiency
Removes updated enforcement rules the government uses to check if appliances meet energy standards

supporters: Supporters say this removes updated certification requirements that add regulatory costs for companies making washing machines, dishwashers, and other appliances.
Supporters say this eliminates new enforcement rules that increase government oversight of appliance manufacturers.
critics: Critics say this removes updated labeling requirements that would tell consumers about energy efficiency of washing machines and dishwashers.
Critics say this eliminates enforcement rules that help ensure appliances actually meet energy efficiency standards.

119-hjres-24.one_liner: Cancel energy efficiency standards for walk-in coolers and freezers
provisions: Cancels a government rule from December 2024
Removes limits on how much energy walk-in coolers and freezers can use
Lets businesses use coolers and freezers that use more energy

supporters: Supporters say this cancels the December 2024 rule that forces businesses to buy more expensive walk-in coolers and freezers.
Supporters say this lets restaurant and grocery store owners choose equipment without government limits on energy use.
critics: Critics say this removes energy limits that would cut electric bills for businesses using walk-in coolers and freezers.
Critics say this cancels rules that would reduce energy waste from thousands of commercial refrigeration units.

119-hjres-25.one_liner: Cancel an IRS rule requiring crypto brokers to report sales to the government
provisions: Cancels an IRS rule that started in December 2024
The rule required companies that help people buy and sell crypto to report sales information to the IRS
These companies no longer have to send these reports to the government

supporters: Supporters say this protects crypto companies from the December 2024 IRS rule that forced them to send sales information to the government.
Supporters say this removes the requirement for DeFi companies to report digital asset sales to the IRS.
critics: Critics say this helps people hide crypto sales from the IRS by canceling the December 2024 reporting rule.
Critics say this makes it harder for the government to track digital asset transactions for tax purposes.

119-hjres-35.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule charging fees for methane emissions from oil and gas companies
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from November 2024 about methane emission fees
The rule charged oil and gas companies fees for releasing too much methane gas
Companies will no longer pay these fees for methane emissions

supporters: Supporters say this bill removes fees that oil and gas companies would have to pay for methane emissions, which could lower energy costs for families.
Supporters say the EPA rule from November 2024 puts extra costs on American energy companies that could hurt jobs in the oil and gas industry.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule means oil and gas companies will not pay fees for releasing methane gas, which contributes to climate change.
Critics say the November 2024 EPA rule held companies accountable for methane emissions above certain limits, and removing it weakens environmental protection.

119-hjres-20.one_liner: Cancel a Department of Energy rule on gas water heater energy use
provisions: Cancels a Department of Energy rule from December 26, 2024
Stops new rules that would require gas water heaters to use less energy
Keeps older rules about how much energy gas water heaters can use

supporters: Supporters say canceling the December 26, 2024 DOE rule will save consumers money because gas water heaters meeting the new energy standards would cost more to buy.
Supporters say the new energy rules force families to buy water heaters with technology that may not work as well as their current models.
critics: Critics say keeping the old energy standards will cost families more on monthly gas bills because water heaters will waste more energy.
Critics say canceling the December 26, 2024 rule will eliminate American manufacturing jobs for companies that make efficient water heater parts.

119-hjres-88.one_liner: Cancel EPA approval for California to set its own car pollution rules
provisions: Cancel the EPA's approval for California to set its own car pollution rules
Require California to follow the same federal car pollution rules as other states
Block California's Advanced Clean Cars II program
Stop California from making car companies meet different pollution standards than other states

supporters: Supporters say this would require California to follow the same federal car pollution rules as other states.
Supporters say this would stop car companies from having to meet different pollution standards in California than in other states.
critics: Critics say this would block California's Advanced Clean Cars II program that sets stricter pollution rules.
Critics say this would cancel California's EPA approval to set its own car pollution rules under the Clean Air Act.

119-hjres-75.one_liner: Cancel a Department of Energy rule setting energy standards for commercial refrigerators and freezers
provisions: Cancels a Department of Energy rule published on January 21, 2025
The rule set new energy efficiency requirements for commercial refrigerators, freezers, and refrigerator-freezers
Prevents these energy requirements from taking effect

supporters: Supporters say this would prevent businesses from having to buy more expensive commercial refrigerators and freezers that meet the January 21, 2025 energy standards.
Supporters say blocking these energy requirements would save small grocery stores and restaurants from costly equipment upgrades.
critics: Critics say canceling the Department of Energy's commercial refrigeration standards would waste energy and increase electricity costs for businesses.
Critics say preventing these energy efficiency rules would block savings that the Department of Energy already determined were economically justified.

119-hjres-87.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule letting California set its own emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from April 2023 that let California set emission standards different from federal rules
Removes California's ability to require its own pollution controls on heavy-duty trucks
Blocks California rules for zero-emission airport shuttles and clean truck requirements

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would create uniform national emission standards instead of letting California set different rules for heavy-duty trucks and airport shuttles.
Supporters say the EPA waiver lets California force truck manufacturers to meet stricter standards that increase costs for trucking companies nationwide.
critics: Critics say this resolution would remove California's ability to require zero-emission airport shuttles and clean truck standards needed to reduce pollution near ports and highways.
Critics say blocking the EPA waiver prevents states from setting stricter emission controls when federal standards are not strong enough to protect public health.

119-hjres-61.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule setting air pollution limits for rubber tire factories
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from November 2024 that limited toxic air pollution from rubber tire factories
Removes rules requiring tire companies to control harmful chemicals released when making rubber

supporters: Supporters say this would remove costly rules that force tire companies to install expensive equipment to control chemicals during rubber processing.
Supporters say the November 2024 EPA rule puts unfair regulatory burden on rubber tire manufacturers that could hurt American jobs.
critics: Critics say this would allow tire factories to release more toxic air pollutants that harm people living near rubber processing plants.
Critics say canceling these rules ignores a 2020 court decision that required EPA to regulate all harmful chemicals from tire manufacturing.

119-hjres-60.one_liner: Cancel a National Park Service rule limiting off-road vehicles at Glen Canyon
provisions: Cancels a Park Service rule from January 2025
The rule limited where people could drive ATVs and off-road vehicles at Glen Canyon National Recreation Area in Arizona and Utah
Canceling the rule lets off-road vehicles back into park areas where they were restricted

supporters: Supporters say this restores access for ATV and off-highway vehicle users who were blocked from Glen Canyon areas by the January 2025 Park Service rule.
Supporters say this gives back recreational rights to off-road vehicle drivers in the Arizona and Utah parts of the park.
critics: Critics say this puts ATVs and off-road vehicles back into Glen Canyon areas that were protected by the January 2025 rule.
Critics say this removes limits on vehicle use that the Park Service created to protect the recreation area from damage.

119-hr-3944.one_liner: Fund military construction and veterans programs for 2026
provisions: Gives money to build military facilities for the Army, Navy, Air Force, and National Guard
Funds veterans healthcare, benefits, and cemeteries through the Department of Veterans Affairs
Pays for building and maintaining military family housing
Funds military programs with NATO and military retirement homes

supporters: Supporters say this funds military construction for Army, Navy, Air Force and National Guard facilities needed to keep forces ready.
Supporters say this provides money for Veterans Health Administration healthcare and Veterans Benefits Administration services that veterans have earned.
Supporters say this pays for building and maintaining military family housing so service members and their families have places to live.
critics: Critics say this continues high spending on military construction projects when other priorities like education and infrastructure need funding.
Critics say the costs for building new military facilities and maintaining family housing add billions more to defense spending.
Critics say this funds NATO Security Investment Program while domestic veterans services and social programs need more resources.

119-hjres-89.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule letting California set pollution limits for trucks
provisions: Cancels an EPA decision made in January 2025
Stops California from requiring trucks to produce less pollution than federal law requires
Takes away California's permission to set different pollution rules for trucks and engines

supporters: Supporters say this prevents trucking companies from having to meet different emission rules in California than in other states.
Supporters say this keeps federal emission standards uniform across all 50 states for heavy-duty trucks and engines.
critics: Critics say this blocks California from reducing NOX pollution from heavy-duty trucks that causes health problems.
Critics say this takes away California's authority under the Clean Air Act to set stricter emission standards than federal law.

provisions: Funds federal agencies through September 2025 to prevent a government shutdown on March 14
Keeps funding for most government programs at 2024 levels
Extends the National Flood Insurance Program
Extends Medicare and Medicaid programs
Extends cash help for families in need through the TANF program
Keeps fentanyl substances illegal as controlled drugs
Extends cybersecurity protections for government computer systems

supporters: Supporters say this bill prevents a government shutdown on March 14 that would stop paychecks for 2 million federal workers and close national parks.
Supporters say extending Medicare and Medicaid programs protects health coverage for 65 million seniors and 80 million low-income Americans.
Supporters say keeping the National Flood Insurance Program running helps 5 million homeowners keep flood coverage and lets them buy and sell homes.
critics: Critics say funding programs at 2024 levels ignores inflation and leaves agencies with less buying power than last year.
Critics say this temporary fix until September 2025 creates uncertainty for federal agencies trying to plan long-term projects and hiring.
Critics say Congress should make hard choices about spending cuts instead of automatically continuing all programs from last year.

119-hr-23.one_liner: Sanction foreign people who help the International Criminal Court prosecute Americans and allies
provisions: Blocks visas and freezes assets of foreign people who help the International Criminal Court investigate or prosecute Americans
Applies sanctions to foreign people who help the court prosecute citizens of US allies that did not join the court
Blocks visas for family members of sanctioned people
Cuts all US funding to the International Criminal Court
Bans future US government funding to the court

supporters: Supporters say this protects Americans from being prosecuted by a foreign court that the US never agreed to join.
Supporters say this saves taxpayer money by cutting all US government funding to the International Criminal Court.
Supporters say this defends citizens of US allies who did not join the court from foreign prosecution.
critics: Critics say this blocks investigations of war crimes by freezing assets and banning visas for people who help the court.
Critics say the visa bans on family members punish innocent relatives who had nothing to do with court work.
Critics say this hurts relationships with US allies who support the International Criminal Court.

119-hr-1.one_liner: Cut taxes while adding work requirements for food assistance and healthcare
provisions: Makes the 2017 tax cuts permanent so tax rates stay low
Requires adults without children to work 80 hours per month to get food assistance
Cuts funding for climate programs from the 2022 climate law
Requires some adults to work to keep government health insurance
Ends government-paid loans for college students starting in 2026
Adds money for military weapons and border security
Raises fees for people seeking asylum and other immigration benefits

supporters: Supporters say making the 2017 tax rates of 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, and 37% permanent will help working families keep more of their paychecks instead of facing tax increases.
Supporters say requiring able-bodied adults without young children to work 80 hours per month for SNAP benefits encourages self-sufficiency and reduces government dependency.
Supporters say cutting unobligated funds from Inflation Reduction Act climate programs eliminates wasteful spending on green energy subsidies that drive up costs for families.
critics: Critics say expanding SNAP work requirements to adults up to age 65 and requiring work when children are only 7 years old will increase hunger among vulnerable families who cannot find adequate employment.
Critics say ending subsidized loans and graduate PLUS loans starting July 2026 will make college unaffordable for millions of students, especially those from low-income families.
Critics say new fees for asylum applications and employment authorization create financial barriers for people fleeing persecution who already face difficult circumstances.

119-s-5.one_liner: Require detention of non-citizens arrested for theft, burglary, or shoplifting
provisions: Requires the government to detain non-citizens who are in the country illegally and have been arrested for break-ins, theft, or shoplifting
Lets states sue the federal government when immigration decisions hurt the state or its people
States can sue when the government releases someone from immigration custody
States can sue when the government fails to properly check people trying to enter the country
States can sue when financial harm to the state exceeds $100

supporters: Supporters say this would keep people who commit break-ins, theft, and shoplifting in detention so they cannot hurt more communities.
Supporters say states need the power to sue the federal government when immigration decisions cost them money or put their residents at risk.
Supporters say the $100 minimum lets states get help even for smaller harms from bad immigration choices.
critics: Critics say requiring detention for arrests means holding people who have not been found guilty of any crime.
Critics say letting states sue over any decision that costs them $100 could flood courts with lawsuits.
Critics say states could sue the federal government for releasing someone from custody even when the release follows proper legal process.

119-s-331.one_liner: Make fentanyl-related substances permanently illegal under federal law
provisions: Makes all fentanyl-related substances permanently illegal under federal drug law
Sets the same prison sentences for these substances as for other fentanyl drugs, including 10 years minimum for 100 grams or more
Creates a new process for researchers to get permission to study these illegal drugs
Lets researchers use one permit for multiple related research locations
Lets researchers make small amounts of controlled substances for research without extra manufacturing permits

supporters: Supporters say this bill closes gaps in federal drug law by permanently making all fentanyl-related substances illegal under Schedule I.
Supporters say the 10-year mandatory minimum sentence for trafficking 100 grams or more will deter people from selling these substances.
Supporters say the new research registration process will help scientists study these substances while keeping them under strict control.
critics: Critics say the 10-year mandatory minimum sentences remove judges' ability to consider individual circumstances in sentencing.
Critics say permanently scheduling all fentanyl-related substances as a class could make future substances illegal even if they have medical value.
Critics say the broad definition of fentanyl-related substances could criminalize people who unknowingly possess substances they don't know are illegal.

119-s-2296.one_liner: Fund the military and set defense policies for the year starting October 2025
provisions: Allows the military to spend money on weapons, ships, aircraft and equipment for the year starting October 2025
Sets how many active duty and reserve troops the military can have
Allows money for building new military facilities and extends deadlines for older construction projects
Requires the Defense Department to make a plan for dealing with new biological technologies that could affect security
Requires the Navy to improve how it maintains and repairs ships at private shipyards
Continues a program to strengthen military forces and help allies in the Pacific region through 2026
Removes diversity, equity and inclusion rules from the Defense Department and eliminates the Chief Diversity Officer position

supporters: Supporters say the bill ensures military readiness by authorizing funds for essential weapons, ships, and aircraft needed to defend the country starting in October 2025.
Supporters say continuing the Pacific Deterrence Initiative through 2026 helps protect allies and counter threats in the Indo-Pacific region where tensions are rising.
Supporters say removing diversity, equity and inclusion rules and the Chief Diversity Officer position eliminates unnecessary bureaucracy and refocuses the military on its core mission.
critics: Critics say the bill authorizes military construction projects and extends deadlines for older projects without requiring detailed cost estimates or completion timelines for taxpayer accountability.

Critics say eliminating the Chief Diversity Officer and diversity programs will harm recruitment and retention of women and minority service members who make up growing portions of military personnel.
Critics say requiring a biotechnology security strategy without providing specific funding or implementation deadlines means the Defense Department may not adequately prepare for biological threats.

119-s-1582.one_liner: Create rules for companies that issue stablecoins
provisions: Only banks and government-approved companies can issue stablecoins to US users
Companies must hold real US dollars equal to every stablecoin they issue
Companies issuing more than $10 billion in stablecoins must get federal approval instead of state approval
Companies must publish monthly reports showing what money they hold to back their stablecoins
Foreign companies can offer stablecoins in the US if Treasury approves their home country rules
Stablecoin companies must follow anti-money laundering laws

supporters: Supporters say requiring only banks and government-approved companies to issue stablecoins will make these digital coins safer for regular people to use.
Supporters say the rule that companies must hold real US dollars equal to every stablecoin they issue will protect users if a company fails.
Supporters say monthly reports showing what money companies hold will let people check if their stablecoins are actually backed by real money.
critics: Critics say limiting stablecoin issuance to only banks and approved companies will reduce competition and block new companies from entering the market.
Critics say the requirement to hold US dollars backing every stablecoin will create high costs that smaller companies cannot afford.
Critics say the $10 billion threshold forcing large issuers to get federal approval instead of state approval will create confusing rules that favor big banks.

119-hr-4.one_liner: Cut $9.4 billion in unspent funding for international programs and public broadcasting
provisions: Cuts $9.4 billion in government money set aside but not yet spent
Reduces funding for health programs in other countries
Cuts money for peacekeeping missions around the world
Reduces funding for public radio and TV stations
Cuts aid money sent to refugee programs and developing countries

supporters: Supporters say cutting $9.4 billion in unspent government money will reduce waste and help balance the federal budget.
Supporters say the United States should focus tax dollars on domestic needs instead of sending billions to foreign countries through aid programs.
Supporters say these cuts target money that agencies have not used yet, so programs can continue with existing funds.
critics: Critics say cutting health program funding will harm disease prevention efforts that protect millions of people in developing countries.
Critics say reducing refugee assistance money will leave fewer resources to help displaced people fleeing wars and disasters.
Critics say cuts to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting will reduce funding for local public radio and TV stations that serve rural communities.

119-s-9.one_liner: Ban male-born students from women's and girls' sports teams in federally funded schools
provisions: Makes it illegal under Title IX for schools that get federal money to let male-born students play on women's or girls' sports teams
Defines sex based on biology and genetics at birth
Applies to public elementary schools, high schools, and colleges

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects opportunities for biological females in women's and girls' sports at federally funded schools by preventing male-born students from competing against them.
Supporters say defining sex based on biology and genetics at birth ensures fair competition and preserves scholarships and records meant for female athletes.
critics: Critics say this bill discriminates against transgender girls by banning them from participating in school sports programs that match their gender identity at public schools and colleges.
Critics say the Title IX violation rule would force federally funded schools to exclude transgender students from athletic activities, harming their ability to participate in school life.

119-sjres-10.one_liner: End the national emergency about energy declared by the President in January 2025
provisions: Ends the national emergency about energy that the President declared on January 20, 2025
The President declared this emergency saying the country does not have enough energy supply and infrastructure
The emergency let government agencies fast-track approvals for oil, gas, and other energy projects
The emergency let the military assess energy needs and use emergency construction powers
Removes the special fast-track powers that agencies got from this emergency

supporters: Supporters say ending this emergency would restore normal environmental permitting rules that agencies bypassed under the January 20, 2025 order.
Supporters say the emergency powers that let agencies fast-track oil and gas projects were too broad and should be removed.
Supporters say normal permitting processes should return instead of the special fast-track approvals for energy infrastructure.
critics: Critics say ending the emergency would slow energy infrastructure projects in the Northeast, West Coast, and Alaska that are being expedited under the current order.
Critics say the energy supply and infrastructure problems identified on January 20, 2025 still exist and need these emergency powers to fix.
Critics say removing the military's emergency construction authority would weaken the country's ability to secure energy resources.

119-s-6.one_liner: Require doctors to provide care to children born alive after abortions
provisions: Requires doctors to give the same care to children born alive after abortions as they would give any other newborn
Requires doctors to send these children to a hospital right away
Makes doctors and hospital staff report any failures to follow these rules to police
Sets penalties of up to 5 years in prison and fines for doctors who don't provide the required care
Makes it murder to intentionally kill a child born alive after an abortion
Protects mothers from being charged with crimes under this law
Lets mothers sue doctors who break these rules

supporters: Supporters say this would require doctors to give the same medical care to babies born alive after abortions as they give to any other newborn of the same age.
Supporters say the 5-year prison sentence and fines would stop doctors from neglecting or harming babies who survive abortions.
Supporters say requiring doctors and hospital staff to report failures to police would ensure these babies get proper protection.
critics: Critics say the 5-year prison penalties would make doctors afraid to provide abortion care, even when it's legal and necessary.
Critics say requiring police reports about medical care decisions would interfere with doctor-patient relationships.
Critics say this creates new criminal laws when existing murder and medical negligence laws already protect newborns.

119-sjres-12.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule charging oil and gas companies for methane emissions
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule that charges oil and gas companies for methane and greenhouse gas emissions
Stops the EPA from collecting annual fees from oil and gas companies whose emissions go above set limits
Ends the waste emissions charge program for petroleum and natural gas systems

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would eliminate annual fees that oil and gas companies must pay when their methane emissions go above EPA limits.
Supporters say ending the waste emissions charge program would reduce regulatory burden on petroleum and natural gas companies.
critics: Critics say canceling this EPA rule would remove financial incentives for oil and gas companies to cut their methane and greenhouse gas emissions.
Critics say stopping the annual emissions charges would let petroleum companies emit methane above set limits without paying environmental costs.

119-sjres-11.one_liner: Cancel rule requiring oil companies to report on historical artifacts before offshore drilling
provisions: Cancels a rule requiring oil and gas companies to check for historical artifacts before all offshore drilling
Returns to the old system where companies only check when the government suspects artifacts might be there
Removes the requirement to look for material remains that are at least 50 years old on the sea floor

supporters: Supporters say this saves oil and gas companies money by removing the requirement to check for 50-year-old artifacts before all offshore drilling.
Supporters say the old system worked fine - companies only need to check for sea floor artifacts when BOEM suspects they might be there.
Supporters say this speeds up drilling permits by removing the archaeological report requirement for all projects.
critics: Critics say this removes protection for underwater historical sites that are at least 50 years old on the sea floor.
Critics say oil and gas companies will destroy artifacts without checking first under the old system.
Critics say fewer archaeological resources will be found and protected when companies only check if BOEM suspects artifacts might be present.

119-sjres-28.one_liner: Cancel a rule letting government check on large payment apps
provisions: Cancels a December 2024 rule that let the government check on large payment apps
The rule covered apps that handle 50 million or more payments per year
The government will no longer check on these apps
Banks and small businesses were not covered by the rule

supporters: Supporters say this would remove the December 2024 rule that required government checks on payment apps with 50 million or more transactions per year.
Supporters say payment apps should not face the same oversight rules that banks follow.
critics: Critics say removing oversight of payment apps with 50 million transactions per year would leave millions of users without protection from fraud or poor practices.
Critics say the December 2024 rule was needed because large payment apps handle billions of dollars but had no government checks.

119-sjres-3.one_liner: Cancel an IRS rule requiring brokers to report cryptocurrency sales to the tax agency
provisions: Cancels an IRS rule from December 30, 2024 about cryptocurrency reporting
Stops brokers who handle crypto trades from having to report sales information to the IRS
Blocks new tax reporting requirements for digital asset transactions

supporters: Supporters say this resolution protects crypto brokers from having to collect and report customer information to the IRS under the December 30, 2024 rule.
Supporters say canceling the rule keeps decentralized finance platforms from being forced to track user transactions they were not designed to monitor.
critics: Critics say blocking the IRS rule will make it harder to track taxes owed on digital asset sales since brokers won't have to report this information.
Critics say without broker reporting requirements, crypto users can more easily avoid paying taxes on their digital asset transactions.

119-sjres-26.one_liner: Block a proposed weapons sale to Israel
provisions: Stops the U.S. from selling weapons and military equipment to Israel
Blocks a specific weapons deal that was already planned

supporters: Supporters say this resolution stops U.S. weapons and military equipment from going to Israel during ongoing conflicts.
Supporters say blocking this specific weapons deal gives Congress power to review arms sales before they happen.
Supporters say stopping the sale of these defense articles prevents U.S. weapons from being used in ways that harm civilians.
critics: Critics say blocking this planned weapons deal weakens Israel's ability to defend itself against security threats.
Critics say stopping the sale of defense articles and services damages the U.S.-Israel military partnership.
Critics say this resolution interferes with an approved arms sale that Israel was counting on for defense.

119-sjres-18.one_liner: Cancel a rule capping overdraft fees at $5 for large banks
provisions: Cancels a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule about overdraft fees
Lets large banks charge more than $5 when customers spend more money than they have in their account
The canceled rule would have capped overdraft fees at $5 at very large banks
Overdraft fees are charged when people spend more than their account balance

supporters: Supporters say canceling this rule lets very large banks set their own overdraft fees instead of being forced to cap them at $5.
Supporters say the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule would hurt large banks' ability to cover the costs of processing overdrafts.
critics: Critics say this lets very large banks continue charging overdraft fees higher than $5 when customers spend more than their account balance.
Critics say canceling the rule removes protections that would have saved consumers money on overdraft fees at large financial institutions.

provisions: Stops the government from selling weapons and military equipment to Israel
Uses Congress's power to reject the planned weapons sale

supporters: Supporters say this resolution uses Congress's constitutional power to disapprove planned weapons exports to Israel.
Supporters say stopping these defense article exports would prevent U.S. weapons from being used in current military operations in Gaza.
Supporters say this measure holds the executive branch accountable for arms sale decisions that affect civilian casualties.
critics: Critics say blocking these defense exports would weaken Israel's ability to defend against rocket attacks and terrorism.
Critics say this resolution undermines the president's authority to conduct foreign policy and maintain security partnerships.
Critics say stopping weapons sales like missile interceptors would leave Israeli civilians more vulnerable to attacks.

119-sjres-33.one_liner: Block a military equipment sale to Israel
provisions: Stops a planned sale of military weapons and equipment to Israel

supporters: Supporters say this congressional disapproval resolution would block the sale of defense articles and services to Israel's government.
Supporters say stopping this foreign military sale keeps Congress from approving weapons transfers without full review.
critics: Critics say the congressional disapproval resolution would cancel defense articles and services that Israel's government needs.
Critics say blocking this planned foreign military sale hurts security cooperation and removes military equipment from an ally.

119-sjres-37.one_liner: Cancel the national emergency that adds extra fees on imports from Canada
provisions: Ends the national emergency declared on February 1, 2025
Removes the extra 25% fee on most goods imported from Canada
Removes the extra 10% fee on Canadian energy imports

supporters: Supporters say removing the extra 25% fee on Canadian goods would lower costs for American businesses that buy supplies from Canada.
Supporters say ending the 10% extra charge on Canadian energy would reduce heating and electricity bills for consumers.
Supporters say terminating the national emergency declared on February 1, 2025 would restore normal trade relations with Canada.
critics: Critics say removing the 25% tariff would hurt American companies that compete with Canadian businesses.
Critics say ending the national emergency would remove protection for American workers in industries that face Canadian competition.
Critics say the 10% fee on Canadian energy helped support domestic energy production.

119-sjres-34.one_liner: Block a planned weapons sale to Israel
provisions: Stops the government from selling weapons and military equipment to Israel

supporters: Supporters say this resolution uses Congress's power to block the transfer of weapons and military equipment to Israel's government.
Supporters say this stops the sale of defense articles and services that were proposed for transfer to Israel.
critics: Critics say this resolution blocks the president's authority to conduct foreign policy through approved military sales to allies.
Critics say this prevents defense articles and services from reaching Israel, undermining security partnerships.

119-sjres-31.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule requiring some factories to keep following stricter pollution limits
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from September 2024
The rule required factories that handle harmful air pollutants to keep following stricter pollution limits even when they become smaller facilities
Without this rule, these factories can follow looser pollution limits when they become smaller facilities

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would allow factories that handle hazardous air pollutants to follow looser pollution limits when they reclassify as smaller area sources.
Supporters say the September 2024 EPA rule imposed continuing major source emission standards on businesses even after they reduced their operations.
critics: Critics say nullifying this rule would allow facilities handling persistent and bioaccumulative hazardous air pollutants to increase emissions by reclassifying as area sources.
Critics say removing the September 2024 rule would weaken Clean Air Act protections for communities near these facilities.

119-sjres-49.one_liner: End the national emergency that imposed 10% tariffs on most imports
provisions: Ends the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025
Removes the 10% tariff on most imports that was imposed under this emergency
Removes additional duties on specified trading partners imposed under this emergency

supporters: Supporters say removing the 10% tariff on most imports would lower prices for American families and businesses.
Supporters say ending additional duties on specified trading partners would improve trade relationships and reduce trade conflicts.
Supporters say terminating the April 2, 2025 national emergency would return trade policy to normal congressional oversight.
critics: Critics say removing the 10% tariff on most imports would hurt American manufacturers who compete with foreign goods.
Critics say ending additional duties on specified trading partners would let unfair traders take advantage of American workers.
Critics say terminating the national emergency declared on April 2, 2025 would remove tools needed to protect American trade interests.

119-sjres-54.one_liner: Block a military weapons sale to the United Arab Emirates
provisions: Stops the United States from selling military weapons to the United Arab Emirates
Blocks the UAE from buying weapons and military equipment from the US
Cancels a weapons sale that was already planned

supporters: Supporters say this resolution stops the UAE from getting US weapons that could be used in conflicts like the war in Yemen.
Supporters say blocking this planned weapons sale prevents military equipment from being misused against civilians.
critics: Critics say canceling this planned weapons sale hurts the US defense partnership with the UAE.
Critics say stopping this military sale costs American defense jobs and revenue from weapon exports.

119-sjres-55.one_liner: Cancel a safety rule for hydrogen-powered vehicles
provisions: Cancels an NHTSA rule about safety standards for hydrogen-powered vehicles
The rule covered safety requirements for fuel systems and hydrogen storage tanks
Stops the safety requirements from taking effect

supporters: Supporters say canceling the NHTSA fuel system safety standards would reduce regulatory costs for hydrogen vehicle manufacturers.
Supporters say the rule could slow down development of hydrogen-powered cars and trucks by adding extra requirements for storage tanks.
critics: Critics say removing safety standards for hydrogen fuel systems would put drivers at risk because hydrogen storage tanks operate under high pressure.
Critics say canceling the rule would eliminate federal oversight of hydrogen vehicle safety standards across all manufacturers.

119-sjres-53.one_liner: Block a weapons sale to Qatar
provisions: Stops the U.S. from selling military equipment to Qatar
Cancels a planned weapons deal with Qatar's government
Prevents Qatar from buying certain military gear from America

supporters: Supporters say stopping this weapons deal prevents Qatar's government from getting U.S. military equipment that could be transferred to other groups
Supporters say blocking Qatar from buying certain military gear keeps advanced American weapons technology from spreading in the region
Supporters say canceling this planned weapons sale shows Congress can block arms deals when needed
critics: Critics say blocking this military sale to Qatar will cost American defense companies revenue and eliminate jobs in the weapons industry
Critics say stopping Qatar from buying U.S. military equipment weakens America's influence with this Gulf ally
Critics say canceling this planned weapons deal could push Qatar to buy weapons from competitors like China or Russia

119-sjres-59.one_liner: End unauthorized U.S. military action against Iran
provisions: Orders the President to end current U.S. military action against Iran
Requires Congress to approve any military action against Iran through a war declaration or specific vote
Removes U.S. military forces from hostilities with Iran that Congress has not authorized

supporters: Supporters say this bill requires Congress to vote before any military action against Iran, giving lawmakers back their constitutional power to decide on war.
Supporters say this bill orders the President to end current military operations against Iran that Congress has not approved.
Supporters say this bill stops the President from using U.S. forces against Iran without getting permission from Congress first.
critics: Critics say this bill limits the President's ability to respond quickly to Iranian attacks on U.S. forces or allies.
Critics say this bill could weaken American security by requiring a congressional vote before military action against Iranian threats.
Critics say this bill removes U.S. forces from operations against Iran even when those operations protect American interests in the region.

119-hconres-30.one_liner: Express Congress's support for local police officers
provisions: Congress officially recognizes local police officers for their work
Congress thanks police officers and their families for their service
Congress honors police officers who died while working
Congress encourages police and communities to work together

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would officially recognize police officers for their daily work protecting communities.
Supporters say honoring officers who died while working shows respect for those who gave their lives in service.
Supporters say encouraging police and communities to work together could help build better relationships between officers and the people they serve.
critics: Critics say this resolution only offers symbolic recognition without changing how police departments operate or hold officers accountable.
Critics say Congress should focus on police reform and oversight rather than just thanking officers.
Critics say this does not address community concerns about police conduct or use of force.

119-sjres-7.one_liner: Cancel a rule letting schools buy cheap Wi-Fi hotspots for students
provisions: Cancels an FCC rule published in August 2024
Stops schools from buying cheap Wi-Fi hotspots for students to take home
Stops libraries from buying Wi-Fi hotspots for users to borrow
Prevents students from getting internet devices for homework through their school

supporters: Supporters say this stops taxpayer money from paying for Wi-Fi devices that students take home, where schools cannot monitor how they use them
Supporters say this prevents the FCC from expanding the E-Rate program beyond its original purpose of connecting schools and libraries to the internet
Supporters say this blocks government-funded hotspots from being used outside school grounds where acceptable use policies are harder to enforce
critics: Critics say this stops schools from helping students who have no internet at home complete their homework assignments
Critics say this prevents libraries from lending Wi-Fi hotspots to families who cannot afford home internet service
Critics say this keeps the homework gap open, leaving students without home internet behind their classmates

119-hjres-104.one_liner: Cancel a rule that blocks coal leasing on 1.7 million acres in Montana
provisions: Cancels a Bureau of Land Management land use rule from November 2024
The rule blocks coal leasing on 1.7 million acres in Montana

supporters: Supporters say this would restore access to coal resources on 1.7 million acres in Montana that the BLM rule blocked from leasing.
Supporters say canceling the November 2024 rule would bring back coal jobs and economic opportunities to local communities in Montana.
critics: Critics say this would open 1.7 million acres of public land in Montana to coal mining and environmental damage.
Critics say canceling the BLM rule would increase coal extraction and pollution that harms air quality and contributes to climate change.

119-hjres-105.one_liner: Cancel a Bureau of Land Management rule limiting oil, gas, and coal development in North Dakota
provisions: Cancels a Bureau of Land Management rule issued in January 2025
Removes limits on oil and gas drilling in certain North Dakota areas
Lets new coal mining happen farther from existing mines

supporters: Supporters say this would remove limits on oil and gas drilling in low-potential areas of North Dakota that were blocked by the 2025 rule.
Supporters say this would let new coal mines open more than four miles from existing mines, instead of being limited to within four miles.
Supporters say this would open up specific North Dakota lands that energy companies could not access under the 2025 restrictions.
critics: Critics say this would cancel environmental protections for North Dakota public lands that were put in place by the 2025 BLM rule.
Critics say this would remove the four-mile limit on new coal mining that was designed to protect land from being spread out over larger areas.
Critics say this overturns the 2025 land management planning process that federal experts completed after studying the environmental effects.

119-hconres-14.one_liner: Set federal spending rules and tell committees to write budget bills
provisions: Sets federal spending and tax collection targets for 2025 through 2034
Orders 11 House committees to write budget bills by March 27, 2025
Lets the tax committee add up to $4.5 trillion to federal debt
Requires other committees to cut federal debt by at least $2 trillion
Raises the limit on how much the government can borrow
Uses special rules that stop Senate delays on these budget bills

supporters: Supporters say the $4.5 trillion allowance for the tax committee would let Congress extend tax cuts for working families and businesses.
Supporters say requiring other committees to cut federal debt by at least $2 trillion shows the plan balances tax relief with spending cuts.
Supporters say the special rules that stop Senate delays would help Congress pass needed budget bills faster.
critics: Critics say allowing the tax committee to add up to $4.5 trillion to federal debt would increase borrowing too much.
Critics say the March 27, 2025 deadline gives committees too little time to write careful budget bills.
Critics say the special rules that limit Senate debate would rush important budget decisions without enough review.

119-hr-1039.one_liner: Require the VA to study and improve benefit notices sent to veterans
provisions: Requires the VA to work with a research center to study the notices they send to veterans applying for benefits
The VA must report what they find and make changes based on the study recommendations
Extends current loan fee rates for VA home loans through June 23, 2034

supporters: Supporters say the research center study of VA notices will help veterans understand their benefit claims better and reduce confusion.
Supporters say implementing the study recommendations will make the claims process clearer for veterans applying for benefits.
Supporters say extending the current loan fee rates through June 2034 gives veterans stable costs when buying homes.
critics: Critics say hiring a federally funded research center to study VA notices will cost taxpayers money without guaranteeing better outcomes.
Critics say extending loan fee rates through June 2034 means veterans will keep paying fees that could be lowered.
Critics say the bill only requires a study and report but doesn't guarantee the VA will actually improve how they communicate with veterans.

119-hjres-106.one_liner: Cancel a Bureau of Land Management rule covering 3.6 million acres in Alaska
provisions: Cancels a federal rule issued November 12, 2024 about managing land in Alaska's Central Yukon area
Removes the designation of 21 special environmental areas covering about 3.6 million acres

supporters: Supporters say this would remove federal land use restrictions from 3.6 million acres in Alaska's Central Yukon area.
Supporters say this would eliminate the 21 special environmental designations that limit mining, drilling, and other commercial activities in the region.
critics: Critics say this would remove conservation protections from 21 designated environmental areas covering 3.6 million acres.
Critics say this would cancel federal management rules that protect research natural areas and wildlife habitat in Alaska's Central Yukon planning area.

119-hr-1048.one_liner: Require colleges to report foreign money and block contracts with China and Russia
provisions: Colleges must report any gift from China or Russia no matter how small
Colleges must report gifts from other foreign countries worth $50,000 or more, down from the current $250,000 limit
Colleges cannot make contracts with China or Russia without getting government approval first
Some colleges must report when their researchers receive money from foreign sources
Private colleges with large investments must file yearly reports about their holdings
Colleges that break these rules can lose access to federal student aid money

supporters: Supporters say this would protect national security by requiring colleges to report any gift from China or Russia, no matter the amount.
Supporters say lowering the reporting threshold from $250,000 to $50,000 for other foreign countries would catch more foreign influence on American campuses.
Supporters say colleges that break these rules should lose access to federal student aid money because they failed to follow disclosure requirements.
critics: Critics say requiring colleges to report gifts as small as $1 from China or Russia creates unnecessary paperwork for administrators.
Critics say requiring government approval for contracts with China or Russia could slow down research partnerships between American and foreign universities.
Critics say taking away federal student aid hurts students who had nothing to do with their college's reporting failures.

119-hr-1156.one_liner: Extend the time limit to prosecute unemployment fraud from 5 to 10 years
provisions: Changes the time limit to prosecute unemployment fraud from 5 years to 10 years
Applies to fraud in pandemic unemployment programs created during COVID-19
Covers both criminal charges and civil lawsuits for fraud
Does not apply if the 5-year deadline already passed before this bill becomes law
Takes back unspent money from the Department of Labor that was meant for fighting fraud

supporters: Supporters say extending the prosecution timeline from 5 to 10 years gives investigators more time to catch people who stole money from pandemic unemployment programs.
Supporters say the longer timeline helps prosecutors build cases against complex fraud schemes and recover stolen taxpayer money through civil lawsuits.
critics: Critics say extending the deadline from 5 to 10 years creates 5 more years of uncertainty for people who may have made innocent mistakes with their pandemic unemployment claims.
Critics say taking back unspent Department of Labor anti-fraud money removes resources that were meant to help fight unemployment fraud.

119-hjres-78.one_liner: Cancel protection for longfin smelt fish in San Francisco Bay
provisions: Cancels a rule from July 2024 that protected longfin smelt fish as endangered
Removes legal protection for longfin smelt in the San Francisco Bay area
Means the fish no longer gets special protection from being harmed or killed

supporters: Supporters say removing the July 2024 longfin smelt protection rule would eliminate new limits on water management and development projects in the San Francisco Bay area.
Supporters say the rule creates restrictions on activities that could harm or kill longfin smelt, affecting farming and construction near Bay waters.
critics: Critics say removing legal protection for longfin smelt could lead to further decline of the fish population in San Francisco Bay waters.
Critics say nullifying the endangered species status eliminates protections that prevent the fish from being harmed or killed during development projects.

119-hr-1228.one_liner: Move the veterans' survivors assistance office to report directly to the VA Secretary
provisions: Moves the Office of Survivors Assistance to a different part of the VA
This office helps spouses and children of dead veterans get benefits
Takes the office out of the Veterans Benefits Administration
Makes it report directly to the VA Secretary instead

supporters: Supporters say moving the Office of Survivors Assistance directly under the VA Secretary will give war widows and children faster help getting benefits.
Supporters say the current setup buries survivors' needs too deep in the Veterans Benefits Administration where they get less attention from top leaders.
critics: Critics say moving the office that helps spouses and children of dead veterans could disrupt services while staff relocates and learns new rules.
Critics say the Veterans Benefits Administration already knows how to handle survivor benefit cases and moving the office wastes time and money.

119-hr-1286.one_liner: Require the VA to get help making veterans' forms clearer
provisions: The VA must work with a research center to review their forms
The research center will study forms that veterans fill out for benefits
The center will tell the VA how to make the forms clearer and easier to understand
The VA must make some of the suggested changes within two years

supporters: Supporters say this would help veterans get benefits faster because the research center will tell the VA how to make forms clearer and easier to understand.
Supporters say veterans struggle with confusing VA forms, and having experts study these forms will solve this problem.
Supporters say the two-year deadline ensures the VA will actually make the recommended changes to help veterans.
critics: Critics say this will cost money to hire a research center when the VA should fix their own forms.
Critics say the two-year requirement might rush the VA to make changes too quickly.
Critics say this takes resources away from other veteran programs while veterans already get help with forms.

119-hr-1223.one_liner: Require NSF to create a plan for upgrading internet and computer security on research ships
provisions: Makes the National Science Foundation create a plan for upgrading internet and computer security on research ships used by scientists and students
The plan must include cost estimates for the upgrades
The plan must include how long the upgrades will take
NSF must give the plan to Congress within 18 months
NSF must later report to Congress on how the plan is working

supporters: Supporters say this would help scientists and students on research ships get better internet to upload their data and connect to computers on land.
Supporters say the plan with cost estimates and timelines will help Congress decide how to fund these upgrades.
Supporters say better computer security on research ships will protect scientific data from hackers.
critics: Critics say the government should not spend money on upgrading internet for research ships when other priorities need funding.
Critics say the 18-month deadline to create the plan may rush the planning process.
Critics say requiring reports to Congress creates more paperwork for the National Science Foundation.

119-hr-1326.one_liner: Require Energy and Agriculture departments to work together on research projects
provisions: Requires the Energy and Agriculture departments to create an agreement to work together on research
Lets the agencies pay each other back for research work
Allows them to work with other federal agencies on research projects
Requires competitive review for research applications from agencies, labs, colleges, and nonprofits
Research includes artificial intelligence, plant-based fuels, power grids, rural technology, and wildfire prevention
Funds systems to handle large amounts of data on farming, environment, supply chains, and economics
Supports research buildings and worker training
Funds research on making farms more efficient and reducing greenhouse gas pollution

supporters: Supporters say this would help the Energy and Agriculture departments work together on research like artificial intelligence and plant-based fuels instead of doing the same work twice.
Supporters say the competitive review process would make sure colleges, labs, and nonprofits compete for the best research projects.
Supporters say combining data systems for farming and environmental information would help researchers find solutions faster.
critics: Critics say adding another agreement between government agencies would create more paperwork and slow down research on wildfire prevention and rural technology.
Critics say the bill does not include specific dollar amounts, so taxpayers do not know how much this research coordination would cost.
Critics say the Energy and Agriculture departments already do their own research, and forcing them to work together might make them less focused on their main jobs.

119-hr-1263.one_liner: Tell the State Department to work with Japan, Australia, and India on security and economic issues
provisions: Tells the State Department to set up a group with Japan, Australia, and India called the Quad
The Quad focuses on security cooperation and economic issues between the four countries
Requires a report to Congress about past work on economic growth, technology, energy, and trade
Asks Congress for ideas on tools and money needed to strengthen U.S. leadership in this group

supporters: Supporters say the working group with Japan, Australia, and India will help coordinate technology cooperation and strengthen supply chains between the four countries.
Supporters say the required report to Congress will help identify what resources and tools are needed to expand successful Quad initiatives.
Supporters say this bill will boost U.S. leadership in economic growth and energy innovation through closer work with these three allies.
critics: Critics say the bill asks Congress for additional resources and new authorities without saying how much money this will cost taxpayers.
Critics say creating another working group adds more bureaucracy to the State Department's existing operations.
Critics say the reporting requirements will take staff time away from other diplomatic work.

119-hr-1503.one_liner: Block money and ban entry for people who force others to give up organs
provisions: The President must make a list of people who force others to give up their organs
The President must freeze the money and property of people on this list
The President must ban people on this list from entering the United States
The State Department can take away passports from Americans convicted of selling organs if they used their passport or crossed borders during the crime

supporters: Supporters say this would stop people who force others to give up their organs by freezing their money and property.
Supporters say this would protect Americans by banning organ traffickers from entering the United States.
Supporters say taking away passports from convicted American organ sellers would stop them from committing crimes in other countries.
critics: Critics say the President could put people on the sanctions list without enough evidence or a fair trial.
Critics say freezing someone's money and property without a court order violates due process rights.
Critics say taking away an American's passport could leave them unable to return home or travel for emergencies.

119-hr-1442.one_liner: Ban consumer products with 10% or more sodium nitrite
provisions: Makes it illegal to sell consumer products that contain 10% or more sodium nitrite
Sodium nitrite is a chemical that can cause poisoning if consumed
Does not ban medicines, medical devices, makeup, or food products that contain sodium nitrite

supporters: Supporters say this bill would prevent young people from getting poisoned by blocking the sale of consumer products that contain 10% or more sodium nitrite.
Supporters say the exceptions for medicines, medical devices, makeup, and food products mean people can still get sodium nitrite when they need it for safe uses.
critics: Critics say the 10% limit could ban consumer products that people use safely for cleaning or other household tasks.
Critics say businesses that sell these products would lose customers and money if they can no longer sell items with sodium nitrite above 10%.

119-hr-1491.one_liner: Count disaster-related tax deadline delays as extensions for tax refunds
provisions: Treats tax deadline delays from disasters as extensions when calculating refund amounts
Lets people claim refunds on more past tax payments when disasters postpone deadlines
Gives the IRS more time to send payment notices during disaster deadline delays

supporters: Supporters say this would help disaster victims claim refunds on more past tax payments when disasters postpone tax deadlines by treating postponements as extensions for the three-year lookback period.
Supporters say this prevents disaster victims from losing access to their own tax money simply because disasters disrupted normal filing schedules.
critics: Critics say this could cost the federal government money by allowing larger tax refunds for people in disaster areas compared to other taxpayers.
Critics say this creates different tax refund rules for people based on whether they live in disaster-declared areas.

119-hr-144.one_liner: Require the Tennessee Valley Authority to report employee salaries and file annual financial statements
provisions: Brings back the requirement for TVA to file annual financial reports with Congress each March
Changes salary reporting from all employees making over $1,500 per year to only those making more than the top federal GS-13 pay rate
Requires TVA to report names, salaries, and job duties for employees above the salary threshold

supporters: Supporters say bringing back annual financial reports to Congress each March will give lawmakers needed oversight of the government-owned TVA.
Supporters say raising the salary reporting threshold from $1,500 to the federal GS-13 maximum rate makes sense because it focuses on higher-paid employees instead of low-wage workers.
Supporters say taxpayers deserve to know the names and salaries of TVA's top executives since it's a government corporation.
critics: Critics say raising the salary threshold from $1,500 per year to the GS-13 maximum rate will hide thousands of TVA employee salaries from public view.
Critics say the annual reporting requirements will cost TVA money and staff time that could be used for providing electricity.
Critics say fewer TVA workers' pay information will be public under the higher salary reporting threshold.

119-hr-1402.one_liner: Require ticket sellers to show total prices and fees upfront
provisions: The Transparency In Charges for Key Events Ticketing Act requires ticket sellers to show the total price when tickets first appear on screen
Sellers must list the base price and each fee before you complete your purchase
Companies cannot sell tickets they do not actually have
Buyers get full refunds if events are canceled or postponed
The Federal Trade Commission can enforce these rules

supporters: Supporters say requiring ticket sellers to show the total price upfront stops hidden fees that surprise buyers at checkout.
Supporters say blocking companies from selling tickets they do not actually have prevents fans from buying fake tickets.
Supporters say guaranteeing full refunds when events are canceled or postponed protects consumers from losing money.
critics: Critics say forcing ticket companies to list all fees upfront will increase their technology costs and hurt smaller businesses.
Critics say stopping secondary sellers from advertising tickets they plan to get later will reduce the number of available tickets for fans.
Critics say giving the Federal Trade Commission power to enforce these rules adds more government control over private businesses.

119-hr-164.one_liner: Let power companies use emergency money to prevent future damage while fixing power
provisions: Lets power companies use emergency repair money to also do damage prevention work while fixing power after disasters
Allows power companies to get both emergency repair money and separate FEMA disaster prevention money for the same facility

supporters: Supporters say this saves money by letting power companies do hazard mitigation work while already doing power restoration after disasters, instead of separate trips.
Supporters say this helps communities by making power systems stronger against future disasters through combined repair and prevention work.
critics: Critics say this lets electric utilities receive both emergency restoration money and FEMA hazard mitigation money for the same facility, which could increase federal spending.
Critics say this gives power companies more ways to access federal disaster funds without clear limits on total payments.

119-hr-1534.one_liner: Create a program to develop cleaner cement, concrete, and asphalt
provisions: Creates a 7-year program at the Energy Department
Funds research for cleaner ways to make cement, concrete, and asphalt
Picks companies and groups to run test projects
Focuses on ways to capture carbon and use less energy when making these materials
The Energy Department can stop projects if clean materials become available at good prices

supporters: Supporters say this 7-year Energy Department program would cut pollution from cement and concrete plants that create 8% of world carbon emissions.
Supporters say focusing on carbon capture and energy-efficient processes would create American jobs in clean building materials.
Supporters say picking companies and research groups to run test projects would speed up development of cleaner cement and asphalt.
critics: Critics say adding another program to the Energy Department wastes money when existing research funds could support clean cement development.
Critics say the government should not pick which companies get funding to develop cleaner concrete and asphalt production.
Critics say the rule letting the Energy Department stop projects if clean materials become available shows even supporters doubt this program will work.

119-hr-152.one_liner: Require FEMA to streamline disaster aid applications and damage assessments
provisions: FEMA must study how to make disaster aid applications take less time
FEMA must create a plan to track how much disaster money gets handed out
FEMA must form a working group to find duplicate damage reviews after disasters
FEMA must explore using drones for faster damage checks
FEMA must report its plans to Congress and post them online

supporters: Supporters say this would reduce paperwork for disaster victims who now fill out forms multiple times for the same aid.
Supporters say the working group would find duplicate damage reviews that waste time after disasters.
Supporters say using drones for damage checks would get help to victims faster than current ground teams.
critics: Critics say the studies and working groups would cost money that should go directly to disaster victims instead.
Critics say FEMA should help disaster victims now rather than spend two years studying better ways to help.
Critics say using drones to check property damage could invade privacy of homeowners.

119-hr-1526.one_liner: Stop courts from issuing orders that affect people beyond those in the case
provisions: Stops federal courts from issuing court orders that affect people beyond those directly in the case
Requires court orders to only apply to the specific people or groups being sued
Changes current rules that let a single federal court make decisions affecting the whole country

supporters: Supporters say this bill would require federal district courts to limit their injunctions to only the parties directly involved in each case.
Supporters say this bill would end the current practice where one federal court can issue orders affecting people and groups across the entire country.
Supporters say this bill would stop plaintiffs from choosing specific court districts to get nationwide injunctions from single judges.
critics: Critics say this bill would prevent federal courts from issuing injunctions that protect people nationwide from the same government policy.
Critics say this bill would force advocacy groups to file the same lawsuit in dozens of different federal districts to get protection.
Critics say this bill would make it slower to stop government actions that affect people across multiple states through the courts.

119-hr-153.one_liner: Require federal agencies to publish quarterly reports on disaster assistance spending
provisions: Creates a central website where anyone can see how much disaster money federal agencies spend
Requires agencies to publish reports every three months showing their total disaster assistance given out
Requires agencies to list every project or activity that got disaster assistance money
Makes the Small Business Administration and Housing Department follow these new reporting rules

supporters: Supporters say the central website would let disaster victims and taxpayers see exactly where federal disaster money goes and which projects get funded.

Supporters say requiring agencies like the Small Business Administration and Housing Department to report every three months would stop waste and make sure disaster assistance reaches people who need it.
Supporters say listing every project that gets disaster assistance money would help communities track whether their area got fair treatment after disasters.
critics: Critics say forcing agencies to create quarterly reports on every disaster project would pull staff away from actually helping disaster victims get assistance.
Critics say the new reporting requirements would cost the Small Business Administration and Housing Department money that should go directly to disaster relief instead.
Critics say agencies already report disaster spending to Congress and adding another website with quarterly updates creates unnecessary paperwork.

119-hr-1717.one_liner: Create legal authority for a council that advises the FCC on network security
provisions: Gives official authority to a council that advises the FCC on phone and internet security
Requires the council to include people from communications companies, public groups, and government at all levels
Blocks people who work for foreign enemies or pose security threats from joining the council
Makes the council permanent instead of renewing it every 2 years like other advisory groups

supporters: Supporters say this gives legal authority to a council that already advises the FCC on keeping phone and internet networks safe from hackers and foreign attacks
Supporters say the requirement to include people from communications companies, public groups, and all levels of government ensures everyone affected gets a voice in security decisions
Supporters say blocking people who work for foreign enemies from joining the council protects America's communications networks from inside threats
critics: Critics say making this council permanent removes the 2-year review process that keeps other advisory groups accountable to the public
Critics say the membership rules could block experts who don't fit into the required categories of companies, public groups, or government workers
Critics say the ban on foreign adversary representatives could be used too broadly to silence legitimate voices in security discussions

119-hr-1709.one_liner: Require a government study of mobile phone network security
provisions: Requires a government agency to study mobile phone network security
The study must look at how foreign countries can hack phones and spy on calls
The government must report on how well phone companies protect against attacks
The report must show whether companies follow security best practices
The study must measure how much phone companies use encryption

supporters: Supporters say this study will identify security gaps that foreign countries use to hack American phones and spy on calls
Supporters say the report on how much encryption phone companies use will show where networks are most vulnerable to attacks
Supporters say checking whether companies follow security best practices will reveal if stronger rules are needed to protect customers
critics: Critics say the study will cost taxpayer money without requiring phone companies to actually fix any security problems the report finds
Critics say the report on encryption and security practices could give hackers a roadmap of network vulnerabilities
Critics say this creates more government oversight of private phone companies without proof that current security is inadequate

119-hr-1642.one_liner: Require business centers to help small businesses hire trade school graduates
provisions: Makes business help centers teach small businesses about hiring trade school graduates
Connects small businesses with trade schools
Helps trade school students and graduates find jobs

supporters: Supporters say this would help small businesses learn how to hire skilled trade school graduates through their local Small Business Development Centers and Women's Business Centers.
Supporters say connecting small businesses with career and technical education programs would give trade school students more job opportunities at local companies.
critics: Critics say requiring Small Business Development Centers and Women's Business Centers to provide educational information about hiring trade graduates adds new work without extra money.
Critics say making these business centers connect companies with trade schools takes staff time away from helping small businesses with loans and business advice.

119-hr-1770.one_liner: Create an AI pilot program for consumer safety and require technology reports
provisions: Creates a pilot program for the Consumer Product Safety Commission to use artificial intelligence
The AI would track injury trends, find product dangers, watch for recalled product sales, or spot unsafe imports
Requires the Commerce Department to write a report on how blockchain technology protects consumers
Requires the Federal Trade Commission to report on stopping scams involving digital tokens

supporters: Supporters say the AI pilot program would help the Consumer Product Safety Commission find dangerous products faster by tracking injury trends and spotting product hazards.
Supporters say the artificial intelligence system would catch recalled products still being sold to consumers.
Supporters say the required reports on blockchain technology and digital tokens would help agencies fight scams and protect people from fraud.
critics: Critics say the AI pilot program would waste taxpayer money on unproven technology that could miss real product dangers.
Critics say artificial intelligence systems make mistakes and could fail to identify serious consumer product hazards.
Critics say requiring more reports on blockchain and digital tokens won't actually stop scams or protect consumers from fraud.

119-hr-165.one_liner: Give 40 acres in South Dakota to two Sioux tribes for a Wounded Knee memorial
provisions: Transfers ownership of 40 acres in South Dakota to the Oglala Sioux Tribe and Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe
Makes the land a memorial and sacred site for the Wounded Knee Massacre
Prevents the tribes from selling the land or using it as loan collateral
Bans businesses and casinos from being built on the land

supporters: Supporters say this would create a permanent memorial for the 300 Lakota people killed at Wounded Knee in 1890 on the exact location where it happened.
Supporters say this returns 40 acres of historically significant land to the Oglala Sioux Tribe and Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe who have ancestral ties to the site.
Supporters say the ban on businesses and casinos protects the sacred nature of the massacre site from commercial development.
critics: Critics say removing 40 acres from local tax rolls reduces property tax revenue for Oglala Lakota County schools and services.
Critics say the restrictions preventing the tribes from selling the land or using it as collateral limit their economic options for the property.
Critics say the federal transfer process costs taxpayer money to complete the legal actions needed to change the land status.

119-hr-186.one_liner: Require a Medal of Honor monument be located on the National Mall
provisions: Requires an authorized monument honoring Medal of Honor recipients be placed within the Reserve area of the National Mall

supporters: Supporters say Medal of Honor recipients should have their monument in the Reserve area because it is the main part of the National Mall that extends from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial and from the White House to the Jefferson Memorial.
Supporters say the nation's highest military award recipients deserve a monument in the same area as other major national memorials.
critics: Critics say placing the Medal of Honor monument in the Reserve area will take up space in the limited area between the Capitol, Lincoln Memorial, White House, and Jefferson Memorial.
Critics say the monument could honor Medal of Honor recipients in another location on the National Mall outside the Reserve area.

119-hr-1804.one_liner: Require the SBA to report yearly on loan agents helping small businesses
provisions: The Small Business Administration must write a yearly report about loan agents
The report shows how many agents help small businesses get SBA loans
The report shows how many bad loans involved these agents
The report shows how much money in fees these agents received
These agents help businesses apply for SBA loans for a fee

supporters: Supporters say this yearly report will help catch fraud by tracking how many bad loans involved agents who charge fees to help businesses.
Supporters say the report will show how much money in referral fees these agents receive, giving small businesses better information about costs.
Supporters say tracking the purchase rate of loans will help the SBA see if agents are actually helping businesses get approved.
critics: Critics say requiring the SBA to compile and submit annual reports on all loan agents will create extra paperwork and use up agency resources.
