Critics say tracking agents who help small businesses could discourage legitimate professionals from offering these services.
Critics say the new reporting requirements will cost the SBA money to gather data on agent numbers, fees, and loan outcomes.

119-hr-1917.one_liner: Give formal authority to a fish tagging program in the Great Lakes
provisions: Gives formal authority to a fish tagging program that started in 2010
Lets the Fish and Wildlife Service buy equipment to tag more farm-raised fish
Lets the agency hire more workers for the tagging program
The tags help tell the difference between farm-raised fish and wild fish
The data helps state and tribal agencies decide how to manage fishing

supporters: Supporters say this would give formal authority to a fish tagging program that has helped state and tribal agencies make better fishing decisions since 2010.
Supporters say the tags help protect wild fish by letting managers tell the difference between farm-raised and wild fish in the Great Lakes.
Supporters say the data supports tribal, recreational, and commercial fisheries by helping balance predators and prey.
critics: Critics say this expands federal spending by letting the Fish and Wildlife Service buy more equipment and hire additional personnel for a program that has run since 2010 without formal authority.
Critics say this increases federal oversight of fishing management that state and tribal agencies already handle.

119-hr-187.one_liner: Require federal agencies to publish data about waterway access and fishing rules
provisions: The Forest Service and Interior Department must create standards for sharing waterway access data
Both agencies must put waterway maps and fishing rules online within 5 years
Waterway access information gets updated twice per year
Fishing restriction data gets updated in real time when rules change
People can submit questions and comments about the waterway data

supporters: Supporters say this would help recreational users plan trips by putting waterway access maps and fishing rules online within 5 years.
Supporters say fishers would stay informed about changing rules because fishing restriction data gets updated in real time.
Supporters say the public comment process would let people ask questions about waterway access data.
critics: Critics say the 5-year timeline to digitize waterway maps is too slow for people who need access information now.
Critics say requiring both the Forest Service and Interior Department to create new data standards could waste money on duplicate systems.
Critics say updating waterway access information only twice per year may leave boaters with outdated navigation data.

119-hr-1919.one_liner: Block the Federal Reserve from creating a digital dollar
provisions: Stops the Federal Reserve from creating or testing a digital version of the dollar
Prevents the Federal Reserve from opening accounts for regular people
Blocks the Federal Reserve from offering banking services directly to individuals
Stops the Federal Reserve from using digital dollars to control the economy

supporters: Supporters say stopping the Federal Reserve from creating a digital dollar would prevent the government from tracking every purchase Americans make.
Supporters say preventing the Federal Reserve from opening accounts for regular people protects private banks from unfair competition.
Supporters say blocking the Federal Reserve from using digital dollars to control the economy stops new forms of government control over spending.
critics: Critics say preventing the Federal Reserve from testing digital dollars could put America behind other countries building digital money systems.
Critics say stopping the Federal Reserve from offering direct banking services removes tools that could help Americans without bank accounts.
Critics say blocking the Federal Reserve from using digital currency for monetary policy takes away options to fight economic problems.

119-hr-2096.one_liner: Cancel stricter police discipline rules in Washington DC
provisions: Brings back a 90-day time limit for starting discipline cases against DC police officers
Lets police unions negotiate discipline rules in their contracts
Stops the police chief from increasing punishments recommended by police trial boards
Cancels the rule requiring police to publish online schedules of firing hearings

supporters: Supporters say the 90-day time limit ensures police discipline cases move quickly instead of dragging on for months or years.
Supporters say allowing police unions to negotiate discipline rules in contracts gives officers the same rights as other workers.
Supporters say stopping the police chief from increasing punishments recommended by trial boards prevents unfair penalties.
critics: Critics say the 90-day time limit makes it nearly impossible to investigate complex police misconduct cases that take months to review.
Critics say letting police unions negotiate discipline rules in contracts will weaken accountability for officer misconduct.
Critics say eliminating the requirement to publish online schedules of firing hearings hides police discipline from the public.

119-hr-2056.one_liner: Require Washington DC to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement
provisions: Stops DC from refusing to share people's immigration status with federal agencies
Requires DC jails to hold people up to 48 extra hours when immigration agents request it
Lets DC protect crime victims and witnesses from these sharing requirements

supporters: Supporters say this ensures DC follows federal immigration law by requiring local jails to hold people for up to 48 hours when immigration agents request it.
Supporters say the bill prevents DC from blocking federal agencies from getting immigration status information they need to enforce the law.
Supporters say this makes sure local governments cannot ignore federal detainer requests from the Department of Homeland Security.
critics: Critics say the 48-hour detention requirement could keep people in jail longer even when they should be released.
Critics say forcing DC to share immigration information could make crime victims afraid to report crimes to police.
Critics say this turns local police and jails into immigration enforcement agents instead of focusing on local public safety.

119-hr-1998.one_liner: Ban foreign pirates from U.S. visas and freeze their money
provisions: Requires the President to ban foreign pirates from getting U.S. visas
Lets the government freeze the money and property of foreign pirates
Creates fines and jail time for people who break these rules

supporters: Supporters say this gives the U.S. tools to freeze the money and property of foreign pirates who attack ships.
Supporters say this creates visa bans that stop foreign pirates from entering the U.S.
Supporters say this adds fines and jail time for people who help pirates avoid these sanctions.
critics: Critics say this gives the President broad authority to decide who counts as a pirate without clear standards.
Critics say this lets the government freeze property before proving someone committed piracy in court.
Critics say this could hurt innocent people if the President wrongly labels someone as a pirate.

119-hr-192.one_liner: Require Amtrak to reveal executive pay and bonuses to the public
provisions: Amtrak must reveal how much it pays its top executives each year
This includes both base salary and any bonus money
Amtrak must explain how it decides who gets bonuses and how much
This information goes in their yearly report to Congress
Amtrak must put this report on their website for everyone to see

supporters: Supporters say this would let taxpayers see how much Amtrak pays its top executives since Amtrak gets public funding.
Supporters say putting executive pay and bonus information on Amtrak's website would help the public track how their tax dollars are spent.
Supporters say requiring Amtrak to explain how it decides on bonuses would help Congress oversee the company's spending choices.
critics: Critics say making executive salaries and bonuses public could make it harder for Amtrak to hire qualified leaders who want privacy.
Critics say requiring Amtrak to post detailed pay information on their website creates extra paperwork and administrative costs.
Critics say the current annual report to Congress already provides enough oversight without needing public website disclosure.

119-hr-2035.one_liner: Require all Transportation Department cargo shipped by sea to use U.S.-flagged ships
provisions: Changes the rule from 50% to 100% of Transportation Department cargo that ships by sea must use U.S.-flagged ships
Applies when the Transportation Department buys equipment or materials that ship by sea
Applies when the Transportation Department gives money to others who ship cargo by sea
Only applies when U.S.-flagged ships are available at fair prices

supporters: Supporters say doubling the requirement from 50% to 100% would create more jobs for American ship crews and port workers.
Supporters say requiring all Transportation Department cargo to use U.S.-flagged ships keeps taxpayer money supporting American maritime companies.
Supporters say this strengthens America's shipping industry by guaranteeing more business for domestic vessels.
critics: Critics say requiring 100% instead of 50% could increase shipping costs for Transportation Department projects and infrastructure.
Critics say the stricter rule could delay projects if U.S.-flagged ships aren't available when cargo needs to be moved.
Critics say higher shipping costs could reduce funding available for roads, bridges, and other transportation projects.

119-hr-2215.one_liner: Change Salem Maritime National Historic Site to a national historical park
provisions: Changes Salem Maritime National Historic Site in Massachusetts to Salem Maritime National Historical Park
Orders a government study on expanding the park to include more land and buildings
The study will look at adding nearby places connected to ships, coastal defenses, and military history

supporters: Supporters say the redesignation would give Salem Maritime park status instead of site status, which could help with funding and protection.
Supporters say the boundary study would identify important maritime and military history locations that should be preserved as part of the park.
critics: Critics say the government boundary study will cost taxpayer money to evaluate adding more land to the park.
Critics say expanding the park boundaries could limit private property rights and local development near the historic sites.

119-hr-2240.one_liner: Require Justice Department reports on attacks against police and mental health resources
provisions: Requires the Justice Department to report on attacks against police officers
Requires a report on whether these attacks can be tracked in existing crime systems
Requires a report on mental health resources available to police officers

supporters: Supporters say the Justice Department reports would help identify patterns in attacks against police officers to better protect them.
Supporters say tracking mental health resources available to officers would show where more support is needed.
Supporters say adding attacks on police to existing crime systems would give better data on officer safety.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires reports but does not provide funding for new mental health programs for officers.
Critics say the Justice Department already tracks crime data and adding more reporting requirements wastes time.
Critics say creating reports without requiring action to fix problems identified will not actually help police officers.

119-hr-2243.one_liner: Let qualified law enforcement officers carry guns in more places
provisions: Lets qualified active law enforcement officers carry hidden guns in school zones
Lets qualified retired law enforcement officers carry hidden guns in school zones
Lets these officers carry guns in national parks
Lets these officers carry guns on state, local, or private property open to the public
Lets these officers carry guns in some federal buildings open to the public
Lets states reduce how often retired officers must meet shooting tests

supporters: Supporters say this lets trained officers stop school shooters faster because active and retired law enforcement can carry guns in school zones.
Supporters say retired and active officers get better protection when they visit national parks and public places since they can carry concealed weapons.
Supporters say letting states reduce how often retired officers take shooting tests saves money while still allowing trained people to protect themselves.
critics: Critics say allowing guns in school zones puts children at risk from accidents or mistakes by officers who are not school security.
Critics say reducing shooting test requirements for retired officers means less-trained people will carry guns in public places and federal buildings.
Critics say this creates more armed people in national parks and public spaces where gun accidents could hurt visitors.

119-hr-21.one_liner: Require medical care for babies born alive after abortion attempts
provisions: Requires doctors to give the same medical care to babies born alive after abortion attempts as other newborns
Requires babies born alive after abortion attempts be taken to a hospital right away
Requires medical workers to call police if these care rules are not followed
Makes it a crime with up to 5 years in prison for doctors who don't follow these care rules
Makes killing a baby born alive after an abortion attempt a murder charge
Protects mothers from being charged with crimes under this law
Lets mothers sue doctors or staff who break these rules

supporters: Supporters say this would protect babies born alive after abortion attempts by requiring doctors to give them the same medical care as other newborns.
Supporters say the requirement to immediately take these babies to hospitals ensures they get proper medical attention.
Supporters say the criminal penalties of up to 5 years in prison will make sure doctors follow the law and don't abandon babies who survive abortion attempts.
critics: Critics say requiring doctors to provide full medical care and immediate hospital transfer for babies with little chance of survival could delay emergency care for women having complications.
Critics say the criminal penalties of up to 5 years in prison could make doctors afraid to perform legal abortions.
Critics say forcing medical workers to call police violates the private relationship between doctors and patients.

119-hr-22.one_liner: Require documents proving US citizenship to register to vote in federal elections
provisions: Requires people to show documents proving they are US citizens when registering to vote in federal elections
States must create programs to find and remove non-citizens from voter lists
Creates criminal penalties for election officials who register people without citizenship proof
Allows people to sue election officials who register voters without proper citizenship documents

supporters: Supporters say requiring documentary proof of US citizenship when registering to vote will prevent non-citizens from illegally voting in federal elections.
Supporters say the criminal penalties for election officials who register people without citizenship proof will ensure the law is followed.
Supporters say allowing citizens to sue election officials who register voters without proper documents gives people a way to enforce these citizenship requirements.
critics: Critics say requiring citizenship documents will prevent eligible US citizens who lack these papers from registering to vote in federal elections.
Critics say the criminal penalties could make election officials afraid to help people register to vote.
Critics say the programs to find and remove non-citizens from voter lists could mistakenly remove eligible US citizens from voting rolls.

119-hr-26.one_liner: Stop the President from banning fracking without Congress approval
provisions: Stops the President from banning fracking unless Congress votes to allow it
Says states should control fracking rules on state and private land
Defines fracking as injecting water, sand, and chemicals into wells to get oil and gas

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects American energy jobs by stopping the President from banning fracking without Congress voting to allow it.
Supporters say states should control fracking rules on their own land because they understand local conditions better than Washington.
critics: Critics say removing the President's power to ban fracking could prevent quick action during environmental emergencies.
Critics say letting states control all fracking rules on private land could lead to weaker safety standards for workers and communities.

119-hr-2483.one_liner: Fund drug addiction and mental health programs through 2030
provisions: Continues funding for programs that help pregnant women with drug addiction through 2030
Keeps funding programs that prevent drug use and help young people recover
Continues paying for housing for people recovering from drug addiction
Keeps loan forgiveness programs for doctors and nurses who treat addiction
Continues funding programs that prevent drug overdose deaths
Expands money for first responders to buy drugs that treat overdoses from substances other than opioids
Creates a federal team to study fentanyl mixed into illegal drugs

supporters: Supporters say continuing funding through 2030 for programs helping pregnant women with drug addiction and youth recovery will save lives and keep families together.
Supporters say keeping loan forgiveness for doctors and nurses who treat addiction will help recruit more healthcare workers to fight the drug crisis.
Supporters say expanding money for first responders to buy drugs that treat overdoses from substances other than opioids will help save more lives as new dangerous drugs spread.
critics: Critics say continuing funding for all these programs through 2030 will cost taxpayers billions of dollars without clear proof the programs work.
Critics say requiring cybersecurity protections for the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline creates new costly federal rules that states and local groups must follow.
Critics say creating a new Federal Interagency Work Group on Fentanyl adds another layer of federal bureaucracy instead of giving money directly to local treatment programs.

119-hr-27.one_liner: Make all substances similar to fentanyl permanently illegal with same penalties as fentanyl
provisions: Makes all substances similar to fentanyl permanently illegal
Sets minimum 10-year prison sentence for having 100 grams or more of these substances
Uses the same penalties as current fentanyl laws
Creates easier permit process for researchers studying these drugs

supporters: Supporters say this bill closes dangerous loopholes by making all fentanyl-like substances permanently illegal instead of waiting for each new drug to be banned separately.
Supporters say the 10-year minimum prison sentence for having 100 grams or more will stop drug dealers from selling these deadly substances.
Supporters say the new research registration process will help scientists study these drugs safely while keeping them away from criminals.
critics: Critics say the 10-year mandatory minimum prison sentence for 100 grams is too harsh and will fill prisons with non-violent drug users.
Critics say automatically making all similar substances illegal could accidentally ban legitimate medicines or research chemicals that help sick people.
Critics say the broad classification of fentanyl-related substances could hurt medical research and slow down development of new pain medicines.

119-hr-2255.one_liner: Let federal law enforcement officers buy their retired work guns
provisions: Requires the General Services Administration to create a gun purchase program
Lets federal law enforcement officers buy their work guns when the guns get retired
Officers can only buy guns their agency gave them

supporters: Supporters say this program lets federal officers keep service weapons they trained with for years after the guns are retired.
Supporters say the bill only allows officers to buy guns their own agency issued to them, not any weapon.
Supporters say this gives retired federal law enforcement weapons a practical use instead of disposal.
critics: Critics say the General Services Administration program will cost taxpayer money to set up and manage.
Critics say allowing federal officers to buy retired weapons puts more guns into private ownership.
Critics say the bill does not set limits on how many retired weapons each officer can purchase from their agency.

119-hr-249.one_liner: Rename park facilities at Paterson Great Falls National Historical Park for Congressman Bill Pascrell Jr
provisions: Renames the Great Falls Scenic Overlook Trail Bridge to the Bill Pascrell Jr Scenic Overlook Trail Bridge
Renames Overlook Park to Bill Pascrell Jr Overlook Park
Both facilities are at Paterson Great Falls National Historical Park in New Jersey

supporters: Supporters say renaming the Great Falls Scenic Overlook Trail Bridge and Overlook Park would honor Congressman Pascrell's decades of service representing Paterson in Congress.
Supporters say Congressman Pascrell has represented the Paterson district in Congress since 1997, making it fitting to name these local facilities after him.
Supporters say the congressman has worked to secure federal funding for Paterson projects, so naming these park facilities recognizes his efforts for the community.
critics: Critics say taxpayers will have to pay for new signs, maps, and brochures showing the new names for both the trail bridge and park.
Critics say the original names Great Falls Scenic Overlook Trail Bridge and Overlook Park should be kept to preserve the historic character of the national park.
Critics say the money spent on renaming these facilities could be used instead for park maintenance or visitor services.

119-hr-276.one_liner: Rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America
provisions: Changes the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America
Requires federal agencies to update their documents and maps with the new name

supporters: Supporters say renaming the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America will better represent American territory in the region.
Supporters say the new name will honor America as the largest country that borders the gulf.
critics: Critics say requiring federal agencies to update all their documents and maps will cost taxpayers money for reprinting and administrative work.
Critics say changing the name from Gulf of Mexico could create confusion since Mexico also borders the gulf and the current name is used worldwide.

119-hr-275.one_liner: Require monthly reports on non-citizens trying to enter illegally who may pose security risks
provisions: Requires Homeland Security to write a report every month
The report covers non-citizens who try to enter the country illegally and might be security risks
The report must say how many people were caught
The report must list what countries these people are from
The report must say where they were found

supporters: Supporters say this bill would give Congress monthly numbers on people who might threaten security and try to cross the border illegally.
Supporters say the reports showing what countries people come from help spot patterns in where threats start.
Supporters say monthly reports ensure the public gets regular updates on border security encounters.
critics: Critics say reporting people's countries in monthly public reports could cause unfair treatment of certain nationalities.
Critics say the bill does not explain what makes someone a security risk, letting Homeland Security decide without clear rules.
Critics say monthly reporting will cost tax money for government workers to write these reports.

119-hr-2931.one_liner: Force Small Business Administration offices out of cities that don't help immigration officials
provisions: Forces Small Business Administration offices to move out of cities that don't help immigration officials
Gives offices 60 days to move after the SBA decides a city limits immigration help
Stops the SBA from opening new offices in cities that don't share citizenship information
Affects cities and states that ignore federal requests about immigrants

supporters: Supporters say this forces cities to follow federal immigration law by making SBA offices move out of places that won't help immigration officials.
Supporters say this stops federal tax dollars from paying for offices in cities that ignore requests from the Department of Homeland Security about immigrants.
Supporters say the 60-day deadline ensures cities can't delay choosing between their local policies and keeping federal business services.
critics: Critics say small businesses will lose access to SBA loans and services when offices move within 60 days of being in sanctuary cities.
Critics say this punishes local business owners for their city government's decision not to share citizenship information with federal officials.
Critics say major cities with thousands of small businesses could lose SBA offices if they restrict sharing immigration status with other government agencies.

119-hr-29.one_liner: Require holding non-citizens arrested for theft or break-ins
provisions: Requires holding non-citizens who are in the country illegally and have been arrested for theft, break-ins, or shoplifting
Lets states sue the federal government when immigration decisions cost the state more than $100
Allows states to sue when the government releases someone from custody
Allows states to sue when the government fails to properly interview people asking for asylum
Allows states to sue when the government keeps giving visas to countries that won't take back their own citizens
Allows states to sue when the government fails to hold someone who was ordered to leave the country

supporters: Supporters say this bill will keep communities safer by holding people who are in the country illegally and have been arrested for crimes like theft, break-ins, and shoplifting.
Supporters say the law gives states power to sue the federal government when immigration decisions cost them more than $100, making the federal government more accountable.
Supporters say this targets people who commit property crimes and are already breaking immigration law by being in the country without permission.
critics: Critics say the bill requires holding people who have only been arrested for minor crimes like shoplifting, not people who have been found guilty in court.
Critics say the $100 threshold for state lawsuits is so low it will flood courts with cases over small costs to states.
Critics say this expands detention to include people charged with non-violent property crimes, keeping more people locked up without trial.

119-hr-28.one_liner: Ban students born male from competing in women's sports at federally funded schools
provisions: Makes it against federal civil rights law for schools that get federal money to let students born male compete in women's sports
Applies to schools from elementary through college that receive federal funding
Lets students born male practice with women's teams but not compete in games
Orders a government study on how male participation affects female athletes

supporters: Supporters say this protects competition opportunities for female athletes in schools that receive federal funding from elementary through college.
Supporters say the bill allows students born male to practice with women's teams while preserving female-only competition slots.
Supporters say the required government study will document how male participation affects girls in sports programs.
critics: Critics say this excludes transgender female students from competing in women's sports at federally funded schools.
Critics say schools could lose federal funding if they allow students born male to compete in women's programs.
Critics say the bill creates different treatment based on biology at birth rather than gender identity.

119-hr-2966.one_liner: Limit Small Business Administration loans to US citizens and permanent residents
provisions: Requires people applying for Small Business Administration loans to prove they are US citizens or permanent residents
Makes refugees, asylees, visa holders, and DACA recipients ineligible for these business loans
Requires applicants to provide their date of birth on loan applications
Blocks people without legal immigration status from getting Small Business Administration loans

supporters: Supporters say this ensures taxpayer-funded Small Business Administration loans go to US citizens and permanent residents instead of people without legal status.
Supporters say blocking refugees, asylees, and visa holders from these loans helps American entrepreneurs compete for limited funding.
Supporters say requiring proof of citizenship prevents fraud and ensures government benefits go to legal residents.
critics: Critics say blocking refugees and asylees from Small Business Administration loans hurts people who are legally in the US and trying to build businesses.
Critics say making DACA recipients ineligible prevents young people who grew up in America from starting companies and creating jobs.
Critics say reducing the number of entrepreneurs eligible for these loans will slow economic growth and limit new business creation.

119-hr-33.one_liner: Cut tax rates for Taiwan residents on income from U.S. sources
provisions: Cuts tax rate from 30% to 10% for Taiwan residents on interest, royalties, and some investment gains from U.S. sources
Cuts dividend tax rate from 30% to 15% for Taiwan residents
Cuts dividend tax rate to 10% for Taiwan corporations that own at least 10% of a U.S. company
Eliminates tax on wages paid to Taiwan residents who are not U.S. residents

supporters: Supporters say cutting Taiwan residents' tax rates from 30% to 10% on interest and investment gains would bring more Taiwan money into U.S. markets.
Supporters say eliminating taxes on wages for Taiwan residents working in the U.S. would make it easier for Taiwan companies to send workers here.
Supporters say reducing dividend taxes to 15% for Taiwan residents would strengthen economic ties between the U.S. and Taiwan.
critics: Critics say cutting tax rates for Taiwan residents would reduce U.S. government revenue from these investments and wages.
Critics say giving Taiwan special tax treatment that other countries don't get creates unfair advantages.
Critics say lowering Taiwan corporations' dividend taxes to 10% when they own at least 10% of U.S. companies gives them better deals than other foreign investors.

119-hr-3095.one_liner: Give unique ZIP codes to 74 communities across the United States
provisions: Requires the Postal Service to give each of 74 specific communities their own unique ZIP code
Covers communities in over 20 states from California to Wisconsin
These communities currently share ZIP codes with other nearby areas

supporters: Supporters say this would eliminate mail delivery errors in the 74 communities that currently share ZIP codes with nearby areas.
Supporters say this would help emergency services locate addresses faster in these specific communities.
Supporters say this would give these 74 communities clearer postal identity for business and resident mail delivery.
critics: Critics say this would cost taxpayers money to create and implement 74 new ZIP codes across more than 20 states.
Critics say this would require Postal Service staff time and resources that could address other postal service issues.
Critics say this targets only 74 specific communities while thousands of other areas also share ZIP codes with nearby towns.

119-hr-30.one_liner: Block and deport non-citizens who commit crimes against women and children
provisions: Blocks non-citizens from entering the US if they committed stalking, child abuse, sex crimes, or domestic violence
Makes sex crimes and conspiracies to commit sex crimes new reasons to deport non-citizens
Expands domestic violence crimes that lead to deportation to include physical abuse, sexual abuse, and controlling behavior

supporters: Supporters say this would block non-citizens who committed stalking, child abuse, sex crimes, or domestic violence from entering the US to protect American women and children.
Supporters say making sex crimes and conspiracies to commit sex crimes new reasons to deport non-citizens closes gaps in current law.
Supporters say expanding domestic violence crimes that lead to deportation to include physical abuse, sexual abuse, and controlling behavior gives clearer rules for removing dangerous people.
critics: Critics say the bill blocks non-citizens from entering if they only admitted to crimes without being convicted, which could punish people unfairly.
Critics say the expanded domestic violence definition including coercive behavior could affect people in complex family situations where the facts are unclear.
Critics say this could hurt asylum seekers who are themselves victims of domestic violence trying to escape dangerous situations.

119-hr-2987.one_liner: Limit for-profit lenders that can make government-backed small business loans to 16 companies
provisions: Sets a cap of 16 companies that can make government-backed small business loans
Applies only to for-profit lending companies
Covers loans where the government guarantees repayment to reduce risk for lenders

supporters: Supporters say limiting the number to 16 for-profit companies would ensure only the most experienced lenders can make government-backed 7(a) loans.
Supporters say this cap would reduce the government's risk because fewer companies would be handling loans that taxpayers guarantee.
critics: Critics say limiting access to just 16 for-profit companies would reduce competition and make it harder for small businesses to find loans.
Critics say this cap would create an unfair advantage for the 16 companies that get to make government-backed 7(a) loans.

119-hr-3422.one_liner: Expand an SEC office that helps small businesses raise money
provisions: Gives an SEC office more jobs helping small businesses raise money
Requires the office to provide educational materials for businesses owned by underrepresented groups, rural businesses, and businesses hurt by natural disasters
Requires the office to host events about ways small businesses can raise money
Requires the office to meet yearly with state regulators to work together

supporters: Supporters say this would help underrepresented small businesses and rural businesses learn about ways to raise money through new educational resources and events.
Supporters say this would create yearly meetings between SEC staff and state regulators to better coordinate help for small businesses.
Supporters say this would give businesses hurt by natural disasters specific resources to help them rebuild and find funding.
critics: Critics say this expands an existing SEC office's duties without clear evidence that current services are insufficient for small businesses.
Critics say this requires the SEC to spend time and money on educational events that private groups and state agencies already provide.
Critics say this creates new federal mandates for yearly meetings with state regulators that may not lead to meaningful improvements.

119-hr-3351.one_liner: Remove paperwork rules for a government office that helps small businesses get money
provisions: Removes certain paperwork rules for a government office that helps small businesses get money
This office works inside the Securities and Exchange Commission
The office can now collect information from people without following some government paperwork rules
The office still must tell people why it is collecting information from them

supporters: Supporters say removing paperwork rules for the Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation will help small businesses get funding faster.
Supporters say this change lets the office collect information from people without delays caused by government paperwork requirements.
Supporters say small businesses need this office to work more quickly when helping them find money to grow.
critics: Critics say removing Paperwork Reduction Act rules takes away protections for people who have to give information to this government office.
Critics say the Securities and Exchange Commission office should follow the same paperwork rules as other government agencies.
Critics say this change reduces oversight of how government offices collect information from the public.

119-hr-35.one_liner: Make it a federal crime to flee Border Patrol agents within 100 miles of the border
provisions: Makes it a federal crime to drive away from Border Patrol agents or police helping them within 100 miles of the border
Sets mandatory minimum prison sentences if someone dies or gets badly hurt during the chase
Bans non-citizens who commit this crime from getting asylum or other immigration help
Makes non-citizens who commit this crime eligible for deportation

supporters: Supporters say this law would protect Border Patrol agents from dangerous car chases within 100 miles of the border.
Supporters say the mandatory prison sentences would deter people from fleeing when someone dies or gets seriously hurt.
Supporters say making non-citizens deportable for this crime would stop border crossers from putting officers at risk.
critics: Critics say the 100-mile zone covers too much area and would affect legal residents who live near the border.
Critics say mandatory minimum sentences take away judges' ability to consider individual cases.
Critics say blocking asylum eligibility is too harsh for people fleeing persecution who make this mistake.

119-hr-3357.one_liner: Require companies to disclose voting power of executives and major shareholders
provisions: Companies with different classes of shares must reveal voting power information in shareholder meeting materials
Companies must disclose how many shares each director and executive owns
Companies must reveal the voting power each director and executive holds
Companies must disclose share ownership and voting power of anyone who owns 5% or more of the company
Multi-class shares mean some shares get more votes than others, often giving founders more control than regular investors

supporters: Supporters say this helps regular investors see how much voting power company founders and executives really have when some shares get more votes than others.
Supporters say this makes companies tell shareholders exactly how many shares each director and top executive owns and how much voting control they have.
Supporters say this requires companies to reveal when someone owns 5% or more of voting shares, so investors know who controls the company.
critics: Critics say this forces companies to spend extra money and time gathering detailed ownership information for every shareholder meeting.
Critics say this creates new paperwork requirements for companies that already report ownership information in other government filings.
Critics say this adds reporting burdens only on companies that use different classes of shares, which could discourage this business structure.

119-hr-3394.one_liner: Expand who can invest in certain private investment deals to include people with professional knowledge
provisions: Lets people with professional knowledge or education invest in certain private investment deals even if they don't meet wealth requirements
Keeps existing wealth and income requirements for qualifying to invest in these deals
Keeps existing rules that let licensed financial professionals invest in these deals
Requires the SEC to update regulations to match the new law

supporters: Supporters say this would let people with professional knowledge or education invest in private deals even if they don't have enough wealth under current rules.
Supporters say licensed financial professionals and people with relevant experience should have the same investment access as wealthy people.
critics: Critics say people without wealth requirements could lose money they can't afford to lose on risky private investments.
Critics say the wealth rules protect people from losing too much money, and removing them for some investors could lead to bigger losses.

119-hr-375.one_liner: Fund research and control of a fungus killing trees in Hawaii
provisions: Requires government agencies to work together to control a tree disease called Rapid Ohia Death in Hawaii
Continues research on how the fungus spreads between trees
Manages deer and other animals that might spread the disease on government and private land
Gives money to prevent the fungus from spreading and restore Hawaii's native forests
Provides staff and funding to a research institute to study the fungus

supporters: Supporters say research on how deer and other animals spread the fungus will help scientists protect Hawaii's ohia trees.
Supporters say financial assistance will help restore native forests and prevent the disease from spreading to more areas.
Supporters say government agencies working together will create better control of Rapid Ohia Death.
critics: Critics say funding staff and infrastructure for the research institute adds to federal spending.
Critics say requiring private landowner consent to manage animals on private land could limit disease control efforts.
Critics say coordinating multiple government agencies could slow response to the tree disease.

119-hr-3633.one_liner: Create rules for trading digital currencies like Bitcoin and other crypto assets
provisions: Puts the CFTC in charge of regulating digital currency exchanges and brokers
Digital currencies can only trade on exchanges if their technology is mature or companies file reports
Some digital currencies do not have to register with the SEC if sales stay under certain amounts
Digital currency companies must follow anti-money laundering rules
Sets up temporary rules until the new system starts working

supporters: Supporters say this gives the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) clear authority to regulate digital currency exchanges and brokers, creating federal rules that don't exist now.
Supporters say digital currencies on mature blockchains can skip Securities and Exchange Commission registration if their annual sales stay under set limits, reducing costs for smaller companies.
Supporters say all digital currency companies must follow anti-money laundering rules, helping prevent criminals from using these markets.
critics: Critics say allowing digital currencies on mature blockchains to skip SEC registration if sales stay under certain amounts could reduce investor protections.
Critics say requiring digital currencies to have mature blockchain technology or file reports before trading on exchanges could prevent emerging digital currencies from reaching markets.
Critics say giving the CFTC instead of the SEC primary control over digital currency regulation could create confusion between the two agencies.

119-hr-359.one_liner: Require Energy Department to report when it reduces company contributions to federally-funded energy projects
provisions: Requires the Energy Department to report when it reduces how much companies must contribute to federally-funded energy projects
Reports must be submitted within 120 days of this law passing
Reports must continue every three months after that
Covers energy research, development, demonstration, and commercial application projects under the Energy Policy Act of 2005

supporters: Supporters say the quarterly reports would let Congress and taxpayers know when companies pay less than planned for Energy Department research projects.
Supporters say the 120-day reporting deadline would quickly reveal how often the Energy Department reduces cost-sharing requirements for energy projects under the Energy Policy Act of 2005.
critics: Critics say the quarterly reporting requirements would create extra paperwork that could delay energy research and development projects.
Critics say the 120-day deadline and ongoing reports could make Energy Department officials less likely to adjust cost-sharing when projects need help.

119-hr-3937.one_liner: Sell 14 acres of Wisconsin forest land to Tony's Wabeno Redi-Mix
provisions: Requires the Forest Service to sell 14 acres of Wisconsin forest land to Tony's Wabeno Redi-Mix if they offer market value
Gives the company 180 days after the land appraisal to make an offer
Makes the company pay market value plus all costs to buy the land
Requires the Interior Department to review federal rules for stone, sand, and gravel permits

supporters: Supporters say this helps Tony's Wabeno Redi-Mix get the 14 acres they need while requiring them to pay market value plus all costs to taxpayers.
Supporters say the 180-day deadline gives the company a clear timeline while the Interior Department review could help other stone and gravel businesses get permits faster.
critics: Critics say this gives special treatment to one company by requiring the Forest Service to sell them public forest land from the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest.
Critics say the 14 acres of public land will be lost forever and the 180-day deadline could pressure officials to accept a low market value appraisal.

119-hr-36.one_liner: Require sanctions on Georgian officials who block Georgia's path to join NATO and EU
provisions: Blocks visas for Georgian officials who hurt Georgia's security or stability
Lets the President freeze assets of people who make Georgia unstable
Targets parliament members and government officials who use corruption or violence to block Georgia's path to join NATO and the EU
Includes family members who benefit from the banned official's conduct
Requires the President to identify foreign persons who engage in major corruption in Georgia

supporters: Supporters say blocking visas for Georgian officials who undermine security will stop corrupt leaders from traveling to the US.
Supporters say freezing assets of people who make Georgia unstable will cut off their money and reduce their power.
Supporters say targeting parliament members and officials who use violence to block Georgia's NATO and EU membership will help Georgia join these groups.
critics: Critics say blocking visas for Georgian officials could damage diplomatic relations between the US and Georgia.
Critics say including family members in sanctions punishes relatives who may not be involved in corruption.
Critics say giving the President power to freeze assets of foreign persons could be used too broadly against people who are not actually threats.

provisions: Gives money to pay military personnel for the year starting October 2025
Pays for military operations and equipment
Funds military health care programs
Pays for military research and weapons development
Pays to destroy old chemical weapons
Funds CIA employee retirement benefits
Sets rules for how the money can be spent

supporters: Supporters say the military personnel funding ensures troops receive their pay starting October 2025
Supporters say the military health care programs provide medical coverage for service members and their families
Supporters say the chemical weapons destruction funding safely eliminates dangerous weapons stockpiles
critics: Critics say the weapons research and development spending increases military capabilities that could escalate conflicts with other countries
Critics say the CIA retirement fund creates special pension benefits that cost more than regular government employee retirement plans
Critics say the military health programs duplicate services already available through civilian health care systems

119-hr-43.one_liner: Let Alaska Native village corporations keep their lands instead of giving them to municipalities
provisions: Stops requiring Alaska Native village corporations to give certain lands to city governments or to Alaska
Lets village corporations take back lands that Alaska currently holds for future cities
Village corporations and village residents can vote together to regain control of their lands

supporters: Supporters say this would give Alaska Native village corporations control over their own lands instead of being forced to give them to city governments or Alaska.
Supporters say village corporations and village residents can vote together to take back lands that Alaska currently holds for future cities.
Supporters say this removes the requirement that forces village corporations to give away certain lands.
critics: Critics say this could prevent future municipalities from getting lands they need to operate as cities.
Critics say removing the trust requirement could hurt planning for new city governments in Alaska Native villages.
Critics say this could make land ownership more complicated when villages want to become cities.

119-hr-4216.one_liner: Review which military equipment companies can sell directly to foreign countries
provisions: The State Department must review military sales rules every year
The review finds equipment that companies could sell directly to foreign governments instead of only through the U.S. government
The review compares how long each type of sale takes to complete
The review looks at how company sales would change the government's workload
The review studies benefits to U.S. security and business competition
The State Department reports results to Congress within 30 days of finishing each review

supporters: Supporters say the annual review would find military equipment that companies could sell directly to foreign governments instead of only through the U.S. government, which could speed up sales to allies.
Supporters say allowing more direct company sales would reduce the workload on the State Department and Defense Department by moving some sales away from government workers.
Supporters say the review of benefits to U.S. competitiveness would help American defense companies compete better against foreign companies for military contracts.
critics: Critics say moving military sales from government control to direct company sales could reduce oversight of sensitive weapons transfers to foreign governments.
Critics say the annual review requirement adds new paperwork and tasks for State Department staff every year.
Critics say government-to-government sales give the U.S. better diplomatic control over which countries receive advanced military equipment.

119-hr-4553.one_liner: Fund energy and water programs for the year starting October 2025
provisions: Funds Army Corps of Engineers to build and maintain dams, levees, and flood control projects
Pays for Department of Energy programs including renewable energy research and nuclear weapon maintenance
Supports water projects in western states through the Bureau of Reclamation
Funds cleanup of old nuclear weapons sites and radioactive waste disposal
Pays for agencies that regulate nuclear power plants and energy markets

supporters: Supporters say the Army Corps flood control projects will protect millions of people from floods and storms.
Supporters say DOE clean energy research will help create jobs and reduce air pollution.
Supporters say Bureau of Reclamation water projects will help western communities get water during droughts.
critics: Critics say funding for nuclear weapons maintenance costs billions that could go to schools or healthcare.
Critics say Army Corps projects mostly help coastal and river communities while all taxpayers pay for them.
Critics say nuclear waste cleanup has no permanent solution but keeps getting more expensive each year.

119-hr-4275.one_liner: Fund the Coast Guard and create a Secretary of the Coast Guard position
provisions: Funds Coast Guard operations and equipment
Creates a Secretary of the Coast Guard position
Lets Coast Guard members take family leave
Pays for maternity uniforms for female officers
Requires reports on Coast Guard Academy safety
Sets rules for buying Coast Guard ships and planes
Gives travel money to Coast Guard members in Alaska

supporters: Supporters say the family leave provision would help Coast Guard members care for new babies and sick relatives.
Supporters say creating a Secretary of the Coast Guard position would give the service better leadership and more say in government decisions.
Supporters say paying for maternity uniforms and travel money for Alaska members shows the government cares about Coast Guard families.
critics: Critics say creating a new Secretary position would add more government bureaucracy and cost taxpayers money for another high-level job.
Critics say the bill spends money on things like maternity uniforms and Alaska travel costs without showing these are the most important needs.
Critics say the bill requires more reports on Academy safety but doesn't fix the actual problems that need reports.

119-hr-517.one_liner: Let the IRS postpone tax deadlines for state-declared disasters and extend automatic extensions
provisions: Lets the IRS postpone tax deadlines for state-declared disasters when governors request it
Increases automatic tax deadline extensions from 60 days to 120 days for disaster victims
Covers people whose homes, businesses, or tax records are in disaster areas
Includes relief workers and people killed or injured in disasters

supporters: Supporters say the 120-day extension (up from 60 days) gives disaster victims more time to file taxes when their homes or businesses are destroyed.
Supporters say allowing state-declared disasters to get the same tax relief as federal disasters helps more people affected by floods, fires, and explosions.
Supporters say this helps relief workers and people whose tax records are lost in disasters get extra time without penalties.
critics: Critics say extending tax deadlines from 60 to 120 days could delay tax revenue collection for the federal government.
Critics say allowing any state governor to request tax deadline postponements might lead to overuse of this relief.
Critics say the expanded definition of disasters could create more administrative work for the IRS.

119-hr-530.one_liner: Require the VA to study cancer rates in veterans who flew military aircraft
provisions: Requires the VA to hire a research group called the National Academies to do a study
The study focuses on veterans who worked as crew members on military planes
The study will count cancer cases and deaths among these veterans

supporters: Supporters say this would help find out if veterans who worked as crew members on military planes get cancer more often than other people.
Supporters say the study by the National Academies would give the VA the facts needed to better care for aircrew veterans with cancer.
critics: Critics say this costs taxpayer money to pay the National Academies to do a study the VA could do itself.
Critics say this focuses on research instead of giving aircrew veterans with cancer the medical care they need now.

119-hr-495.one_liner: Require annual reports on border tunnel defense plans
provisions: Requires border patrol to report every year on tunnel defense plans
Currently they only have to report once
The reports cover plans to stop underground tunnels at the border

supporters: Supporters say annual reporting will help Congress track how well CBP is stopping underground tunnels at the border each year.
Supporters say the current one-time report requirement does not give lawmakers enough information about ongoing tunnel defense efforts.
Supporters say yearly reports will show whether CBP's tunnel defense plans are working over time.
critics: Critics say requiring CBP to write reports every year will cost money and time that could be spent on actual border security operations.
Critics say the current one-time reporting requirement already provides Congress with the needed information about tunnel defense plans.
Critics say annual paperwork creates more government bureaucracy without improving border security.

119-hr-471.one_liner: Change forest management rules to reduce wildfire risk
provisions: Creates fire risk zones on federal land called fireshed management areas
Sets up a government center to track wildfires and predict where they might happen
Speeds up approval for tree cutting and forest management projects
Removes some environmental review requirements for forest work
Limits lawsuits that can challenge forest management projects
Funds programs to help firefighters and prevent wildfires

supporters: Supporters say creating fireshed management areas on federal land will help prevent dangerous wildfires by identifying high-risk zones.
Supporters say speeding up approval for tree cutting and forest management projects will reduce wildfire risks faster.
Supporters say funding programs for wildland firefighters will help protect the people who risk their lives fighting fires.
critics: Critics say removing environmental review requirements for forest work could harm wildlife and water quality.
Critics say limiting lawsuits that challenge forest management projects takes away people's right to protect public lands in court.
Critics say reducing consultation requirements for threatened and endangered species could push more animals toward extinction.

119-hr-586.one_liner: Require the VA to study bile duct cancer rates in Vietnam veterans
provisions: Requires the VA to study bile duct cancer rates in Vietnam veterans
Compares cancer rates in Vietnam veterans to rates in all Americans
Tracks bile duct cancer cases using the VA's cancer registry
Requires the VA to report study results to Congress

supporters: Supporters say the epidemiological study comparing Vietnam veterans to U.S. residents would reveal if veterans face higher bile duct cancer risks.
Supporters say using the VA Central Cancer Registry to track cholangiocarcinoma cases would help identify veteran health patterns.
Supporters say the required Congressional reports would ensure lawmakers know about veteran cancer rates.
critics: Critics say the VA should focus resources on cancer treatment for veterans instead of funding epidemiological studies.
Critics say comparing Vietnam veterans to all Americans may not account for age and health differences between groups.
Critics say adding more Congressional reporting requirements creates paperwork that diverts VA staff from patient care.

119-hr-736.one_liner: Extend deadline for companies to file ownership information by one year
provisions: Extends the deadline for companies to tell the government who owns them
Companies formed before January 1, 2024 get until January 1, 2026 instead of January 1, 2025
This gives companies one extra year to file this ownership information

supporters: Supporters say the one-year extension to January 1, 2026 gives small businesses more time to understand and follow the new beneficial ownership rules.
Supporters say companies formed before January 1, 2024 did not have enough notice about these filing requirements and need the extra year to comply.
critics: Critics say pushing the deadline to January 1, 2026 delays important ownership information that law enforcement needs to fight financial crimes.
Critics say the original January 1, 2025 deadline gave companies enough time to file their beneficial ownership information with FinCEN.

119-hr-695.one_liner: Increase monthly pension for Medal of Honor recipients and create pension for surviving spouses
provisions: Raises monthly pension for living Medal of Honor recipients from $1,407 to $8,333
Creates a monthly pension of $1,407 for spouses of deceased Medal of Honor recipients
Adjusts both pension amounts each year for inflation

supporters: Supporters say the increase from $1,407 to $8,333 per month provides Medal of Honor recipients with more financial support.
Supporters say the new $1,407 monthly payment helps surviving spouses of deceased Medal of Honor recipients.
Supporters say the annual inflation adjustments protect the value of these payments over time.
critics: Critics say raising monthly payments from $1,407 to $8,333 for living Medal of Honor recipients will cost the government significantly more money.
Critics say adding $1,407 monthly payments for surviving spouses creates new government spending.
Critics say the automatic inflation adjustments will increase costs each year.

119-hr-758.one_liner: Require the postal service to track and report traffic deaths involving mail trucks
provisions: Makes the postal service track deaths and injuries from crashes involving mail trucks
Requires postal workers to report crashes within three days if someone gets hurt or dies
Creates a database to store information about these crashes
Requires a yearly public report about mail truck crashes

supporters: Supporters say the three-day reporting rule will help families of crash victims get information faster about what happened to their loved ones.
Supporters say the annual public reports will help identify dangerous routes and patterns that could prevent future mail truck crashes.
Supporters say creating a database of mail truck crashes will give the public transparency about postal service safety that does not exist today.
critics: Critics say the new reporting requirements will cost the postal service money and staff time that should be used for delivering mail.
Critics say the three-day reporting deadline is too short and will burden postal workers who are already required to report crashes to police and insurance companies.
Critics say this creates duplicate paperwork since mail truck crashes are already reported to state and federal transportation agencies.

119-hr-747.one_liner: Expand sanctions to Chinese companies and officials linked to fentanyl trafficking
provisions: Lets the President sanction Chinese companies that make fentanyl ingredients and don't try to stop drug trafficking
Lets the President sanction Chinese government officials who help drug trafficking or don't stop it
Brings back a rule requiring the President to report to Congress each year on drug traffickers and sanctions until 2029
Requires the President to study costs and benefits before making new economic rules during drug trafficking emergencies

supporters: Supporters say this would let the President sanction Chinese companies that make fentanyl ingredients but fail to stop drug trafficking, targeting the source of deadly drugs killing Americans.
Supporters say this would hold Chinese government officials accountable for helping drug trafficking or doing nothing to stop it, closing a gap in current law.
Supporters say bringing back the annual reporting requirement until 2029 gives Congress oversight of who gets sanctioned and why.
critics: Critics say sanctioning Chinese companies and officials could hurt trade relations with China and lead to economic retaliation against American businesses.
Critics say the cost-benefit study requirement could slow down emergency action when the President needs to act fast during drug trafficking crises.
Critics say the broad power to sanction Chinese officials for 'intentional inaction' could be misused against officials who are not directly involved in drug trafficking.

119-hr-692.one_liner: Require the U.S. to pressure China on currency policies at the IMF
provisions: Requires the U.S. to push China to be more open about how it manages its currency at the IMF
Focuses on how China controls its currency value, including through banks and government-owned companies
Calls for more watching of China's currency policies by the IMF
Links China's openness to its voting power at the IMF
Ends after 7 years or sooner if China becomes more open about its currency

supporters: Supporters say this would force China to reveal how it uses banks and state-owned companies to control its currency value.
Supporters say this would give the IMF more power to watch China's currency policies through enhanced surveillance.
Supporters say this would link China's voting power at the IMF to how open it is about its currency management.
critics: Critics say this could harm U.S.-China relations by threatening China's voting shares at the IMF.
Critics say this gives the U.S. too much control over how the IMF evaluates China's currency policies.
Critics say this could take up to 7 years to work and China might not change its behavior during that time.

119-hr-818.one_liner: Require agencies to track first-time contracts to veteran-owned and minority-owned small businesses
provisions: Requires federal agencies to add new information to their yearly small business contracting reports
Agencies must count how many small businesses get their first government contract each year
The count must include businesses owned by disabled veterans, minorities, women, and businesses in special economic areas

supporters: Supporters say tracking first-time contracts for businesses owned by disabled veterans, minorities, women, and businesses in special economic areas would help agencies see if their programs are reaching new small businesses.
Supporters say adding this information to yearly reports would give Congress better data on whether government contracting is expanding to include more diverse small businesses.
critics: Critics say requiring agencies to track and count first-time contracts for these specific groups would create new paperwork and administrative costs.
Critics say the new reporting requirements would burden federal agencies without directly helping small businesses win more contracts.

119-hr-776.one_liner: Continue funding states to control nutria and restore marshes through 2030
provisions: Continues a program that gives money to states to control nutria through 2030
Nutria are rodents that damage wetlands and marshes
States can use the money to kill nutria and restore damaged marshes

supporters: Supporters say this gives states money to remove nutria that eat and destroy wetlands and marshes.
Supporters say this helps fix marshes that nutria have already damaged.
Supporters say this continues protection of wetlands through 2030 by controlling these invasive rodents.
critics: Critics say this spends federal tax money on pest control that states should pay for themselves.
Critics say this continues a program that has been running since 2003 without proving it has solved the nutria problem.
Critics say this money could go to other priorities instead of rodent control programs.

119-hr-804.one_liner: Require outreach to rural small businesses for disaster assistance
provisions: Requires the Small Business Administration to help rural small businesses get disaster assistance
The agency must reach out to rural areas when disasters happen
The agency must create outreach materials for rural communities

supporters: Supporters say this would ensure rural small businesses get the same disaster assistance as urban businesses by requiring the Small Business Administration to actively reach out to rural areas.
Supporters say the outreach materials would help rural communities learn about disaster programs they might not know exist.
critics: Critics say requiring the Small Business Administration to create new outreach materials and programs would cost taxpayer money without providing new funding.
Critics say the bill's requirements are too vague and could force the agency to spend unlimited amounts on rural outreach.

119-hr-788.one_liner: Require the Energy Department and Small Business Administration to work together on research
provisions: Makes the Energy Department and Small Business Administration sign an agreement to work together on research projects
Requires these projects to include small businesses when possible
Makes both agencies write reports about what research they completed together
Requires reports about ways to improve their technical abilities

supporters: Supporters say requiring the Energy Department and Small Business Administration to work together gives small businesses access to energy research they could not afford alone.
Supporters say the collaboration agreement prevents both agencies from doing the same research twice, saving taxpayer money.
Supporters say the required reports ensure the agencies actually work together and show Congress what they accomplished.
critics: Critics say the required reports create more paperwork and take staff time away from actual research work.
Critics say forcing the Energy Department and Small Business Administration to sign an agreement wastes resources because the agencies have different missions.
Critics say requiring small business participation in energy research projects slows down important scientific work.

119-hr-77.one_liner: Let Congress cancel multiple government rules at once instead of one at a time
provisions: Congress can currently cancel government rules one at a time with separate votes
This bill would let Congress cancel multiple rules with a single vote
Only applies to rules made in the last year of a president's term
Makes it easier for Congress to undo rules from an outgoing president

supporters: Supporters say this bill saves Congress time by allowing one vote to cancel multiple rules instead of requiring separate votes for each rule made in the final year of a president's term.
Supporters say the current system is too slow because Congress must vote separately on each rule from an outgoing president.
critics: Critics say combining multiple rules in one vote could force lawmakers to cancel good rules along with bad ones.
Critics say this makes it too easy for Congress to quickly remove rules that protect workers and consumers without reviewing each rule carefully.

119-hr-875.one_liner: Make drunk driving a reason to deport non-citizens or block them from entering
provisions: Lets the government deport non-citizens who are convicted of drunk driving
Blocks non-citizens from entering the US if they were convicted of drunk driving
Also blocks non-citizens from entering if they admit to drunk driving even without a conviction

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects communities by giving immigration officials the power to deport non-citizens convicted of drunk driving.
Supporters say the law stops people with drunk driving convictions from entering the U.S. in the first place.
Supporters say this removes dangerous drivers who could hurt American families on the roads.
critics: Critics say the bill allows deportation even for first-time drunk driving offenses, which can break up families with U.S. citizen children.
Critics say non-citizens can be blocked from entering the country just for admitting to drunk driving without ever being convicted in court.
Critics say the law treats all drunk driving cases the same way, even when no one was injured.

119-hr-859.one_liner: Require companies to tell buyers about cameras and microphones in smart devices before purchase
provisions: Companies that make devices connected to the internet must tell buyers if the device has a camera or microphone
This applies to smart appliances and similar devices but not phones or laptops
Companies must give this information before someone buys the device

supporters: Supporters say this would help people learn if their smart appliances have cameras or microphones before they buy them.
Supporters say many consumers don't know that devices like smart TVs and thermostats can record them in their homes.
Supporters say requiring companies to share this information lets families make better choices about their privacy.
critics: Critics say manufacturers would face new costs to update their labels and marketing materials for internet-connected devices.
Critics say the rule is unclear about which devices count as ones consumers would 'reasonably expect' to have cameras.
Critics say compliance costs could make smart appliances more expensive for buyers.

119-hr-825.one_liner: Block people convicted of COVID loan fraud from getting Small Business Administration help
provisions: Stops people convicted of financial crimes or lying about COVID business loans from getting Small Business Administration money
Blocks Small Business Administration help for businesses owned by people convicted of these crimes
Covers crimes involving Paycheck Protection Program loans, Restaurant Revitalization Fund grants, and Shuttered Venue Operators grants
Still allows disaster loans

supporters: Supporters say this stops people who lied about Paycheck Protection Program loans or Restaurant Revitalization Fund grants from getting more Small Business Administration money.
Supporters say this protects taxpayer dollars by blocking financial assistance to businesses owned by people convicted of COVID loan fraud.
Supporters say the bill still allows disaster loans so legitimate businesses can get help during emergencies.
critics: Critics say blocking all Small Business Administration programs except disaster loans is too harsh for businesses with convicted owners.
Critics say this punishes innocent employees and business partners when only one owner or director committed financial crimes.
Critics say small businesses that need legitimate Small Business Administration programs will lose access because of one person's past conviction.

119-hr-832.one_liner: Expand Small Business Administration advocacy to include international work
provisions: Gives the Small Business Administration's advocacy office new international duties
The office will study how small businesses work in the global economy
The office will represent small businesses to foreign governments
The office will work on international trade and rule issues affecting small businesses

supporters: Supporters say this would give the Office of Advocacy new power to represent small businesses before foreign governments on trade and regulatory issues.
Supporters say requiring the office to study small businesses in the international economy would help find ways to boost overseas sales.
Supporters say small businesses currently have no official voice in international trade talks that affect their ability to export.
critics: Critics say expanding the Office of Advocacy's duties to include international work would increase government spending without proof of benefits.
Critics say the Small Business Administration should focus on domestic small business needs instead of taking on international trade roles.
Critics say other agencies like the Commerce Department already handle international trade issues for businesses.

119-hr-856.one_liner: Require a study on whether federal buying rules create security risks
provisions: Requires the Office of Management and Budget to study how federal agencies buy things
Looks at whether rules that require buying the cheapest option create security risks
Requires a report to Congress with the findings

supporters: Supporters say this Office of Management and Budget study would find security risks in Federal Acquisition Regulation rules that require buying the cheapest option.
Supporters say Congress needs this report to know if lowest price technically acceptable rules let unsafe suppliers sell to the government.
critics: Critics say this study could lead to higher costs for taxpayers if agencies stop using lowest price technically acceptable rules.
Critics say the Office of Management and Budget evaluation will slow down federal purchasing while the review takes place.

119-hr-881.one_liner: Stop DHS funding to colleges with ties to Chinese government programs
provisions: Stops the Department of Homeland Security from giving money to colleges that work with Chinese cultural institutes
Blocks DHS funding to universities connected to Chinese technology and education programs
Cuts DHS money to schools with ties to Chinese universities that help with military or police work
Colleges can get their DHS funding back if they end these relationships

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects American colleges from Chinese government influence by blocking DHS funding to schools that work with Chinese cultural institutes or military-linked universities.
Supporters say the bill gives colleges a clear choice between keeping partnerships with Chinese entities of concern and receiving DHS money.
Supporters say this stops Chinese intelligence and military organizations from accessing American university research through the Thousand Talents Program and other partnerships.
critics: Critics say this bill forces colleges to lose DHS funding if they want to keep academic partnerships with Chinese universities and cultural programs.
Critics say cutting DHS money from universities could hurt school budgets and research programs that depend on federal funding.
Critics say this bill limits academic cooperation between American and Chinese schools, even for non-military research.

119-hr-901.one_liner: Require DHS to create security policies for research and report on compliance
provisions: Requires DHS to create rules protecting research from unauthorized access
Makes DHS protect sensitive information in research contracts
Orders an audit of whether DHS follows 2021 rules about research reporting
Checks if DHS reports conflicts of interest involving foreign governments

supporters: Supporters say this bill would protect DHS research from unauthorized access by requiring new security rules for the Science and Technology Directorate.
Supporters say the audit would ensure DHS follows 2021 rules about reporting conflicts of interest involving foreign governments in research contracts.
critics: Critics say the new security policy requirements could slow down DHS research and add paperwork for contractors.
Critics say the GAO audit would cost taxpayer money to check compliance with rules that are already in place.

119-hr-993.one_liner: Require border patrol to plan new AI and sensor technology for border security
provisions: Requires border patrol to plan how to use AI, sensors, and other new technology for border security
Lets border patrol create research teams to test technology from private companies
Border patrol must give the plan to Congress within 6 months
The plan must explain how new surveillance technology affects privacy in border communities
Border patrol must report to Congress each year about the research teams

supporters: Supporters say this would modernize border security by requiring border patrol to use AI, sensors, and other new technology to better protect the border.
Supporters say the Innovation Teams would help border patrol find the best technology from private companies to improve security operations.
Supporters say the plan must be finished within 6 months, which ensures border patrol acts quickly to improve security.
critics: Critics say this expands surveillance technology like AI and sensors that could violate privacy rights of people living in border communities.
Critics say the Innovation Teams working with private companies could lead to expensive contracts that waste taxpayer money.
Critics say the new surveillance technology could harm border communities even though the plan must study privacy impacts.

119-hr-973.one_liner: Require safety rules for lithium-ion batteries in electric bikes and scooters
provisions: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to create a safety rule for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes and electric scooters
Makes manufacturers and distributors follow safety standards set by the American National Standards Institute, the Standards Council of Canada, and UL Solutions Inc.
