supporters: Supporters say requiring the Consumer Product Safety Commission to create safety rules for lithium-ion batteries in electric bikes and scooters would prevent fires and explosions that have injured riders.
Supporters say making manufacturers follow standards from the American National Standards Institute and UL Solutions would ensure batteries meet proven safety requirements.
critics: Critics say forcing manufacturers and distributors of electric bikes and scooters to comply with new Consumer Product Safety Commission rules would raise production costs and make these vehicles more expensive.

Critics say requiring compliance with standards from the American National Standards Institute, Standards Council of Canada, and UL Solutions could delay new electric bike and scooter models from reaching the market.

119-hr-884.one_liner: Stop non-citizens from voting in Washington DC elections
provisions: Stops non-citizens from voting in Washington DC local elections
Cancels a DC law from 2022 that let non-citizens vote in local elections
The DC law started in February 2023 and let non-citizens vote if they lived there long enough
Federal law already stops non-citizens from voting for president and Congress

supporters: Supporters say this would make DC election rules match federal law, which already prohibits non-citizens from voting for president and Congress.
Supporters say this would ensure only U.S. citizens can vote in all DC elections.
Supporters say this cancels the 2022 DC law that allowed non-citizens to vote in local elections starting February 2023.
critics: Critics say this takes away voting rights from non-citizens who have been able to vote in DC local elections since February 2023.
Critics say this removes voting access for non-citizens who met residency and other requirements under the 2022 DC law.

119-hr-997.one_liner: Let the office that helps taxpayers hire their own lawyers
provisions: The National Taxpayer Advocate can hire lawyers who report directly to them
Right now, all Treasury lawyers report to Treasury's top lawyer
The National Taxpayer Advocate gets more control over all workers in their office
The office helps people who have problems with the IRS

supporters: Supporters say letting the National Taxpayer Advocate hire lawyers who report directly to them would remove conflicts of interest when helping taxpayers fight the IRS.
Supporters say giving the Advocate control over all Taxpayer Advocate Service workers instead of just local advocates would help them better serve people with IRS problems.
critics: Critics say breaking Treasury's current rule that all lawyers report to the General Counsel could weaken legal oversight and create confusion about who is in charge.
Critics say creating independent legal counsel for the Taxpayer Advocate Service could lead to higher costs and duplicate the work already done by Treasury's Legal Division.

119-hres-161.one_liner: Allow House votes on canceling two environmental rules and setting the federal budget
provisions: Allows the House to vote on canceling Department of Energy efficiency standards for gas water heaters
Allows the House to vote on canceling EPA methane emission fees on oil and gas companies
Allows the House to vote on setting the federal budget for 2025 and spending levels through 2034

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows Congress to vote on canceling Department of Energy efficiency standards for gas water heaters that could increase appliance costs for homeowners
Supporters say this rule allows Congress to vote on canceling EPA methane emission fees on oil and gas companies that could raise energy prices
Supporters say this rule allows Congress to vote on a budget plan that sets federal spending limits for 2025 through 2034
critics: Critics say canceling the gas water heater efficiency standards would cost families more on energy bills and reduce household energy savings
Critics say canceling the methane emission fees would let oil and gas companies emit greenhouse gases without paying cleanup costs
Critics say setting federal spending levels for 10 years through 2034 limits Congress's flexibility to respond to future economic needs or emergencies

119-hres-177.one_liner: Set up House votes to cancel three federal agency rules

One measure would cancel rules protecting underwater historical sites

supporters: Supporters say this gives the House an efficient way to review three federal agency rules that may go too far.
Supporters say this allows one hour of debate on each measure to cancel rules on appliance energy labels, tire factory air pollution, and underwater site protection.
Supporters say this lets Congress use its oversight powers to disapprove rules from the Energy Department, EPA, and Bureau of Ocean Energy Management.
critics: Critics say this limits debate to just one hour on each measure that could weaken environmental protections.
Critics say this rushed process reduces scrutiny of votes that would cancel rules protecting air quality at tire factories and underwater historical sites.
Critics say this streamlined approach gives too little time to discuss measures affecting appliance energy standards and pollution limits.

119-hres-189.one_liner: Vote to criticize Representative Al Green
provisions: Votes to criticize Representative Al Green
Records the criticism in the House proceedings

supporters: Supporters say the formal vote holds Representative Green accountable for his actions through official House criticism.
Supporters say recording this criticism in House proceedings creates a proper official record of the rebuke.
critics: Critics say the censure vote targets Representative Green without giving him adequate due process protections.
Critics say recording the criticism in House proceedings creates a permanent negative mark on Green's official record.

119-hres-282.one_liner: Schedule House votes on canceling bank rules and requiring citizenship proof to vote
provisions: Sets up a House vote to cancel a rule limiting overdraft fees at large banks
Sets up a House vote to cancel a rule about digital payment companies
Sets up a House vote to limit federal courts' power to block government actions
Sets up a House vote to require proof of US citizenship to register to vote in federal elections
Gives each bill one hour of debate time split between party leaders

supporters: Supporters say canceling the overdraft fee rule would give large banks more flexibility to offer payment services to customers who need short-term credit.

Supporters say requiring proof of US citizenship for federal voter registration would ensure only eligible citizens participate in federal elections.
critics: Critics say canceling the overdraft fee rule would allow large banks to charge consumers higher fees for insufficient funds.
Critics say removing oversight of digital payment applications would reduce consumer protections for personal financial data.
Critics say limiting federal courts' power to block government actions would reduce judicial review of government decisions.

119-hres-211.one_liner: Allow House votes on digital asset tax rules, unemployment fraud limits, and government funding
provisions: Sets up a House vote on canceling an IRS rule that requires brokers to report digital asset sales
Sets up a House vote on giving prosecutors more time to charge people with unemployment fraud
Sets up a House vote on continuing government funding through September 2025

supporters: Supporters say this allows the House to vote on three separate issues that affect taxpayers and government operations.
Supporters say canceling the IRS digital asset reporting rule would protect privacy and reduce compliance costs for cryptocurrency traders.
Supporters say extending the statute of limitations for unemployment fraud cases would give prosecutors more time to recover the $163 billion lost to pandemic fraud.
critics: Critics say bundling these three unrelated issues into one procedural vote prevents proper debate on each topic.
Critics say blocking the IRS reporting rule would make it easier for digital asset traders to hide income from tax collectors.
Critics say this procedural process delays action on government funding that expires soon.

119-hres-294.one_liner: Set up House votes on four bills about financial rules, courts, and voting
provisions: Allows a vote to cancel a bank rule about overdraft fees
Allows a vote to cancel a rule about digital payment companies
Allows a vote on limiting federal courts' power to issue orders stopping government actions
Allows a vote on requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote

supporters: Supporters say this allows Congress to vote on canceling CFPB rules that impose overdraft fee limits on large financial institutions.
Supporters say this allows a vote to remove CFPB oversight rules for digital payment companies.
Supporters say this allows Congress to vote on requiring proof of United States citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.
critics: Critics say this could lead to removing consumer protections that limit overdraft fees charged by large banks.
Critics say this could remove oversight rules for digital payment applications used by millions of Americans.
Critics say this could make it harder for eligible citizens to register to vote by requiring additional documentation.

119-hres-242.one_liner: Set up House votes on energy rules and college foreign money disclosure
provisions: Allows the House to vote on canceling energy efficiency standards for walk-in coolers and freezers
Allows the House to vote on canceling energy efficiency standards for commercial refrigerators and freezers
Allows the House to vote on requiring colleges to report foreign money and banning some foreign contracts

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows Congress to vote on canceling energy efficiency standards for walk-in coolers and freezers that would require costly equipment upgrades for restaurants and grocery stores.
Supporters say this rule enables a vote on requiring colleges to report foreign money and banning contracts with countries of concern.
critics: Critics say this rule tries to block energy efficiency standards for commercial refrigerators and walk-in coolers that would reduce electricity bills for businesses.
Critics say canceling these energy standards would increase energy costs for restaurants and grocery stores using walk-in freezers and coolers.

119-hres-313.one_liner: Set House rules to vote on Senate budget changes and pause a national emergency countdown
provisions: Lets the House vote on Senate changes to the government budget for 2025-2034

Stops the countdown to end a national emergency from April through September 2025

supporters: Supporters say the 1 hour of debate time will let the House vote on the Senate budget changes quickly without delays

critics: Critics say 1 hour of debate is too short for discussing a budget that covers 10 years from 2025-2034

Critics say this rushes the House vote on Senate budget changes without enough time to study the details

119-hres-352.one_liner: Ask elected officials and community leaders to condemn antisemitism
provisions: Calls on elected officials to condemn acts of antisemitism

Calls for educating the public about Jewish American contributions

supporters: Supporters say this would help reduce antisemitism by getting elected officials and faith leaders to publicly condemn antisemitic acts.
Supporters say educating the public about Jewish American contributions would build understanding and reduce prejudice in communities.
critics: Critics say the resolution provides no funding or specific requirements for how officials should educate the public about Jewish American contributions.
Critics say asking faith leaders and civil society leaders to counter antisemitism gives them a responsibility without clear guidance on what actions to take.

119-hres-426.one_liner: Set up House votes to cancel two federal rules about bank mergers and air pollution
provisions: Allows the House to vote on canceling a Treasury rule about reviewing bank merger applications
Allows the House to vote on canceling an EPA rule about classifying air pollution sources
Skips normal House procedures to speed up these votes

supporters: Supporters say this rule lets Congress vote quickly to block Treasury regulations on bank mergers that could hurt community banks.
Supporters say the rule allows lawmakers to stop EPA air pollution rules that could force businesses to follow stricter regulations.
Supporters say waiving normal House procedures speeds up votes to overturn federal agency rules that exceed their authority.
critics: Critics say skipping normal House procedures under rule XIII removes time for lawmakers to fully study the Treasury bank merger oversight rules before voting.
Critics say rushing votes on EPA air pollution source classifications could weaken protections for the 25 million Americans living near major pollution sources.
Critics say the rule bypasses standard debate processes that ensure Congress understands the impact of disapproving federal agency regulations.

119-hres-354.one_liner: Set up House votes to cancel five environmental rules
provisions: Sets up House votes on canceling five environmental rules from federal agencies
Would cancel a rule about motor vehicles in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
Would remove endangered species protections for a type of smelt fish in California
Would block California from using stricter pollution standards for trucks and cars

supporters: Supporters say these rules hurt trucking companies and auto manufacturers by forcing them to meet California's expensive emission standards nationwide.
Supporters say the Glen Canyon vehicle restrictions limit access for families who want to use motorized recreation in the park.
Supporters say removing the longfin smelt protections would help California farmers and water users get more reliable water supplies.
critics: Critics say blocking California's vehicle emission standards would increase air pollution that causes asthma and heart disease in communities near highways.
Critics say removing endangered species protection for the longfin smelt could push the fish species toward extinction.
Critics say canceling these emission rules would increase greenhouse gas pollution from trucks and cars when the country needs to cut climate pollution.

119-hres-405.one_liner: Allow House votes on three bills about police officer safety and weapons
provisions: Lets the House debate a bill requiring reports on attacks against police officers
Lets the House vote on a bill expanding where police can carry hidden guns
Lets the House consider a bill allowing federal police to buy their old service weapons

supporters: Supporters say requiring reports on attacks against police officers would help track violence against law enforcement and improve officer safety.
Supporters say expanding where police can carry hidden guns would better protect officers when they are off-duty.
Supporters say allowing federal police to buy their old service weapons would save taxpayer money and let officers keep guns they know how to use.
critics: Critics say requiring new reports on attacks against police officers would create more paperwork for the Attorney General without clear benefits.
Critics say expanding where police can carry hidden guns could increase the risk of accidents or misuse of weapons in public places.
Critics say allowing federal officers to buy their service weapons would put more guns into circulation among private citizens.

119-hres-489.one_liner: Set up House votes on four bills about DC voting, immigration, police, and fentanyl
provisions: Sets the rules for the House to debate and vote on a bill that would stop non-citizens from voting in Washington DC elections
Sets the rules for the House to vote on a bill that would make Washington DC follow federal immigration laws
Sets the rules for the House to vote on a bill that would let DC police unions negotiate about officer discipline again
Sets the rules for the House to vote on a bill that would change how fentanyl-related drugs are classified under federal law

supporters: Supporters say stopping non-citizens from voting in DC elections protects the right of US citizens to choose their representatives.
Supporters say requiring DC to follow federal immigration laws would help enforce immigration rules that Congress has already passed.
Supporters say letting police unions negotiate officer discipline again would give officers fair representation when facing punishment.
critics: Critics say blocking non-citizens from voting in DC takes away rights that DC voters gave to legal residents who pay taxes but cannot vote for Congress.
Critics say forcing DC to follow federal immigration laws removes local control over police priorities in a city that chose different policies.
Critics say bringing back police union talks about discipline would make it harder to fire officers who break rules or hurt people.

119-hres-481.one_liner: Condemn antisemitic attacks and reaffirm commitment to protecting religious freedom
provisions: Condemns the June 1, 2025 attack in Boulder, Colorado
Condemns attacks on Jewish people across the United States
Says Congress supports people's right to practice their religion without fear of violence

supporters: Supporters say this resolution condemns the June 1, 2025 Boulder attack and shows Congress stands against rising attacks on Jewish Americans.
Supporters say this reaffirms that Jewish people have the right to practice their religion without fear of violence.
critics: Critics say this resolution only makes statements but does not create new laws or funding to prevent future attacks on Jewish people.
Critics say Congress should focus on passing bills with real action instead of symbolic resolutions about the Boulder attack.

119-hres-458.one_liner: Allow the House to debate four bills about opioids, small business, and immigration
provisions: Allows the House to debate a bill that would reauthorize opioid prevention and treatment programs
Allows the House to debate a bill that would move Small Business Administration offices out of sanctuary cities
Allows the House to debate a bill that would require citizenship documents for SBA loan applications
Allows the House to debate a bill that would limit the number of small business lending companies

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows Congress to reauthorize opioid treatment programs that help people recover from drug addiction.
Supporters say this rule lets Congress move SBA offices out of sanctuary cities that don't cooperate with immigration enforcement.
Supporters say this rule allows Congress to require citizenship documents for SBA loans to ensure taxpayer money goes to legal applicants.
critics: Critics say this rule would let Congress move SBA offices away from immigrant communities that rely on small business support.
Critics say this rule allows Congress to create citizenship barriers that make it harder for immigrants to get SBA loans.
Critics say this rule lets Congress limit the number of small business lending companies, reducing access to business loans.

119-hres-488.one_liner: Condemn the antisemitic terrorist attack in Boulder, Colorado
provisions: Condemns the antisemitic terrorist attack in Boulder, Colorado
Expresses sympathy for the victims and affected community

supporters: Supporters say this resolution officially condemns the antisemitic terrorist attack in Boulder and shows Congress stands with Jewish communities.
Supporters say expressing sympathy for Boulder victims gives them important recognition from the federal government.
critics: Critics say this resolution only offers sympathy to Boulder victims but provides no money or real help.
Critics say Congress should pass laws to prevent antisemitic attacks instead of just condemning them after they happen.

119-hres-436.one_liner: Set rules for the House to vote on budget bill H.R. 1
provisions: Lets the House vote on budget reconciliation bill H.R. 1

Removes procedural barriers that could block the vote
Allows one attempt to send the bill back to committee

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to vote on budget reconciliation bill H.R. 1.
Supporters say the 2-hour debate between party leaders provides discussion time while moving the legislation forward.
critics: Critics say the 2-hour debate limit reduces time for lawmakers to discuss the reconciliation bill.
Critics say limiting attempts to send H.R. 1 back to committee to just one reduces review options.

119-hres-516.one_liner: Condemn June 2025 riots in Los Angeles and thank law enforcement
provisions: Condemns riots that happened in Los Angeles in June 2025
Thanks law enforcement agencies that responded to the riots
Thanks Immigration and Customs Enforcement for their work during the riots

supporters: Supporters say this resolution properly condemns the violent riots that damaged property and hurt people in Los Angeles in June 2025.
Supporters say thanking law enforcement agencies for their response recognizes officers who risked their safety to protect communities.
Supporters say including Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the thanks shows all federal agencies that helped restore order deserve recognition.
critics: Critics say calling the June 2025 events 'riots' unfairly labels what some view as legitimate protests against injustice.
Critics say thanking Immigration and Customs Enforcement could encourage more immigration enforcement during civil unrest.
Critics say this resolution takes sides in a complex situation without addressing underlying causes of the demonstrations.

119-hres-53.one_liner: Let the House vote on two bills about forest management and immigration detention

Lets the House vote on a bill that would require jailing non-citizens charged with theft

Supporters say this enables consideration of immigration enforcement measures that would require detention of non-citizens charged with theft.
Supporters say this provides structured debate rules so the House can efficiently consider both forest management and immigration enforcement bills.
critics: Critics say this limits debate time on complex environmental and immigration issues that affect millions of acres of federal land and thousands of people.
Critics say this combines unrelated forest management and immigration bills under one rule, preventing separate consideration of each issue.
Critics say the debate rules restrict the House's ability to fully discuss environmental impacts on tribal lands and detention requirements for non-citizens.

119-hres-519.one_liner: Condemn attacks on Minnesota lawmakers and call for unity

Honors Speaker Emerita Melissa Hortman and her husband Mark Hortman who were killed
Honors Senator John Hoffman and his wife Yvette Hoffman who were hurt
Honors police officers who responded and caught the suspect

supporters: Supporters say this resolution sends a clear message against political violence by condemning the June 14, 2025 attacks on Minnesota lawmakers.

Supporters say this recognizes the law enforcement officers who responded quickly and caught the suspect.
critics: Critics say this resolution does not provide funding for increased security measures to protect lawmakers from future attacks.
Critics say this does not create new policies or training programs to prevent political violence against elected officials.
Critics say this calls for unity and peaceful democracy but does not establish specific steps to identify or stop threats before they happen.

119-hres-499.one_liner: Set up a vote on canceling government spending the President wants to cut
provisions: Sets up a vote on whether to cancel certain government spending
The President sent Congress a list of spending cuts he wants on June 3, 2025
Uses a budget law that lets the President ask Congress to cancel spending
If approved, the government would spend less money on those programs

supporters: Supporters say this follows the proper legal process under the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 to review the President's June 3, 2025 spending cut requests.
Supporters say this would reduce government spending and help control the federal deficit by canceling programs the President identified as unnecessary.
Supporters say this ensures Congress has proper oversight over which specific programs would lose their funding rather than letting the President cut spending alone.
critics: Critics say the bill does not specify which government programs would lose funding from the President's June 3, 2025 spending cut list.
Critics say this could reduce funding for essential services like Medicare, education programs, or infrastructure projects that communities depend on.
Critics say this fast-track voting process might not give Congress enough time to review how the spending cuts would affect specific programs and the people they serve.

119-hres-5.one_liner: Set operating rules for the House of Representatives for 2025-2026

critics: Critics say requiring 9 majority party members to remove the Speaker makes it too hard to get rid of a bad Speaker who loses support.
Critics say closing the House Office of Diversity and Inclusion eliminates programs that help underrepresented groups get jobs and advance in Congress.

119-hres-530.one_liner: Allow the House to vote on military funding and immigration bills

119-hres-566.one_liner: Let the House accept or reject a Senate amendment to H.R. 1

119-hres-580.one_liner: Allow the House to debate and vote on defense funding and three digital currency bills

Lets the House vote on stopping the Federal Reserve from making a digital dollar

critics: Critics say this rule waives House rule requirements for considering certain resolutions.
Critics say this rule combines unrelated issues like defense spending and digital currency regulation in one procedural vote.
Critics say this rule allows votes on bills that would prohibit the Federal Reserve from offering certain products to individuals.

119-hres-672.one_liner: Set up votes on energy spending and canceling three federal land plans
provisions: Sets up a vote on energy and water spending for the year starting October 2025
Sets up a vote to cancel a federal land plan for the Miles City area
Sets up a vote to cancel a federal land plan for North Dakota
Sets up a vote to cancel a federal land plan for Central Yukon

supporters: Supporters say this allows Congress to vote on energy and water spending for fiscal year 2026.

critics: Critics say overturning the Bureau of Land Management plans could remove protections for wildlife and natural resources in Miles City, North Dakota, and Central Yukon.

119-s-1596.one_liner: Rename the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge in Texas to the Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge
provisions: Renames the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge in Texas to the Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge

119-s-146.one_liner: Ban posting intimate images without consent and require website removal

Critics say determining whether someone intended to cause harm when posting intimate images could be difficult for prosecutors and courts.
Critics say requiring platforms to remove content within 48 hours could lead to removal of legal content due to rushed decisions.

119-hres-590.one_liner: Approve cuts to government spending that the President requested

117-hconres-119.one_liner: Correct a law to include seven days of sick leave for railroad workers

119-sres-195.one_liner: Request information about human rights practices in El Salvador
provisions: Asks the government to provide information about human rights conditions in El Salvador
Uses a provision in foreign aid law that lets Congress request reports on human rights practices
Targets a country that receives U.S. foreign assistance

supporters: Supporters say this would provide Congress with reports on human rights conditions in El Salvador under section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act.
Supporters say this would give Congress information to review before making decisions about foreign aid to El Salvador.
Supporters say this would ensure Congress can oversee countries that receive U.S. assistance.
critics: Critics say this could harm diplomatic relations between the U.S. and El Salvador.
Critics say this might create duplicate reporting since the State Department already tracks human rights practices.
Critics say this could be viewed as U.S. interference in El Salvador's internal policies.

117-hjres-100.one_liner: Require railroads and unions to accept negotiated contracts without worker votes
provisions: Requires railroad companies and unions to accept work contracts they negotiated but workers have not approved
Applies to all contract negotiations that were finished before this bill becomes law
Ends ongoing labor disputes by making both sides accept these agreements

supporters: Supporters say this would end railroad labor disputes that have been ongoing by requiring both companies and unions to accept contracts they already negotiated.
Supporters say this would prevent railroad strikes that could stop freight and passenger trains across the country.
critics: Critics say this takes away workers' right to vote on contracts that affect their pay and working conditions.
Critics say this forces railroad workers to accept agreements they have not approved through their normal voting process.

119-sconres-7.one_liner: Set spending and borrowing limits for the federal government for 10 years
provisions: Sets how much the federal government can spend and borrow from 2025 through 2034
Tells congressional committees to write bills that change the deficit by specific amounts by March 7, 2025
Creates rules for how Congress handles budget bills over the next 10 years
Sets spending levels for Social Security and Postal Service administrative costs

supporters: Supporters say this resolution provides fiscal discipline by setting specific spending and deficit limits for the next 10 years through 2034.
Supporters say the reconciliation instructions will allow Congress to quickly pass deficit reduction bills by March 7, 2025 without Senate filibusters.
Supporters say establishing clear budget levels for Social Security and Postal Service administrative expenses will improve government financial planning.
critics: Critics say the 10-year spending limits could prevent Congress from responding to economic emergencies or unexpected needs between 2025 and 2034.
Critics say the reconciliation process bypasses normal Senate debate rules and could rush important budget changes through Congress by the March 7, 2025 deadline.
Critics say setting specific administrative spending levels for Social Security and the Postal Service could limit funding for services that help seniors and mail delivery.

117-hr-1799.one_liner: Extend the Paycheck Protection Program for small businesses through June 30, 2021
provisions: Extends the Paycheck Protection Program from March 31, 2021 to June 30, 2021
Lets small businesses apply for loans for three more months
Stops accepting new applications after June 1, 2021
Only processes applications already submitted during the final month

supporters: Supporters say small businesses need the three-month extension from March 31 to June 30 because many are still struggling to recover from COVID-19 shutdowns.
Supporters say the June 1st application deadline gives businesses one more month to apply while allowing the Small Business Administration time to process existing applications through June 30th.
critics: Critics say extending the program for three more months will add billions more to federal spending when the economy is already recovering.
Critics say the June 1st cutoff for new applications creates confusion and may leave some businesses unable to apply during the final month.

117-hr-1652.one_liner: Add new funding sources to the Crime Victims Fund from legal deals
provisions: Sends money from legal deals with companies that broke laws to the Crime Victims Fund instead of the general Treasury
Increases the percentage used to calculate state grants from 60% to 75% of what states paid crime victims the year before
Lets states skip requiring local matching funds during pandemics and allows states to set their own waiver rules

supporters: Supporters say this would send money from corporate legal settlements directly to help crime victims instead of going to the general Treasury.
Supporters say increasing the grant calculation from 60% to 75% means states get more federal money to pay crime victims.
Supporters say allowing states to waive matching requirements during pandemics helps victims when state budgets are tight.
critics: Critics say redirecting corporate settlement money from the Treasury to the Crime Victims Fund takes away funding from other federal programs.
Critics say increasing the grant percentage from 60% to 75% increases federal spending on victim compensation.
Critics say letting states set their own waiver policies could reduce local investment in victim services.

117-hr-1437.one_liner: Require weather agency to update rainfall predictions and create guidance
provisions: Requires the weather agency to update rainfall predictions for the US every 5 years
Makes rainfall prediction studies available to the public
Orders a study on how to improve rainfall predictions
Creates guidance for government agencies on rainfall predictions

supporters: Supporters say this bill would help communities prepare for floods and droughts by requiring NOAA to update rainfall predictions every 5 years with current data.
Supporters say making rainfall studies available to the public would help local governments and businesses plan better for weather risks.
Supporters say the guidance for government agencies would create consistent standards for rainfall predictions across the country.
critics: Critics say this bill would waste taxpayer money on studies that NOAA already conducts as part of its regular work.
Critics say the requirement for updates every 5 years would create unnecessary paperwork and costs for the weather agency.
Critics say federal agencies should not tell state and local governments how to handle their own weather planning through mandatory guidance.

117-hr-1868.one_liner: Stop automatic cuts to Medicare and other health programs
provisions: Lets the government spend pandemic aid money without cutting other programs
Protects Medicare from automatic spending cuts until December 31, 2021
Stops unemployment payments from counting when deciding who qualifies for Medicaid
Sets how much rural health clinics get paid if they joined Medicare during the pandemic
Keeps higher Medicaid payments for public hospitals in California

supporters: Supporters say this stops automatic Medicare cuts that would reduce payments to doctors and hospitals until December 31, 2021.
Supporters say this helps rural health clinics that joined Medicare during the pandemic get proper payments for treating patients.
Supporters say this prevents unemployment money from counting against people who want Medicaid coverage.
critics: Critics say this lets the government spend pandemic aid money without cutting other programs, adding to the national debt.
Critics say this turns off automatic spending controls that help limit government spending.
Critics say this gives California public hospitals special higher Medicaid payments that other states don't get.

117-hr-2471.one_liner: Update how the U.S. tracks its work in Haiti
provisions: Cancels rules about reporting on Haiti earthquake recovery
Requires the State Department to focus on protecting human rights in Haiti
Requires the State Department to protect journalists and press freedom in Haiti
Requires the State Department to fight corruption in Haiti
Creates a plan for helping Haiti after disasters and the pandemic

supporters: Supporters say this would protect journalists in Haiti by requiring the State Department to focus on press freedom.
Supporters say this would fight corruption in Haiti through new State Department anti-corruption efforts.
Supporters say this would help Haiti recover from disasters and the pandemic by creating a new recovery plan.
critics: Critics say this would eliminate important oversight by canceling existing earthquake recovery reporting rules.
Critics say this would burden the State Department with new human rights and corruption requirements without clear funding.
Critics say this would create more bureaucracy instead of direct aid to Haiti.

117-hr-3233.one_liner: Create a commission to investigate the January 6 attack on the Capitol
provisions: Creates a commission to investigate the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol
Gives the commission power to force people to testify and provide documents
Requires the commission to hold public hearings and write public reports
The commission will study what caused the attack and how to prevent similar attacks
The commission will recommend ways to improve Capitol security

supporters: Supporters say the commission's power to force people to testify and provide documents will help uncover the full truth about the January 6 attack.
Supporters say public hearings and reports will give Americans transparency about what caused the attack on the Capitol.
Supporters say the commission's security recommendations could prevent future attacks on government buildings.
critics: Critics say the commission's power to force testimony and seize documents could violate people's privacy rights.
Critics say public hearings about January 6 will divide the country further instead of helping it heal.
Critics say the commission duplicates work already done by other investigations of the Capitol attack.

117-hr-335.one_liner: Let a military officer become Secretary of Defense after 4 years instead of 7
provisions: Changes the waiting period from 7 years to 4 years for one Secretary of Defense appointment
Only applies to the first person picked for the job after January 20, 2021
Lets a former military officer take the job sooner than normal rules allow

supporters: Supporters say this would let more qualified former military officers serve as Secretary of Defense by cutting the waiting time from 7 years to 4 years.
Supporters say the 4-year wait time still keeps enough separation between military and civilian leadership.
Supporters say this only affects one appointment after January 20, 2021, so it won't change the rules for future picks.
critics: Critics say cutting the waiting period from 7 years to 4 years weakens the rule that keeps civilian control over the military.
Critics say letting former military officers take the job sooner could blur the line between military and civilian leadership.
Critics say this sets a bad example that Congress can change the 7-year rule whenever they want for political reasons.

117-hr-3237.one_liner: Give $1.9 billion to fix Capitol damage and boost security after January 6th attack
provisions: Gives $1.9 billion in emergency money to respond to the January 6th Capitol attack
Pays to fix damage to Capitol buildings from the attack
Funds security upgrades at the Capitol
Pays back agencies for costs of responding to the attack
Creates a quick reaction force in the D.C. National Guard to help Capitol Police
Requires Capitol Police officers who talk to the public to wear body cameras
Funds COVID-related expenses for Congress

supporters: Supporters say the $1.9 billion is needed to fix damage to Capitol buildings and pay for security upgrades after the January 6th attack.
Supporters say requiring Capitol Police officers to wear body cameras when talking to the public will make officers more accountable.
Supporters say creating a quick reaction force in the D.C. National Guard will help protect Congress if another attack happens.
critics: Critics say the $1.9 billion cost is too high and bypasses normal budget rules by using the emergency spending label.
Critics say funding COVID expenses for Congress is not related to the January 6th attack and should not be in this bill.
Critics say the bill pays back agencies for costs they already spent responding to the attack instead of focusing only on future security needs.

117-hr-3076.one_liner: Reform postal service finances and worker benefits
provisions: Creates a health insurance program for postal workers and retirees
Stops the postal service from having to prepay future retiree health costs
Lets the postal service offer services besides mail delivery
Makes the postal service post online data about mail delivery performance

supporters: Supporters say the bill creates a dedicated Postal Service Health Benefits Program for postal workers and retirees, separate from other federal employee health plans.
Supporters say ending the annual prepayment requirement for future retiree health benefits would remove a major financial burden from USPS operations.
Supporters say allowing USPS to partner with state, local, and tribal governments to provide non-postal services would create new revenue sources.
critics: Critics say creating a separate health program for postal workers creates unequal treatment compared to other federal employees who remain in existing plans.
Critics say removing the prepayment requirement for retiree health benefits could leave future postal retirees without guaranteed healthcare funding.
Critics say expanding USPS into non-postal services moves the agency beyond its core mission of mail delivery.

117-hr-2617.one_liner: Require government agencies to include more details in performance reports
provisions: Government agencies must give more details about how they plan to reach their goals
Agencies must describe the staff, training, technology, and other resources they need
Changes which government office is responsible for writing these reports

supporters: Supporters say this will force agencies to plan ahead for the staff, training, and technology they need to meet their goals instead of just setting goals without a real plan.
Supporters say moving this job to the chief performance improvement office means someone focused on getting results will write these reports instead of human resources staff.
Supporters say requiring agencies to describe their technology upgrades and stakeholder feedback will help government programs work better for the people they serve.
critics: Critics say this adds detailed reporting requirements about human capital, training, data, and technology systems that will take staff time away from actually doing their jobs.
Critics say requiring agencies to describe technology modernization investments and system upgrades in reports creates more government paperwork without proof it will improve anything.
Critics say moving this responsibility from chief human capital offices to chief performance improvement offices creates unnecessary reorganization and confusion about who does what.

117-hr-350.one_liner: Create new offices to track and investigate domestic terrorism
provisions: Creates new domestic terrorism offices in the Department of Homeland Security, Department of Justice, and FBI
Requires these three agencies to write reports on domestic terrorism incidents
Makes the agencies review their training programs for local police
Creates a team to find white supremacists in the military and federal law enforcement
Puts FBI agents in charge of hate crimes at each FBI office
Lets these offices monitor, investigate, and prosecute domestic terrorism cases

supporters: Supporters say this creates specialized offices in the Department of Homeland Security, Department of Justice, and FBI to better track and stop domestic terrorism threats.
Supporters say the team to find white supremacists in military and federal law enforcement protects the public from officers who might abuse their power.
Supporters say putting FBI agents in charge of hate crimes at each field office will improve investigations of attacks on minority groups.
critics: Critics say the new powers to monitor and investigate domestic terrorism could target peaceful political groups and violate free speech rights.
Critics say creating new offices in three federal agencies will increase government spending without clear limits on the cost.
Critics say the broad authority to investigate domestic terrorism could be misused against protesters or political opponents who are not actual terrorists.

117-hr-3967.one_liner: Expand VA healthcare and benefits for veterans exposed to toxic substances during service
provisions: Lets veterans get VA healthcare if they were exposed to toxic substances during military service
Creates committees within the VA to decide which health problems count as service-related
Makes it easier for veterans to prove their health problems are connected to military service
Requires the VA to give medical exams to veterans who file disability claims related to toxic exposure
Requires the VA to ask veterans about toxic exposure during routine health screenings
Creates registries to track veterans exposed to specific toxic chemicals

supporters: Supporters say this gives VA healthcare access to veterans who participated in toxic exposure risk activities or served in specified contaminated locations.
Supporters say the mandatory medical exams for veterans filing toxic exposure disability claims will help establish service connection when evidence is insufficient.
Supporters say the required toxic exposure screening questionnaires during routine VA care will help identify veterans who may not know about their exposures.
critics: Critics say the broad eligibility criteria for veterans exposed to toxic substances during any military service could include veterans without clear connection to specific contaminated locations.
Critics say the new Formal Advisory Committee on Toxic Exposure and Science Review Board add additional review layers before veterans can get presumptive service connection decisions.
Critics say requiring VA medical exams for all disability claims related to toxic exposure when evidence is insufficient creates new mandatory procedures that could delay claim processing.

117-hr-3684.one_liner: Fund highways, bridges, and transit systems through 2026
provisions: Keeps current funding for highways, buses, and safety programs through 2022
Sets new funding for roads, bridges, and trains from 2023 to 2026
Creates a program to fix bridges in rural areas
Requires American-made materials for highway and transit projects
Adds new safety rules for all types of transportation
Tests charging drivers by the mile instead of gas taxes to fund road repairs

supporters: Supporters say the rural bridge program would fix dangerous bridges in small communities that cannot afford repairs on their own.
Supporters say the Buy America requirements would create jobs for American workers in steel, concrete, and manufacturing.
Supporters say the per-mile fee pilot would make drivers who use roads more pay more, which is fairer than gas taxes.
critics: Critics say the Buy America requirements would increase costs for highway and transit projects by limiting competition.
Critics say the per-mile fee pilot would burden rural drivers who must travel long distances for work and services.
Critics say the new safety rules would force trucking and transit companies to spend money on compliance instead of operations.

117-hr-4346.one_liner: Fund Congress and related offices for the year starting October 2021
provisions: Funds House of Representatives operations for the year starting October 2021
Funds Capitol Police for the year starting October 2021
Funds Congressional Budget Office for the year starting October 2021
Funds Architect of Capitol for the year starting October 2021
Funds Library of Congress for the year starting October 2021
Funds Government Accountability Office for the year starting October 2021
Sets rules for how these funds can be used

supporters: Supporters say funding the Capitol Police protects lawmakers and staff after security threats like the January 6th attack on the Capitol.
Supporters say the Library of Congress and Government Accountability Office provide research and oversight services that help Congress make informed decisions for the public.
Supporters say these funds keep basic House operations running so representatives can serve their districts and pass laws.
critics: Critics say Congress should not increase its own funding while many Americans struggle with rising costs and inflation.
Critics say the Government Accountability Office already has enough money and adding more wastes taxpayer dollars on bureaucracy.
Critics say funding should go to border security or military instead of congressional office buildings and staff.

117-hr-3755.one_liner: Block state and local laws that restrict abortion services
provisions: Stops governments from banning abortion before the baby could survive outside the womb
Stops governments from banning abortion when the mother's life or health is at risk
Stops governments from requiring doctors to do unnecessary medical procedures before abortions
Stops governments from requiring patients to visit the doctor in person before abortion medication
Stops governments from requiring doctors to give patients wrong medical information about abortion
Lets the Justice Department, patients, and doctors sue states that break these rules
Applies to laws that states passed before and after this bill becomes law

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects women when their life or health is at risk by stopping states from banning abortion after fetal viability in those cases.
Supporters say this stops states from requiring doctors to give patients wrong medical information about abortion.
Supporters say this removes barriers like unnecessary medical procedures and required in-person visits that delay abortion care.
critics: Critics say this bill overrides state laws by applying to laws that states passed before and after this bill becomes law.
Critics say this removes state requirements for in-person visits before abortion medication and other safety measures.
Critics say this lets the Justice Department sue states over their abortion laws, taking away states' rights to regulate medical procedures.

117-hr-4350.one_liner: Fund the military and set troop numbers for the year starting October 2021
provisions: Gives money to the Defense Department to pay troops and run military programs for the year starting October 2021
Lets the military buy weapons, aircraft, missiles, and ammunition
Sets how many people can serve in the Army, Navy, Air Force, and other military branches
Funds military research to develop new technology and equipment
Covers military training programs and base operations

supporters: Supporters say this bill makes sure troops get paid and military programs can run starting in October 2021.
Supporters say the money for research helps develop new technology to protect soldiers and keep America safe.
Supporters say setting how many people can serve in each military branch ensures the country has enough troops for defense.
critics: Critics say the Defense Department funding takes money away from schools, roads, and healthcare that Americans need.
Critics say buying weapons, aircraft, and missiles wastes money on equipment the military doesn't need.
Critics say the military personnel limits allow too many people in the armed forces and cost too much.

117-hr-4521.one_liner: Create a government research program for engineering biology
provisions: Creates a new research program across government agencies to study engineering biology
Gives money to research centers, scientists, and training programs
Requires eight agencies including NASA and the EPA to work together on the research
Makes agencies send reports to Congress every three years through 2028
Has the National Science Foundation study safety and ethics questions about the research
Encourages partnerships between big universities and smaller colleges

supporters: Supporters say this creates research jobs and training programs by funding centers across eight agencies including NASA and the EPA.
Supporters say this helps smaller colleges access research opportunities through required partnerships with large universities.
Supporters say this studies safety and ethics through the National Science Foundation review of these issues.
critics: Critics say this costs taxpayer money to fund research centers and training programs across eight government agencies.
Critics say this adds reporting requirements by making agencies send reports to Congress every three years through 2028.
Critics say this overlaps with research programs that already exist at these agencies.

117-hr-5305.one_liner: Fund the government through December 2021 and suspend the debt limit
provisions: Funds federal agencies through December 3, 2021 to prevent a government shutdown
Keeps funding at 2021 levels while Congress writes the 2022 budget
Suspends the debt limit through December 16, 2022
Gives extra money for natural disaster relief and helping Afghan evacuees
Extends flood insurance and food assistance programs that were set to expire

supporters: Supporters say this bill prevents a government shutdown on October 1, 2021 by funding federal agencies through December 3, 2021.
Supporters say suspending the debt limit through December 16, 2022 prevents the U.S. from defaulting on its debts and protects the economy.
Supporters say the extra money for natural disaster relief and Afghan evacuees helps people who lost their homes and need emergency aid.
critics: Critics say suspending the debt limit through December 16, 2022 lets the government borrow more money without setting a clear spending limit.
Critics say funding agencies at 2021 levels through December 3, 2021 does not let Congress set new budget priorities for 2022.
Critics say this bill just delays budget decisions for two months instead of solving the funding problem.

117-hr-5376.one_liner: Fund education and healthcare programs while raising taxes
provisions: Makes community college free for up to 6 semesters
Makes child care free for children under 6 years old
Makes preschool free for all children
Gives workers up to 12 weeks of paid family and medical leave
Expands Medicare to cover dental, hearing, and vision care
Raises taxes on corporations and people making over $400,000 per year
Charges oil and gas companies a fee for methane pollution

supporters: Supporters say the free community college program would help millions of students get job training without debt.
Supporters say free child care for children under 6 and 12 weeks of paid leave would help working parents stay in jobs.
Supporters say expanding Medicare to cover dental, hearing, and vision care would help seniors get needed health services.
critics: Critics say the free community college and child care programs would cost taxpayers hundreds of billions of dollars.
Critics say raising taxes on corporations and people making over $400,000 would hurt business growth and job creation.
Critics say the methane fees on oil and gas companies would raise energy costs for families.

117-hr-4373.one_liner: Fund State Department and international aid programs
provisions: Provides money for State Department operations and embassies overseas
Funds foreign aid programs through USAID
Pays for U.S. membership in international organizations
Supports democracy and human rights programs in other countries

supporters: Supporters say this funds State Department embassies and operations that protect American citizens traveling and working overseas.
Supporters say USAID foreign aid programs build partnerships with other countries that help prevent costly wars.
Supporters say democracy and human rights programs spread American values that make the world safer for trade and travel.
critics: Critics say this spends taxpayer money on foreign aid programs while Americans face high costs and problems at home.
Critics say membership fees for international organizations drain resources that could help American communities instead.
Critics say democracy programs in other countries waste money that should go to American schools and roads.

provisions: Stops imports of Russian oil, gas, and other energy products
Lets the President waive this ban for national security reasons if Congress agrees
Tells trade officials to consider removing Russia from the World Trade Organization
Expands sanctions to target people who commit serious human rights abuses
Lets the President sanction corrupt foreign government officials
Lets the President sanction people who support these activities

supporters: Supporters say stopping imports of Russian oil and gas would cut off funding that Russia uses for military actions.
Supporters say the expanded sanctions would target people who commit serious human rights abuses, holding more violators accountable than current law.
Supporters say removing Russia from the World Trade Organization would isolate them from global trade benefits.
critics: Critics say stopping Russian oil imports could raise gas prices for American drivers and businesses.
Critics say requiring Congressional approval for the President's waiver could delay responses to energy emergencies.
Critics say lowering the sanctions standard from 'gross' to 'serious' human rights violations could target too many people.

117-hr-6617.one_liner: Extend government funding through March 11, 2022 to prevent shutdown
provisions: Keeps government agencies open through March 11, 2022
Prevents government workers from being sent home without pay
Funds most federal programs at 2021 spending levels
Provides extra money for building new military submarines
Extends the rule keeping fentanyl-related drugs illegal until later in 2022
Continues collecting special fees from people convicted of sex trafficking

supporters: Supporters say this bill prevents government workers from being sent home without pay and keeps essential services running through March 11, 2022.
Supporters say the extra money for military submarines protects national security.
Supporters say extending the rule that keeps fentanyl-related drugs illegal until later in 2022 saves lives.
critics: Critics say funding programs at 2021 levels does not account for rising costs or new needs in 2022.
Critics say the March 11 deadline just pushes the same budget fight to next month.
Critics say the extra submarine funding increases military spending without full budget review.

117-hr-6833.one_liner: Set a $35 monthly cap on insulin costs for Medicare and private insurance
provisions: Caps insulin costs at $35 per month for all people with Medicare in 2023
Starting in 2024, caps insulin costs at $35 per month for people with Medicare who have not hit their yearly out-of-pocket limit
Caps insulin costs for people with private insurance at either $35 per month or 25% of the plan's price, whichever is less
Replaces a voluntary Medicare program ending in 2025 with these permanent caps

supporters: Supporters say this would save money for the 3.3 million Medicare beneficiaries who use insulin by capping their monthly costs at $35 starting in 2023.
Supporters say this would help people with private insurance by limiting their monthly insulin costs to either $35 or 25% of their plan's negotiated price, whichever is less.
Supporters say this would make permanent the insulin savings that are currently only available through a voluntary Medicare program that ends in 2025.
critics: Critics say the $35 Medicare cap will increase costs for taxpayers and other Medicare beneficiaries because the program will have to cover the difference between the cap and actual insulin prices.
Critics say private insurance premiums could go up for everyone to cover the cost of the $35 monthly caps, as insurers pass along these costs to all customers.
Critics say the 25% minimum cost-sharing requirement for private insurance means some people could end up paying more than $35 per month if their plan's negotiated price is high.

provisions: Keeps government funded until February 18, 2022 or until the regular budget passes
Prevents a government shutdown that would happen on December 3, 2021
Funds most programs at 2021 spending levels
Provides money to help people evacuated from Afghanistan
Extends the rule that lets drug agents treat fentanyl-like drugs as illegal
Keeps the pay freeze for top government officials

supporters: Supporters say this prevents a government shutdown on December 3, 2021 that would stop essential services and hurt federal workers.
Supporters say this provides needed money to help people evacuated from Afghanistan who need housing and services.
Supporters say extending the fentanyl scheduling rule until February 18, 2022 keeps dangerous drugs off the streets.
critics: Critics say funding programs at 2021 levels until February 18, 2022 wastes money by continuing old spending without congressional review of what programs still need funding.
Critics say extending the deadline to February 18, 2022 lets Congress avoid making hard budget choices for another two and a half months.
Critics say the pay freeze for senior officials hurts the government's ability to hire good leaders.

117-hr-5746.one_liner: Extend NASA's authority to lease its property through 2031
provisions: Lets NASA continue leasing its non-excess real property through 2031
Covers both real property and related personal property
Continues an existing authority that would otherwise expire

supporters: Supporters say this lets NASA earn money from leasing its non-excess real property through 2031 to help fund space programs.
Supporters say the extension covers both buildings and related equipment, giving NASA more leasing options.
Supporters say this continues an existing authority that would expire without this bill.
critics: Critics say extending NASA's leasing authority through 2031 is too long without Congressional review.
Critics say this lets private companies profit from NASA property and equipment that taxpayers funded.
Critics say the bill extends leasing of non-excess property without checking if rental terms are fair to taxpayers.

117-hr-7.one_liner: Strengthen rules against paying women less than men for the same work
provisions: Limits reasons companies can give for paying women less than men for the same job
Bans companies from stopping workers from talking about their pay
Increases fines for companies that break equal pay rules
Creates training programs to help women negotiate better pay
Requires companies to report worker pay by gender and race
Protects workers from punishment if they complain about unequal pay

supporters: Supporters say this would help close the gender pay gap by limiting certain justifications companies can use to pay women less for the same work.
Supporters say allowing workers to discuss their wages would help them discover pay gaps that exist in their workplace.
Supporters say the negotiation training programs for women and girls would help them ask for equal pay more effectively.
critics: Critics say the increased fines and new reporting requirements would raise costs for businesses of all sizes.
Critics say limiting the reasons companies can give for pay differences could prevent them from rewarding workers based on skills, experience, or performance.
Critics say requiring companies to report worker pay by gender and race would create burdensome paperwork that takes time away from running their business.

117-hr-7691.one_liner: Send $40.1 billion to help Ukraine respond to Russia's invasion
provisions: Gives $40.1 billion to US agencies to help Ukraine respond to Russia's invasion in 2022
Funds military equipment for Ukraine
Funds assistance for Ukrainian refugees
Funds food aid for Ukraine
Funds money for Ukraine's economy
Gives money to Justice, Defense, State, and other departments to run Ukraine aid programs

supporters: Supporters say the $40.1 billion gives Ukraine the military equipment it needs to defend against Russia's invasion.
Supporters say this funding provides food aid and refugee assistance for millions of Ukrainians forced from their homes by the war.
Supporters say the economic assistance helps Ukraine's government keep running basic services during the Russian attack.
critics: Critics say the $40.1 billion cost is too much for American taxpayers when the US faces high inflation and other domestic problems.
Critics say this money should go to American priorities like border security or infrastructure instead of foreign aid.
Critics say sending military equipment to Ukraine could escalate the conflict and risk drawing America into a larger war with Russia.

117-hr-7776.one_liner: Lets the Army Corps of Engineers build water and flood control projects
provisions: Lets the Army Corps of Engineers carry out water resources development projects
Covers water supply, wastewater systems, flood control, and navigation projects
Includes ecosystem restoration and shoreline restoration work
Changes how inactive water projects are canceled

supporters: Supporters say this bill would help protect communities from flooding by letting the Army Corps build flood control projects.
Supporters say the water supply and wastewater system projects would provide clean water to more Americans.
Supporters say the new process for canceling inactive projects would save taxpayer money by getting rid of old projects that aren't being built.
critics: Critics say Army Corps water projects cost billions of dollars that add to federal spending.
Critics say some Corps navigation and flood control projects harm wetlands and fish habitats.
Critics say these federal water projects should be handled by states and local governments instead.

117-s-1301.one_liner: Require the health department to publish physical activity guidelines every 10 years
provisions: Requires the health department to publish physical activity guidelines every 10 years
Bases the guidelines on current science and medical research
Requires the health department to publish reports between each set of guidelines
Reports must include proven ways to increase physical activity
Reports must highlight ongoing physical activity problems

supporters: Supporters say the 10-year requirement ensures Americans get physical activity advice based on the newest science and medical research.
Supporters say the reports between guidelines will help doctors and health workers use proven methods to get more people active.
Supporters say tracking ongoing physical activity problems through regular reports will help identify which groups need more help.
critics: Critics say requiring HHS to publish reports every few years between the 10-year guidelines creates extra government spending without clear benefits.
Critics say medical organizations and private health groups can provide physical activity advice without requiring federal guidelines every 10 years.
Critics say the bill does not specify how much the new reporting requirements will cost taxpayers.

117-s-1260.one_liner: Create a technology research office and fund innovation programs
provisions: Creates a new technology research office within the National Science Foundation
Funds research in artificial intelligence, computing, and manufacturing
Sets up regional technology centers across the country
Gives grants to help regions develop technology plans
Keeps funding a manufacturing program through 2026 that helps companies make products in America
Creates a program to fix supply chain problems in key industries

supporters: Supporters say the new technology research office would help America compete with China in artificial intelligence and computing by funding research that leads to American-made products.
Supporters say the regional technology hubs would create jobs and economic development in areas outside Silicon Valley by giving grants to help communities develop their own technology plans.
Supporters say the supply chain program would fix vulnerabilities in key industries that were exposed during the COVID-19 pandemic when America couldn't get critical supplies.
critics: Critics say creating a new technology office within the National Science Foundation moves the agency away from basic research toward picking winners and losers in private industry.
Critics say the regional technology hubs would use taxpayer money to subsidize private companies that should fund their own research and development.
Critics say extending the Manufacturing USA Program through 2026 continues government spending on programs that duplicate what private companies already do.

117-s-1251.one_liner: Create a USDA program to help farmers sell carbon credits
provisions: Creates a USDA certification program for companies that help farmers with carbon credits
Publishes rules companies must follow to get certified
Creates an advisory council to make recommendations about the program
Takes money from the American Rescue Plan Act to fund this program
Lets farmers, ranchers, and forest owners access carbon credit markets

supporters: Supporters say this helps farmers, ranchers, and forest owners make money by selling carbon credits from their environmental practices.
Supporters say the USDA certification program gives farmers trusted companies to help them with carbon credit paperwork and rules.
Supporters say this removes barriers that kept agricultural businesses out of environmental credit markets.
critics: Critics say taking money from the American Rescue Plan Act shifts funds away from COVID-19 recovery programs.
Critics say the new USDA certification program creates more government rules and paperwork for businesses.
Critics say the advisory council and certification requirements add administrative costs to the program.

117-hres-24.one_liner: Impeach President Trump and remove him from office for inciting insurrection
provisions: Impeaches President Trump for high crimes and misdemeanors
Charges Trump with inciting the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol
Says Trump made false claims about election fraud before January 6
Says Trump encouraged a crowd that broke into the Capitol building
Says Trump threatened Georgia's Secretary of State about election results
Would remove Trump from office if passed by the Senate
Would bar Trump from holding federal office in the future

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would hold Trump accountable for inciting the January 6, 2021 attack that broke into the Capitol building and killed a law enforcement officer.
Supporters say barring Trump from holding federal office in the future would protect American democracy from someone who threatened Georgia's Secretary of State about election results.
Supporters say Trump's false claims about election fraud and his speech to the crowd before they attacked the Capitol warrant impeachment for high crimes and misdemeanors.
critics: Critics say impeaching a president who is already leaving office divides the country and wastes Congress's time instead of focusing on important issues.
Critics say Trump's speech before January 6 was protected by the First Amendment and did not directly tell people to break into the Capitol building.
Critics say the impeachment process is being rushed without proper investigation into what actually happened during the January 6 events.

117-s-1.one_liner: Expand voter registration and voting access while adding campaign finance and ethics rules
provisions: Makes all states automatically register people to vote when they get driver's licenses
Lets people register to vote on election day in all states
Requires all states to offer early voting and mail-in voting
Makes states use independent groups instead of politicians to draw congressional district maps
Requires campaigns to report more details about who gives them money
Stops House members from sitting on company boards while in office
Makes presidential candidates release 10 years of tax returns

supporters: Supporters say automatic voter registration when getting driver's licenses would add millions of eligible citizens to voter rolls who currently can't vote because they forgot to register.
Supporters say requiring all states to offer early voting and mail-in voting would help working people and parents who can't get to polls on election day.
Supporters say independent redistricting commissions would stop politicians from drawing district maps that favor their own party.
critics: Critics say automatic voter registration could put non-citizens and ineligible people on voter rolls because DMV workers don't check citizenship status.
Critics say forcing all states to allow mail-in voting takes away states' rights to run their own elections and could increase voter fraud.
Critics say requiring presidential candidates to release 10 years of tax returns is a political attack designed to hurt certain candidates.

117-s-3373.one_liner: Move Iraq and Afghanistan education grants into the Pell Grant program
provisions: Moves the Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant program into the Pell Grant program
Changes how education benefits for families of service members killed in Iraq or Afghanistan are given out

supporters: Supporters say moving the Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant into the Pell Grant program would make it easier for Gold Star families to get education benefits through one system.
Supporters say this would streamline the process for families of service members killed in Iraq or Afghanistan to access their education aid.
critics: Critics say folding the Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant into the general Pell Grant program could reduce recognition of the special sacrifice made by families of service members killed in those wars.
Critics say this change might create delays or confusion for Gold Star families trying to get their education benefits.

117-s-2938.one_liner: Name a federal courthouse in Tallahassee after Joseph Woodrow Hatchett
provisions: Names the Federal Building and United States Courthouse at 111 North Adams Street in Tallahassee, Florida as the Joseph Woodrow Hatchett United States Courthouse and Federal Building

supporters: Supporters say this honors Joseph Woodrow Hatchett, who was the first African American to serve on the Florida Supreme Court and broke racial barriers in the federal courts.
Supporters say this recognizes his 15 years of service as a federal appeals court judge and costs taxpayers very little since it only requires new building signs.
critics: Critics say the cost of replacing all building signage and updating official records wastes taxpayer money that could go to court operations.
Critics say the naming process did not include enough public input from Tallahassee residents about honoring Judge Hatchett at this specific building.

117-s-1605.one_liner: Make the Pulse Memorial in Orlando a national memorial
provisions: Makes the Pulse Memorial in Orlando a national memorial

supporters: Supporters say this would honor the 49 people killed in the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting by making their memorial a national site.
Supporters say making the Orlando memorial a national memorial would give it the same federal status as other important American sites.
critics: Critics say turning the Orlando memorial into a national memorial could require federal tax money to maintain it.
Critics say this takes control of the memorial away from Orlando and gives it to the federal government.

117-s-2747.one_liner: Expand voter registration and voting access while changing campaign finance rules
provisions: Requires states to offer automatic voter registration and same-day registration
Requires states to offer vote-by-mail and early voting, makes Election Day a federal holiday
Lets people with felony convictions vote unless they are currently serving their sentence
Requires states to audit federal elections and makes interfering with voter registration a federal crime
Sets new rules for drawing congressional districts and bans redrawing them mid-decade
Bans foreign campaign spending, requires more reporting of campaign money, and creates a public campaign funding option

supporters: Supporters say automatic voter registration and same-day registration would make it easier for eligible citizens to vote in federal elections.
Supporters say banning foreign campaign spending and requiring more disclosure of campaign money would reduce outside influence on American elections.
Supporters say requiring states to offer early voting and vote-by-mail would give working people more ways to cast their ballots.
critics: Critics say requiring states to offer automatic registration, early voting, and vote-by-mail would force states to spend money changing their current election systems.
Critics say federal rules for drawing congressional districts would take away states' control over their own redistricting process.
Critics say making Election Day a federal holiday would cost businesses and taxpayers money for another paid day off.

117-s-2093.one_liner: Expand voter access and add new rules for campaigns and government officials
provisions: Lets people register to vote automatically and on election day and limits removing them from voter lists
Requires all states to allow voting by mail and early voting
Creates independent groups instead of politicians to draw congressional district maps
Shares intelligence information with states and improves cybersecurity to protect election systems
Bans foreign money in campaigns and requires more disclosure of campaign donors and spending
Requires Supreme Court justices to follow a code of conduct and presidents to release 10 years of tax returns

supporters: Supporters say automatic voter registration and same-day registration would make it easier for millions of Americans to vote who currently face barriers.
Supporters say independent redistricting commissions would stop politicians from drawing unfair congressional district maps to help their own party win elections.
Supporters say requiring disclosure of campaign donors and spending would let voters see who is funding political ads and candidates.
critics: Critics say the bill forces states to change their election systems and violates the Constitution's rule that states run their own elections.
Critics say automatic voter registration and mail voting in all states could lead to more voter fraud and registration mistakes.
Critics say creating independent redistricting commissions takes redistricting power away from elected officials chosen by voters.

117-s-4822.one_liner: Require more disclosure of campaign spending and block foreign money in elections
provisions: Blocks non-citizens from spending money on web political ads and federal judge nomination campaigns
Makes it illegal for non-citizens to give money to ballot measure campaigns
Requires organizations to report campaign spending over $10,000 within 24 hours
Forces political ads to show which donors gave the most money to that organization in the last year
Makes hiding non-citizen election contributions through fake companies a crime with up to 5 years in prison
Orders a government watchdog to study foreign money in federal elections every 4 years

supporters: Supporters say the 24-hour reporting rule for spending over $10,000 gives voters quick access to who funds campaigns during elections
Supporters say blocking non-citizens from web political ads and ballot measure campaigns stops foreign interference in American elections
Supporters say requiring ads to show top donors helps voters know which groups or companies are behind political messages
