critics: Critics say the 24-hour reporting deadline for spending over $10,000 creates paperwork burdens that smaller organizations cannot handle as easily as large groups
Critics say forcing political ads to name top donors could expose supporters to harassment and reduce political participation
Critics say the broad restrictions on non-citizens could affect legal immigrants and businesses with foreign ownership who want to participate in ballot measure campaigns

117-s-4008.one_liner: Fund grants for restaurants and other businesses hurt by COVID-19
provisions: Gives grants to restaurants to keep their operations running
Gives grants to gyms, minor league sports teams, and live event businesses
Gives grants to businesses near border crossings
Gives grants to transportation companies
Requires the government to track how businesses spend the grant money
Limits each business to grants from only one program

supporters: Supporters say this would help restaurants, gyms, minor league sports teams, and live event businesses stay open after COVID hurt their income.
Supporters say the weekly tracking reports and audit plans will make sure businesses use the grants properly.
Supporters say transportation companies and border businesses that lost customers during the pandemic need this money to keep workers employed.
critics: Critics say this emergency spending adds to the federal debt because it is exempt from normal spending limits.
Critics say limiting businesses to only one grant program means some companies that qualify for multiple programs will get less help than they need.
Critics say the government should not pick which types of businesses get grants while others that were also hurt by COVID get nothing.

117-s-4132.one_liner: Stop governments from blocking abortion services
provisions: Stops governments from blocking doctors who provide abortion services through video calls
Stops governments from making patients visit a doctor in person before getting an abortion
Stops governments from requiring doctors to give patients false medical information about abortions
Stops governments from banning abortions before the fetus can survive outside the womb
Stops governments from banning abortions when the pregnancy threatens the patient's life or health
Lets the Justice Department, patients, or doctors sue states that break these rules

supporters: Supporters say this would help women in rural areas by stopping governments from blocking doctors who provide abortion services through video calls.
Supporters say this would protect women whose pregnancies threaten their life or health by banning governments from blocking emergency abortion care.
Supporters say this would stop governments from making patients make unnecessary in-person visits before getting abortion services.
critics: Critics say this would override state laws and take away states' rights to regulate abortion clinics and procedures.
Critics say this would let the Justice Department sue any state that requires waiting periods or in-person visits before abortions.
Critics say this would stop governments from requiring safety measures they believe protect women getting abortion care.

117-s-3436.one_liner: Impose sanctions on companies involved in the Nord Stream 2 pipeline
provisions: Blocks companies that plan, build, or run Nord Stream 2 from accessing US money and property
Stops company leaders of these companies from getting US visas
Nord Stream 2 is a pipeline that carries Russian gas to Germany
Requires the President to tell Congress before canceling any Russia sanctions
Lets Congress block the President from canceling Russia sanctions if they disagree

supporters: Supporters say blocking Nord Stream 2 companies from US property and money stops Russia from controlling Germany's energy supply
Supporters say requiring the President to ask Congress before removing Russia sanctions keeps America tough on Russia
Supporters say banning company leaders from getting US visas punishes people who help Russia sell more gas to Europe
critics: Critics say blocking Nord Stream 2 hurts Germany, a US ally that wants cheaper Russian gas through the pipeline
Critics say making the President ask Congress before removing sanctions takes away his power to make deals with Russia
Critics say sanctioning pipeline companies could hurt US businesses that work with these firms

117-s-4.one_liner: Require some states to get federal approval before changing voting rules
provisions: Requires states with 15 or more voting violations in 25 years to get federal approval before changing voting rules
Requires states with 10 or more violations in 25 years to get approval if the state committed at least one violation
Requires local areas with 3 or more voting violations in 25 years to get federal approval
Makes states tell the public when they change voting rules
Lets the Justice Department ask states for documents about voting rights
Protects election workers and polling places
Expands voting access on tribal lands

supporters: Supporters say this would stop states with 15 or more voting violations from changing voting rules without federal approval for 10 years.
Supporters say the bill would protect election workers and polling places from threats and violence.
Supporters say this would expand voting access for Native Americans on tribal lands.
critics: Critics say the 10-year federal approval requirement takes away states' right to run their own elections.
Critics say forcing states with 10 or more violations to get Washington's permission for voting changes creates delays and bureaucracy.
Critics say the 3-violation threshold for local areas is too low and punishes communities unfairly.

117-s-610.one_liner: Give money for healthcare worker mental health programs and suicide prevention training
provisions: Gives money to programs that train healthcare workers on suicide prevention
Gives money to create mental health programs for healthcare workers who treated COVID-19 patients
Requires the health department to study what causes healthcare worker burnout and write solutions
Requires the CDC to run campaigns encouraging healthcare workers to get mental health help

supporters: Supporters say this would reduce suicide rates among healthcare workers by funding training programs on suicide prevention.
Supporters say this would help healthcare workers who treated COVID-19 patients get mental health support through new programs.
Supporters say this would solve healthcare worker burnout by requiring the health department to study the causes and write solutions.
critics: Critics say this would cost taxpayer money for grants to train healthcare workers on suicide prevention instead of other priorities.
Critics say this would create new government spending on mental health programs for healthcare workers who treated COVID-19 patients.
Critics say this would require the CDC to spend money on campaigns encouraging healthcare workers to seek mental health help.

117-s-937.one_liner: Require DOJ to speed up review of COVID-19 hate crimes
provisions: Makes DOJ assign someone to review COVID-19 hate crimes faster
Defines COVID-19 hate crimes as violent crimes motivated by a person's race or ethnicity during the pandemic
Requires DOJ to help local police set up online hate crime reporting in multiple languages
Makes DOJ expand education campaigns about hate crimes
Requires DOJ and health officials to give guidance on describing COVID-19 without language that targets specific groups

supporters: Supporters say assigning a DOJ officer to review COVID-19 hate crimes faster will help Asian Americans and other groups who faced attacks during the pandemic.
Supporters say requiring online hate crime reporting in multiple languages will help victims who don't speak English report crimes to local police.
Supporters say the guidance on describing COVID-19 without targeting specific groups will prevent language that leads to more attacks.
critics: Critics say creating a new DOJ position to review these crimes wastes money when existing hate crime laws already cover violent crimes based on race.
Critics say the federal government should not tell local police how to set up their reporting systems.
Critics say the definition of COVID-19 hate crimes is too vague and could confuse law enforcement about which cases qualify.

provisions: Gives government agencies money for programs that provide safe drinking water through 2026
Gives government agencies money for programs that treat wastewater and sewer overflows through 2026
Continues a program that loans money to communities for clean water projects
Continues a program that loans money to communities for drinking water systems

supporters: Supporters say the drinking water programs through 2026 will help protect public health by ensuring communities have safe water to drink.
Supporters say the loan programs will help small towns and cities afford to fix old water pipes and treatment plants that many cannot pay for on their own.
Supporters say the wastewater treatment funding will stop sewer overflows that dump raw sewage into rivers and lakes.
critics: Critics say the federal spending on water programs through 2026 will add billions to the national debt when states should pay for their own water systems.
Critics say the revolving loan funds have operated for decades but many communities still have unsafe drinking water and failing sewers.
Critics say local water utilities should raise rates to pay for upgrades instead of relying on federal taxpayer money.

117-sjres-13.one_liner: Cancel an EEOC rule about sharing discrimination case details with employers
provisions: Cancels a rule that would make the EEOC share more information with employers during discrimination case settlements
The rule would have required the EEOC to tell employers the facts and legal reasons behind discrimination findings
By canceling the rule, the EEOC can keep this information private during settlements

supporters: Supporters say canceling this rule protects workers who file discrimination complaints by letting the EEOC keep settlement details private.
Supporters say requiring the EEOC to share its legal reasoning with employers during settlements could make it harder to reach agreements.
critics: Critics say employers need to know the specific facts and legal reasons behind discrimination findings to properly respond during settlements.
Critics say the rule would make the EEOC settlement process more transparent by requiring the agency to share its reasoning with employers.

117-sjres-14.one_liner: Cancel a 2020 EPA rule about oil and gas emissions
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from September 2020 about pollution from oil and gas facilities
The rule applied to new, rebuilt, and modified oil and gas facilities
Restores methane emission limits that the 2020 rule removed

supporters: Supporters say this bill would restore methane emission limits on new, rebuilt, and modified oil and gas facilities that the 2020 EPA rule removed.
Supporters say canceling the EPA rule would bring back pollution controls that protect air quality from oil and gas operations.
critics: Critics say restoring methane emission limits would add new costs and rules for oil and gas companies building or changing their facilities.
Critics say the bill would hurt energy production by putting back pollution rules that the EPA removed in 2020.

117-sconres-41.one_liner: Set the federal government's spending goals for the years 2023 through 2032
provisions: Sets spending goals for the government for each year from 2023 through 2032
Sets goals for how much the government will collect in taxes each year
Sets limits on how much new debt the government can take on
Creates rules that Congress must follow when making spending decisions
Allows some changes to these rules for health savings account bills
Sets spending amounts for running Social Security offices

supporters: Supporters say this creates a 10-year spending plan that helps Congress make organized decisions about the federal budget through 2032.
Supporters say the budget enforcement rules will prevent overspending by requiring Congress to follow set limits on new debt and spending.
Supporters say the reserve funds allow Congress to adjust spending for health savings account bills and government efficiency measures.
critics: Critics say the 10-year spending goals are too uncertain because economic conditions and needs change over such a long time period.
Critics say the debt limits could force cuts to Social Security administrative spending and other programs that people depend on.
Critics say the budget enforcement procedures could make it harder for Congress to respond quickly to emergencies or unexpected costs.

117-sconres-5.one_liner: Set the federal budget plan for 2021 through 2030
provisions: Sets spending and tax collection targets for the federal government from 2021 to 2030
Lets Congressional committees write special budget bills that spend more money than the government takes in
Gives budget committee leaders power to change spending limits for certain bills
Removes budget rules that would normally block some spending bills
Requires committees to submit their budget bills by February 16, 2021

supporters: Supporters say this lets committees write budget bills by February 16, 2021 that can pass the Senate without filibuster rules, allowing Congress to act quickly on pandemic relief.
Supporters say this gives budget committee chairs power to adjust spending limits for emergency bills, helping the government respond to crises.
Supporters say this sets federal spending and tax targets through 2030, giving the government a long-term budget plan.
critics: Critics say this removes budget rules that normally block deficit spending, letting Congress spend more money than the government takes in without fiscal controls.
Critics say this lets committees bypass normal Senate debate rules through reconciliation, limiting opposition input on major spending bills.
Critics say this allows budget committee leaders to change spending limits without full Congressional votes, concentrating too much budget power in committee chairs.

117-sjres-31.one_liner: Block a planned military weapons sale to Saudi Arabia
provisions: Stops a planned sale of military weapons to Saudi Arabia

supporters: Supporters say this would stop weapons from going to Saudi Arabia, which has been linked to civilian deaths in Yemen's conflict
Supporters say blocking these defense articles would pressure Saudi Arabia to improve its human rights record
critics: Critics say stopping the planned military sale would hurt American defense jobs and weapons manufacturers
Critics say this would damage the strategic partnership with Saudi Arabia needed for Middle East security

117-sjres-29.one_liner: Cancel a workplace rule requiring COVID-19 vaccination or weekly testing
provisions: Cancels a Department of Labor rule from November 2021
The rule required employers with 100 or more employees to mandate COVID-19 vaccination or weekly testing
Employers would no longer have to require vaccination or testing from employees
This affects workplaces with 100 or more employees

supporters: Supporters say this resolution stops the government from forcing employers with 100 or more workers to require vaccination or weekly testing.
Supporters say canceling the November 2021 rule gives businesses back the right to set their own COVID policies.
critics: Critics say removing this rule takes away safety protections for employees at companies with 100 or more workers.
Critics say canceling the vaccination and testing requirement could increase COVID spread in large workplaces.

117-sjres-32.one_liner: Cancel a rule requiring COVID vaccines for healthcare workers
provisions: Cancels a rule requiring healthcare workers to get COVID vaccines
Healthcare workers at hospitals and nursing homes that take Medicare or Medicaid money would no longer need shots
The rule started in November 2021

supporters: Supporters say this would protect healthcare workers at hospitals and nursing homes from losing their jobs if they don't get COVID vaccines.
Supporters say this would end the rule that forces healthcare facilities taking Medicare and Medicaid money to require staff vaccinations.
critics: Critics say this would put nursing home residents and hospital patients at risk by allowing unvaccinated healthcare workers to care for them.
Critics say this would remove COVID safety rules for healthcare facilities that serve Medicare and Medicaid patients.

117-sjres-15.one_liner: Cancel a 2020 rule about when banks count as lenders
provisions: Cancels a banking rule from October 2020
The rule said banks must be named in loan agreements or fund the loans to count as lenders
Without this rule, banks can count as lenders in more situations

supporters: Supporters say this removes the October 2020 rule that required banks to be named in loan agreements or fund loans to count as lenders.
Supporters say this gives banks more ways to participate in lending beyond just the two methods allowed under the 2020 rule.
critics: Critics say removing this rule makes it harder for borrowers to know which bank is actually responsible for their loan.
Critics say this lets banks avoid the requirement to be named as lenders or fund loans while still claiming to be lenders.

117-sjres-33.one_liner: Increase the debt limit by $2.5 trillion
provisions: Lets the government borrow $2.5 trillion more money
Allows the government to keep paying its bills and debts
Prevents the government from running out of money to pay what it owes

supporters: Supporters say this $2.5 trillion debt limit increase would let the government keep paying money it owes.
Supporters say this prevents the government from running out of money to pay its bills and debts.
critics: Critics say the $2.5 trillion increase adds to the government's debt.
Critics say this lets the government borrow more money without any spending limits.

117-sjres-35.one_liner: Block a military weapons sale to Egypt
provisions: Stops the U.S. government from selling military equipment to Egypt
Cancels a weapons sale that was planned but not yet completed

supporters: Supporters say this would prevent Egypt from receiving the defense articles and services in the proposed sale.
Supporters say this would ensure Congress can block military sales to Egypt when it disagrees with them.
critics: Critics say this would cancel defense articles and services that Egypt was expecting to receive from the U.S.
Critics say this would damage the U.S.-Egypt security partnership by stopping the planned weapons transfer.

117-sjres-37.one_liner: End the requirement to wear masks on planes, trains, and buses
provisions: Ends the requirement for people to wear masks on planes, trains, buses, and other public transportation
Ends the requirement for people to wear masks at airports, train stations, and bus stations
Cancels a CDC rule from February 2021 that created these requirements
The rule was meant to stop the spread of COVID-19

supporters: Supporters say this would end federal government requirements for masks on planes, trains, buses and at airports and train stations.
Supporters say this restores personal choice for millions of travelers who use public transportation daily.
Supporters say the February 2021 CDC rule went too far in requiring masks nationwide on all forms of public transportation.
critics: Critics say removing mask requirements on crowded planes, trains and buses puts public health at risk during COVID-19 outbreaks.
Critics say this takes away CDC authority to protect vulnerable people who rely on public transportation.
Critics say ending these requirements at airports and transportation hubs removes safety measures where large numbers of people gather.

117-sjres-38.one_liner: End the COVID-19 national emergency declared in March 2020
provisions: Ends the COVID-19 national emergency that started on March 13, 2020
Stops any special government powers that were active under this emergency
Returns government operations to normal non-emergency rules

supporters: Supporters say this would end special government powers that have been active since March 13, 2020.
Supporters say this would return government operations to normal non-emergency rules after six years.
critics: Critics say ending the March 13, 2020 emergency could remove health protections that people still need.
Critics say stopping special government powers could hurt programs that help people with COVID.

117-sjres-39.one_liner: End vaccine and mask requirements in Head Start programs
provisions: Cancels a health rule from November 2021
Ends vaccine requirements in Head Start programs
Ends mask requirements in Head Start programs
Head Start programs provide early education to low-income children

supporters: Supporters say this would end the November 2021 vaccine and mask rules in Head Start programs that serve low-income children.
Supporters say this would let parents decide about vaccines and masks for their children instead of the government.
Supporters say this would remove health mandates so Head Start programs can focus on education.
critics: Critics say this would remove vaccine and mask protections for low-income children in Head Start programs.
Critics say this would eliminate safety rules that helped prevent COVID-19 spread in Head Start programs since November 2021.
Critics say this would put Head Start staff and children at higher risk for illness.

117-sjres-41.one_liner: Cancel a health department rule about abortion counseling at family planning clinics
provisions: Brings back restrictions on abortion counseling at government-funded family planning clinics
Requires family planning clinics to physically separate abortion services from other health services
Changes family planning clinic rules back to how they were in May 2019

supporters: Supporters say this would restore restrictions on abortion counseling and referrals at government-funded family planning clinics.
Supporters say this would bring back the physical separation requirements between abortion-related activities and family planning services that were in place before May 2019.
critics: Critics say this would reduce access to complete pregnancy counseling options for women at federally funded family planning clinics.
Critics say this would require women to visit separate locations for different reproductive health services due to the physical separation requirements.

117-sjres-63.one_liner: End the COVID-19 national emergency declared in March 2020
provisions: Ends the COVID-19 national emergency declared on March 13, 2020

supporters: Supporters say this ends emergency procurement rules from March 13, 2020 that let agencies buy supplies without normal bidding rules and oversight.
Supporters say this restores regular government operations by ending powers that allow federal agencies to waive standard regulations.
Supporters say this signals the COVID crisis phase is over and returns the country to normal legal framework.
critics: Critics say this could end Medicare waivers that allow doctors to provide telehealth services and give hospitals flexibility in staffing and bed rules.
Critics say this might cut FEMA authorities that provide federal funding to states and cities for ongoing COVID-related emergency costs.
Critics say this could affect public health programs and emergency response systems that depend on the March 13, 2020 emergency powers.

117-sjres-60.one_liner: Cancel a rule about how charter schools get federal grants
provisions: Cancels a Department of Education rule from July 2022 about charter school funding
Removes requirements for how states get charter school grants
Eliminates rules for how charter school companies get money to open or expand schools

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would remove federal requirements that states must follow to get charter school grants
Supporters say this would eliminate rules that charter school companies must follow to get federal money
Supporters say this would give states more control over their charter school programs
critics: Critics say the 2022 rule provides oversight for how charter school grant money is spent
Critics say removing these requirements would reduce accountability for federal charter school funding
Critics say the rule helps ensure charter schools meet standards before getting federal money

117-sjres-55.one_liner: Cancel a 2022 environmental review rule for federal projects
provisions: Cancels a 2022 rule on environmental reviews for federal projects
Keeps 2020 rules that set time limits for environmental studies
Affects how federal agencies review projects before approval

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would keep the 2020 rules that set time limits for environmental studies, helping federal agencies approve projects faster.
Supporters say canceling the 2022 rule prevents delays that hurt businesses and infrastructure projects waiting for federal approval.
critics: Critics say the 2020 time limits for environmental studies rushed reviews and missed important environmental problems.
Critics say keeping the 2020 rules weakens protection for air, water, and wildlife that federal projects might harm.

117-sjres-46.one_liner: Cancel a 2022 rule that changed asylum screening procedures
provisions: Cancels a rule from March 2022 about asylum fear screenings
Brings back the screening process that existed before March 2022
The old process had more ways for people to pass the fear screening
Affects people in removal proceedings who claim they will face persecution

supporters: Supporters say bringing back the pre-March 2022 screening process would give asylum seekers three ways to pass fear screenings instead of two.
Supporters say people in removal proceedings who claim persecution would have more chances to avoid deportation under the old system.
critics: Critics say nullifying the March 2022 rule would bring back a more complex screening system for asylum officers to use.
Critics say the 2022 rule improved efficiency by reducing asylum fear screening categories from three to two.

117-sres-16.one_liner: Set up rules and deadlines for Donald Trump's impeachment trial
provisions: Sets deadlines for when lawyers must file trial documents
Sets a date for the Senate to consider the impeachment charge
Lists what issues both sides must address in their legal arguments

supporters: Supporters say this resolution provides clear deadlines for lawyers to file trial documents so the impeachment process can proceed in an orderly way.
Supporters say this resolution sets a specific date for the Senate to consider the impeachment charge so there is certainty about when the trial will happen.
critics: Critics say this resolution diverts Senate resources from other legislative priorities by establishing deadlines for trial documents and setting a specific consideration date for the impeachment charge.
Critics say this resolution creates additional procedural steps by requiring both sides to address specific legal issues in their arguments when the Senate could focus on other business.

118-hconres-21.one_liner: Remove U.S. troops from Syria within 180 days
provisions: Directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from Syria
Sets a 180-day deadline for the troop removal
Applies to all U.S. military personnel currently in Syria

supporters: Supporters say this would bring all American troops home from Syria within 180 days.
Supporters say removing U.S. Armed Forces from Syria would end America's military role in the conflict.
critics: Critics say removing all U.S. forces from Syria within 180 days could hurt efforts to fight ISIS.
Critics say the 180-day withdrawal deadline could abandon Kurdish allies who helped American forces.

118-hconres-30.one_liner: Remove US troops from Somalia within one year
provisions: Requires the President to pull all US troops out of Somalia within 365 days
Lets troops assigned to guard the US embassy stay in Somalia
Uses Congress's war powers to force this troop withdrawal

supporters: Supporters say this would end US military involvement in Somalia by requiring all troops to leave within 365 days, except those protecting the US embassy.
Supporters say this uses Congress's war powers to control where the military fights overseas.
Supporters say this would bring American troops home from another foreign conflict.
critics: Critics say removing all US forces within 365 days would hurt efforts to fight terrorist groups in Somalia.
Critics say this would take away the President's ability to respond quickly to threats in East Africa.
Critics say pulling out US troops could make Somalia and nearby countries less stable.

118-hconres-3.one_liner: Condemn attacks on pro-life groups and churches
provisions: Condemns recent attacks on pro-life facilities, groups, and churches
Asks the president to use law enforcement to keep these groups safe

supporters: Supporters say this resolution condemns attacks on pro-life facilities, groups, and churches.
Supporters say this asks the president to use law enforcement authorities to protect these groups.
critics: Critics say this resolution creates no new laws or funding since it expresses Congress's opinion.
Critics say this focuses on pro-life facilities while not addressing attacks on other groups or facilities.

117-sres-47.one_liner: Set rules for Donald Trump's impeachment trial in the Senate
provisions: Sets deadlines for filing papers in the impeachment trial
Sets time limits for arguments for and against impeachment
Sets rules for what evidence can be used in the trial
Sets rules for voting on the impeachment charge

supporters: Supporters say the filing deadlines ensure both the House managers and Trump's lawyers have equal time to submit their legal papers
Supporters say the time limits for arguments ensure the Senate can complete the trial efficiently
Supporters say the evidence rules ensure the trial follows proper legal procedures
critics: Critics say the time limits for arguments could prevent Trump's lawyers from presenting a complete defense
Critics say the filing deadlines rush the preparation of legal documents
Critics say the evidence rules could exclude important information that should be considered

118-hconres-25.one_liner: Let Congress use Emancipation Hall for a Holocaust remembrance ceremony
provisions: Lets Congress use Emancipation Hall on April 20, 2023
The hall is in the Capitol Visitor Center
The ceremony remembers victims of the Holocaust

supporters: Supporters say using Emancipation Hall on April 20, 2023 honors Holocaust victims and ensures their memory is preserved in an important federal building.
Supporters say holding the ceremony in the Capitol Visitor Center educates the public about genocide and helps prevent future atrocities.
Supporters say using Emancipation Hall, which celebrates freedom from slavery, is the right place to remember Holocaust victims who suffered under Nazi persecution.
critics: Critics say Congress should focus on current problems like the budget and inflation instead of spending time on ceremonial activities in federal buildings.
Critics say using the Capitol Visitor Center for the April 20, 2023 ceremony costs taxpayer money for security and staff that could be used for other priorities.
Critics say authorizing specific dates and locations for commemorative events sets a precedent for other groups to demand similar use of federal facilities.

118-hconres-7.one_liner: Condemn Iran's crackdown on protesters and encourage US sanctions
provisions: Condemns Iran's violent response to protesters in over 133 cities
Commends Iranian protesters risking their lives to defend human rights
Condemns the beating and death of Mahsa Amini
Calls for accountability for all protesters killed by Iranian security forces
Encourages the Biden Administration to continue sanctioning Iran's morality police

supporters: Supporters say this resolution stands with Iranian women and men protesting for basic rights in over 133 cities and condemns the beating and death of Mahsa Amini.
Supporters say it calls for accountability for protesters killed by Iranian security forces and encourages continued sanctions against Iran's morality police.
Supporters say Congress should speak out against human rights abuses and support people risking their lives for freedom.
critics: Critics say this resolution only makes statements but doesn't authorize new sanctions, military action, or funding to help Iranian protesters.
Critics say congressional resolutions are non-binding and don't create enforceable policy changes compared to legislation that could impose new sanctions or provide aid.

118-hconres-40.one_liner: Say Congress supports police and opposes defunding police departments
provisions: Says Congress supports local police officers
Says Congress opposes efforts to defund police departments
Says Congress opposes efforts to get rid of police departments

supporters: Supporters say this resolution shows Congress supports local police officers in their communities.
Supporters say Congress opposes efforts to defund police departments through this resolution.
Supporters say Congress opposes efforts to get rid of police departments entirely.
critics: Critics say this resolution only expresses support but does not provide funding or new laws for police.
Critics say this resolution opposes efforts to defund police departments without addressing reform concerns.
Critics say this resolution blocks discussions about moving police money to other community services.

118-hjres-27.one_liner: Cancel a rule that expanded federal control over waterways and wetlands
provisions: Cancels a 2023 rule that expanded which waterways the federal government controls
Brings back a 2020 rule that gave the federal government control over fewer water bodies
Changes which waterways need federal permits before companies can build near them or dump pollution
Affects rivers, streams, wetlands, and other water bodies across the country

supporters: Supporters say this reduces the number of waterways that need federal permits, making it cheaper and faster for farmers and builders to work near streams and wetlands.
Supporters say this brings back the 2020 rule that gave states more control over water bodies instead of federal agencies controlling more rivers and streams.
Supporters say this cuts federal red tape that makes companies wait longer and pay more to get permits for projects near water.
critics: Critics say this removes federal protection from thousands of streams and wetlands that provide drinking water to communities across the country.
Critics say this allows more pollution near water sources because fewer waterways would need federal permits before companies can dump waste.
Critics say this weakens Clean Water Act protections for rivers, streams and wetlands that wildlife and communities depend on.

118-hjres-24.one_liner: Cancel a DC law that lets non-citizens vote in local elections
provisions: Cancels a 2022 DC law that allowed non-citizens to vote in local elections
Non-citizens who met residency requirements could vote in DC local elections under the canceled law
Returns DC to the previous rule where only citizens can vote in local elections

supporters: Supporters say this cancels the 2022 DC law that allowed non-citizens to vote in local elections.
Supporters say this returns DC to requiring citizenship for voting in mayor and city council races.
critics: Critics say this removes voting rights from non-citizens who met DC residency requirements under the canceled law.
Critics say this prevents non-citizen residents from voting in DC school board and mayoral elections.

118-hjres-26.one_liner: Cancel DC's changes to criminal laws and sentencing rules
provisions: Cancels the District of Columbia's updated criminal code from 2022
Keeps current definitions of crimes and current sentencing guidelines
Keeps current rules that limit jury trials for some misdemeanor cases
Prevents changes to penalties for various crimes in Washington DC

supporters: Supporters say canceling DC's updated criminal code stops changes to criminal penalties the DC Council approved in 2022
Supporters say keeping current rules that limit jury trials for misdemeanor cases maintains existing court procedures
Supporters say this prevents new crime definitions from taking effect in Washington DC
critics: Critics say canceling DC's updated criminal code blocks the District's criminal justice reforms from taking effect
Critics say keeping current rules that limit jury trials for misdemeanors prevents more defendants from getting jury trials
Critics say Congress should not override the District of Columbia Council's local decisions on criminal law

118-hjres-39.one_liner: Cancel a rule that stopped tariffs on solar panels from four Asian countries
provisions: Cancels a 2022 Commerce Department rule about solar panel tariffs
The rule stopped tariffs on solar panels made in Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam that use Chinese parts
Brings back tariffs on these solar panels
Makes solar panels from these four countries more expensive to import

supporters: Supporters say bringing back tariffs on solar panels from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam would protect American solar panel makers from unfair competition.
Supporters say the 2022 rule allowed Chinese companies to avoid tariffs by moving final assembly to these four countries while still using Chinese parts.
critics: Critics say reinstating tariffs on solar panels from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam would make solar panels more expensive for American homeowners and businesses.
Critics say higher solar panel costs would slow down solar energy projects and hurt efforts to reduce carbon emissions.

118-hjres-30.one_liner: Cancel a rule letting retirement plan managers consider climate factors in investments
provisions: Cancels a Department of Labor rule from December 2022
Stops managers of employee retirement plans from considering climate change when picking investments
Stops them from considering environmental and social factors in investment choices
Stops them from using these factors when voting on company decisions

supporters: Supporters say this would stop retirement plan managers from using climate change and social factors when picking investments, so they focus only on making money for retirees.
Supporters say the rule from December 2022 lets politics into retirement investing, and canceling it would keep managers focused on financial returns.
Supporters say this protects millions of workers' retirement savings from being used to push environmental and social goals instead of maximizing returns.
critics: Critics say canceling the December 2022 rule would stop retirement plan managers from considering climate risks that could hurt long-term investment returns.
Critics say this would limit managers' ability to vote on company decisions using environmental and social factors that affect financial performance.
Critics say blocking the Department of Labor rule could harm retirement security by preventing managers from considering all factors that impact investment returns.

118-hjres-42.one_liner: Cancel police reforms in Washington DC from 2022
provisions: Cancels police reforms that Washington DC passed in 2022
Lets DC police go back to using certain neck restraints that were banned
Removes extra rules DC police had to follow for body cameras
Makes it harder for people to see DC police discipline records

supporters: Supporters say DC police need to use neck restraints in dangerous situations to protect themselves and the public.
Supporters say the extra body camera rules cost money and slow down police work.
Supporters say making police discipline records public hurts officers who did nothing wrong.
critics: Critics say neck restraints can kill people and should stay banned to protect DC residents.
Critics say the body camera rules help people see what police do and hold them accountable.
Critics say public access to discipline records helps identify officers who break the rules.

118-hjres-7.one_liner: End the COVID-19 national emergency declared in March 2020
provisions: Ends the COVID-19 national emergency declared on March 13, 2020

supporters: Supporters say this ends the March 13, 2020 emergency powers that were meant to be temporary and restores normal government processes.
Supporters say the COVID-19 emergency declared in March 2020 is no longer needed because the health threat has decreased.
Supporters say ending this emergency returns lawmaking power to Congress from the President.
critics: Critics say ending the March 13, 2020 emergency could eliminate federal powers still needed to respond to COVID-19.
Critics say this could disrupt federal programs that depend on the March 2020 emergency declaration to operate.
Critics say terminating this emergency could leave the government unable to respond quickly if COVID-19 cases rise again.

118-hjres-44.one_liner: Cancel a rule about when guns with stabilizing braces must be registered
provisions: Cancels a 2023 rule about guns with devices called stabilizing braces that help with firing
Removes new requirements to register certain guns with these braces as rifles
Returns gun rules to what they were before January 2023

supporters: Supporters say this would remove the requirement for gun owners to register firearms with stabilizing braces that they legally bought before January 2023.
Supporters say the 2023 ATF rule created confusion about which guns count as rifles under the National Firearms Act.
Supporters say this protects people who own guns with stabilizing braces from new registration rules.
critics: Critics say this removes rules that help decide when firearms with stabilizing braces should be treated as rifles under federal law.
Critics say the 2023 ATF rule closed gaps in gun regulations for weapons that can be fired from the shoulder.
Critics say this weakens enforcement of the National Firearms Act for firearms with attached stabilizing braces.

118-hjres-45.one_liner: End federal student loan payment suspensions and debt forgiveness
provisions: Ends the suspension of federal student loan payments
Stops federal student loan debt forgiveness
Cancels an Education Department rule from October 2022
People with federal student loans would have to start making payments again

supporters: Supporters say this bill stops the October 2022 rule that forgives federal student loan debt without requiring taxpayers to cover the cost.
Supporters say borrowers who took federal student loans should resume making the payments they agreed to make.
critics: Critics say this bill forces millions of federal student loan borrowers to start making payments again after the October 2022 suspension.
Critics say ending the debt forgiveness rule takes away financial relief for people with federal student loans.

118-hjres-68.one_liner: End a 2006 national emergency about Congo conflict
provisions: Ends a national emergency that started October 27, 2006
Unfreezes money and property of people involved in Congo's civil war
The emergency has been in place for nearly 20 years

supporters: Supporters say this would end the asset freezes on individuals sanctioned for contributing to Congo's conflict that have been in place since October 27, 2006.
Supporters say this would terminate the emergency powers that block property and money of Congo conflict contributors after nearly 20 years.
critics: Critics say this would unfreeze the blocked property and money of people who contributed to the civil war in Congo.
Critics say this could allow sanctioned individuals to access their frozen assets while instability may still affect the Democratic Republic of Congo.

118-hjres-71.one_liner: End the Iraq national emergency from 2003
provisions: Ends the national emergency about Iraq that President Bush declared on May 22, 2003

supporters: Supporters say ending the May 22, 2003 emergency declaration would stop presidential powers that have lasted over 20 years without review.
Supporters say Congress should reclaim authority over emergency powers since the Iraq stabilization mission from 2003 has ended.
Supporters say the president no longer needs special emergency authority for Iraq that was declared in 2003.
critics: Critics say ending the May 22, 2003 emergency declaration could remove important presidential tools to respond to security problems in Iraq.
Critics say Iraq still faces threats that may require the emergency powers from the 2003 declaration.
Critics say removing emergency authority for Iraq stabilization could limit U.S. ability to respond to crises in the region.

118-hjres-70.one_liner: End the national emergency about Libya from 2011
provisions: Ends the national emergency about Libya that President Obama declared on February 25, 2011

supporters: Supporters say the emergency was declared during the 2011 uprising against Muammar Gaddafi, but Gaddafi was killed in October 2011, ending the original crisis that prompted the emergency.
Supporters say the Libya emergency has remained active for 15 years without Congressional review, giving the President powers that should be limited in time.
Supporters say Libya is no longer in active civil war like it was in 2011, making the continued emergency declaration unnecessary.
critics: Critics say ending the February 25, 2011 emergency would remove sanctions and asset freezes on Libyan officials and entities that still threaten U.S. interests.
Critics say Libya remains divided between competing governments in Tripoli and eastern Libya, creating ongoing instability that requires emergency powers to address.
Critics say the emergency declaration provides tools to respond quickly to terrorism and human trafficking that operate from Libyan territory.

118-hjres-79.one_liner: End a 2004 emergency rule that blocks trade and property dealing with Syria
provisions: Ends a 2004 rule that stopped trade with Syria
Lets businesses deal with certain Syrian people again
Lets companies sell certain goods to Syria again
These rules were made because Syria supported terrorists in Iraq

supporters: Supporters say this would let American businesses trade with Syria again after the 2004 rules blocked most commerce.
Supporters say this would allow companies to sell goods to Syria that have been banned for over 20 years.
critics: Critics say this would let certain Syrian people who were blocked for supporting terrorists in Iraq access their property again.
Critics say this removes national security protections that were put in place because Syria supported terrorist activity in Iraq.

118-hjres-74.one_liner: End a national emergency from 2012 that freezes money of people threatening Yemen
provisions: Ends a national emergency that President Obama declared on May 16, 2012
Stops freezing the money and property of people who threaten Yemen's stability

supporters: Supporters say this would end a 14-year-old emergency declared on May 16, 2012.
Supporters say this would stop the government from freezing people's money and property under emergency powers.
Supporters say this would return decisions about Yemen threats to normal legal processes instead of emergency rules.
critics: Critics say this would unfreeze the assets of people who threaten Yemen's peace and security.
Critics say this would remove tools that block the property of people who destabilize Yemen.
Critics say this would end protections that have been in place since May 16, 2012.

118-hjres-98.one_liner: Cancel a labor board rule about when two companies are both employers
provisions: Cancels a National Labor Relations Board rule set to take effect February 26, 2024
The canceled rule would have changed when two companies are both considered the employer of the same workers
Under the canceled rule, companies could both be employers if they control pay, schedules, or working conditions together

supporters: Supporters say this joint resolution would protect businesses from unclear rules about when they become responsible for another company's workers.
Supporters say canceling the February 26, 2024 rule prevents companies from facing unexpected legal costs when they contract with other businesses.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule removes protections for workers who have their pay and schedules controlled by multiple companies.
Critics say workers lose the right to organize against all companies that control their working conditions when the joint employer rule is canceled.

118-hr-1093.one_liner: Require a State Department report on defense partnership with Australia and the UK
provisions: Requires the State Department to write a report to Congress about a defense partnership with Australia and the UK
The report must include how long it takes to approve defense exports to Australia and the UK
The report must include information about violations of arms export rules by Australia and the UK
The report must suggest changes to export control laws in all three countries

supporters: Supporters say the report on export license review times will help Congress understand delays in defense sales to Australia and the UK.
Supporters say tracking violations of arms export rules by Australia and the UK will improve oversight of the defense partnership.
Supporters say recommended changes to export control laws could make the trilateral security partnership work better.
critics: Critics say the report requirement adds more work for State Department staff without clear benefits.
Critics say reporting on violations by Australia and the UK could damage relationships with these allies.
Critics say the report could expose sensitive information about defense exports and security partnerships.

118-hr-1.one_liner: Remove restrictions and fees on oil and gas development
provisions: Waives environmental review requirements for energy projects
Eliminates restrictions on importing and exporting oil and natural gas
Stops the President from banning fracking
Requires the Interior Department to sell oil and gas leases on federal land
Cuts royalties that oil and gas companies pay for drilling on federal land
Eliminates charges on methane emissions from oil and gas operations
Cuts funding for energy efficiency programs and greenhouse gas reduction

supporters: Supporters say this cuts energy costs by waiving environmental reviews that slow down oil and gas projects.
Supporters say eliminating import and export restrictions increases energy supply and gives consumers more choices.
Supporters say cutting royalties for drilling on federal land reduces costs for energy companies and lowers gas prices.
critics: Critics say waiving environmental reviews for energy projects puts public health and clean air and water at risk.
Critics say cutting funding for energy efficiency programs and greenhouse gas reduction hurts efforts to fight climate change.
Critics say eliminating charges on methane emissions lets oil and gas companies release pollution without paying for the damage.

118-hr-1076.one_liner: Require a government study on how money flows through illegal drug trafficking
provisions: Orders a government office to study how drug traffickers move money
The study covers fentanyl, methamphetamine, and similar illegal drugs
Includes studying chemicals used to make these drugs
The office must report its findings to Congress

supporters: Supporters say the GAO study would help Congress understand how traffickers fund fentanyl and methamphetamine operations.
Supporters say including precursor chemicals in the study would identify financial weak points in the synthetic drug supply chain.
Supporters say requiring the GAO to report findings to Congress would give lawmakers data needed to write stronger anti-trafficking laws.
critics: Critics say the GAO study on synthetic drug financing duplicates existing work by the DEA and Treasury Department.
Critics say the bill provides no deadline for the GAO study, potentially delaying action on fentanyl and methamphetamine trafficking for years.
Critics say Congress already knows drug traffickers use complex financing schemes and does not need another study to write stronger laws.

118-hr-1096.one_liner: Create coins to celebrate the Marine Corps turning 250 years old
provisions: Creates coins to celebrate the Marine Corps turning 250 years old
Makes up to 50,000 $5 gold coins, 400,000 $1 silver coins, and 750,000 half-dollar coins
Sends money from coin sales to the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation
Uses the money to support the Marine Corps Heritage Center

supporters: Supporters say this honors the Marine Corps' 250 years of service with special commemorative coins.
Supporters say the surcharges from selling up to 1.2 million coins will support the Marine Corps Heritage Center.
critics: Critics say the Treasury should not spend resources making up to 50,000 gold coins, 400,000 silver coins, and 750,000 half-dollar coins.
Critics say the government should not direct coin sale surcharges to the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation.

118-hr-10545.one_liner: Keep the government funded through March 2025 and provide emergency disaster relief
provisions: Keeps the federal government funded through March 14, 2025 to prevent a shutdown
Provides emergency money to help communities recover from hurricanes, wildfires, floods, and storms
Extends health programs like community health centers and diabetes research through March 2025
Extends farm bill programs including crop insurance and food assistance through September 2025
Continues Medicare telehealth rules that let patients see doctors from home through March 2025

supporters: Supporters say this prevents a government shutdown that would disrupt services for millions of Americans by keeping federal agencies funded through March 14, 2025.
Supporters say this provides emergency disaster relief funding to help communities recover from recent hurricanes, wildfires, and floods that damaged homes and businesses.
Supporters say this extends the Community Health Center Fund and National Health Service Corps through March 2025, keeping health care available in underserved areas.
critics: Critics say this short-term funding through March 14, 2025 creates ongoing budget uncertainty instead of passing full-year appropriations bills.
Critics say this adds billions in emergency spending that bypasses normal budget rules and increases the federal deficit.
Critics say this extends farm bill programs through September 2025 without addressing needed reforms to agricultural subsidies.

118-hr-1123.one_liner: Require a government study of cybersecurity risks in mobile phone networks
provisions: Requires a government agency to study security risks in mobile phone networks
The study examines how well phone companies protect against hackers and foreign spies
The report must show how phone companies follow security best practices
The study looks at encryption used to protect phone calls and data

supporters: Supporters say this study would help identify security gaps in mobile networks that foreign adversaries could exploit for surveillance
Supporters say the report would show which phone companies are following cybersecurity best practices and which are leaving Americans vulnerable to hackers
Supporters say examining encryption used in mobile devices and networks would help protect phone calls and data from cyberattacks
critics: Critics say this requires phone companies to spend time and money preparing detailed security reports about their cybersecurity vulnerabilities and best practices for the government
Critics say the study could slow down development of new mobile technologies while companies focus on complying with government reporting requirements
Critics say sharing detailed information about encryption and authentication techniques with the government creates risks if that security data gets leaked

118-hr-1154.one_liner: Impose sanctions on people who traffic human organs and revoke some passports
provisions: Requires the President to make a list of people who harvest organs by force or traffic people for their organs
Blocks those people from entering the US and freezes their property in America
Lets the State Department take away or refuse passports for Americans convicted of organ trafficking crimes
Applies passport punishment only if the person is in prison or supervised release and used a passport or crossed borders while committing the crime

supporters: Supporters say this gives the President tools to block people involved in forced organ harvesting from entering the US and freeze their American property.
Supporters say the passport rules stop convicted organ traffickers from crossing borders to commit more crimes if they used passports or crossed borders during their original crime.
Supporters say the sanctions target people who traffic others specifically for organ harvesting.
critics: Critics say the President can add people to the sanctions list without a trial or court review.
Critics say taking away passports from American citizens convicted of these crimes violates due process rights.
Critics say the bill does not specify how much money or staff would be needed to track down organ traffickers worldwide.

118-hr-1151.one_liner: Allow sanctions on people who run China's surveillance balloon program
provisions: Lets the President block property and visas of foreign people who manage China's surveillance balloon program
Requires the Commerce Department to report on export controls for aerospace technology used by China's military for spying
Requires the State Department to create a plan to tell allies about China's surveillance program and work together against it

supporters: Supporters say this gives the President power to block property and visas of foreign people who manage China's surveillance balloon program.
Supporters say this requires the State Department to build a plan with allies to address China's global surveillance program.
Supporters say this makes the Commerce Department review export controls for aerospace technology that China's military uses for spying.
critics: Critics say sanctioning foreign individuals who manage the balloon program could worsen relations with China and hurt trade.
Critics say the bill does not clearly define who counts as managing China's surveillance balloon program for sanctions.
Critics say requiring new reports from Commerce and State departments adds work without providing extra funding.

118-hr-1149.one_liner: Require companies to report use of risky telecommunications equipment to regulators
provisions: Companies must tell regulators if they use telecommunications equipment that the government says threatens national security
The State Department must support safe telecommunications projects in other countries
The State Department must report to Congress about unsafe equipment used by allies and U.S. embassies
Companies must include this information in their regular financial reports

supporters: Supporters say requiring companies to disclose telecommunications equipment the FCC calls a national security threat would help protect the country.
Supporters say State Department reports to Congress about telecommunications equipment used by allies and U.S. embassies would give lawmakers better information about security issues.
Supporters say State Department support for telecommunications projects overseas would help the U.S. compete with foreign companies in other countries.
critics: Critics say requiring companies to add telecommunications equipment information to their financial reports would create new paperwork and costs.
Critics say the disclosure requirements could hurt American businesses that work with foreign telecommunications equipment makers.
Critics say the State Department's new reporting and project support duties would require government spending without funding specified in the bill.

118-hr-1107.one_liner: Stop China from being classified as a developing country by international organizations
provisions: Requires the State Department to ask international trade groups to change China's status from developing country to developed country
China would lose special trading benefits currently given to developing countries
International organizations must create ways to remove China's developing country status if no process exists
The President can skip this requirement if it serves American interests

supporters: Supporters say China's economy is too large to receive special trading benefits meant for poor countries.
Supporters say removing China's developing country status would create fair competition for American businesses and workers.
Supporters say the State Department should push international trade groups to recognize China as a developed country.
critics: Critics say forcing China to lose developing country status could lead to trade fights that hurt American exporters.
Critics say this requirement could damage US relationships with international trade organizations.
Critics say the President waiver provision shows this policy might not always serve American interests.

118-hr-1226.one_liner: Create an online tool for veterans to request their records from the VA
provisions: The VA must build a safe website where veterans can request copies of their records
Veterans can choose what format they want their records in
The VA must tell veterans within 10 days that they got their request
The VA must send the records within 120 days
When veterans log into VA websites, they see warnings about attorneys who break rules
Veterans see links to report bad attorneys and to find approved attorneys

supporters: Supporters say the 120-day deadline will force the VA to send veterans their records faster instead of making them wait months or years.
Supporters say the online tool will make it easier for veterans to request their files without having to call or visit VA offices.
Supporters say the attorney warnings will protect veterans from lawyers who charge illegal fees or break VA rules.
critics: Critics say the 120-day deadline may be too short for the VA to handle all requests, especially for complex cases with many records.
Critics say building and maintaining the new website will cost taxpayers money that could go to veteran healthcare instead.
Critics say the new requirements will create more paperwork and slow down other VA services for veterans.

118-hr-1163.one_liner: Let states keep part of unemployment overpayments they recover and extend fraud investigation time
provisions: States can keep 25% of fraud money they recover from unemployment benefits
States can keep 5% of extra unemployment payments they recover if they meet data matching rules
States get 10 years instead of 3 years to recover extra pandemic unemployment payments
States can hire temporary staff without the usual hiring process to investigate fraud
Federal government gets 10 years instead of 5 years to charge people with unemployment fraud
Removes funding for unemployment fraud prevention programs

supporters: Supporters say letting states keep 25% of fraud money they recover will motivate them to find more of the billions stolen during the pandemic.
Supporters say extending the recovery time from 3 to 10 years gives states enough time to track down fraudsters who stole pandemic unemployment benefits.
Supporters say allowing states to hire fraud investigators without the usual hiring process will help them move faster to catch criminals.
critics: Critics say letting states keep 25% of recovered fraud money means less goes back to federal taxpayers who were originally cheated.
Critics say allowing states to keep 5% of regular overpayments they recover could push them to go after people who legitimately received benefits.
Critics say removing the fraud prevention funding from the CARES Act takes away money that could stop fraud before it happens.

118-hr-1156.one_liner: Require Treasury to report on China's financial risks to the United States
provisions: Requires Treasury to study how China's financial sector affects the United States
Requires a report on risks China poses to U.S. financial stability
Requires Treasury to describe what the U.S. is doing to protect itself from China
Requires recommendations for working with other countries to reduce risks

supporters: Supporters say the required Treasury study of China's financial sector reforms would help identify specific vulnerabilities in U.S. banks and investment firms before they become financial crises
Supporters say the mandated report on financial stability risks would give Congress concrete data to write laws protecting American financial institutions from Chinese threats
Supporters say the requirement for international cooperation recommendations would help Treasury work with allies to coordinate responses across global financial markets
critics: Critics say the required Treasury report duplicates financial sector assessments already conducted by existing federal agencies and intelligence services
Critics say the study mandate creates bureaucratic paperwork without giving Treasury new legal tools to actually address the risks it identifies
Critics say requiring a report focused specifically on China's financial sector could damage trade relationships and economic cooperation between the two countries

118-hr-1159.one_liner: Require regular State Department reviews of Taiwan policy guidance every two years
provisions: Changes a one-time State Department review of Taiwan policies to reviews every two years
Requires the State Department to report to Congress every two years while the policies are in effect
Reports must describe how the policies consider that Taiwan is governed through free elections
Reports must identify ways to lift limits the U.S. put on itself for relations with Taiwan

supporters: Supporters say the every-two-year reviews will help Congress track changes in the State Department's Taiwan policies instead of just getting one report.
Supporters say requiring reports to identify ways to lift self-imposed restrictions on Taiwan relations could strengthen ties with Taiwan's 23 million people.
Supporters say the reports must acknowledge Taiwan's free elections, which helps Congress understand how democratic values shape U.S. policy.
critics: Critics say the every-two-year reporting requirement will create extra paperwork for State Department staff without clear benefits.
Critics say requiring reports on lifting self-imposed restrictions could anger China and damage U.S.-China relations.
Critics say the focus on Taiwan's democratic government in official reports could be seen as taking sides in the China-Taiwan dispute.

118-hr-1338.one_liner: Set deadlines for satellite licensing decisions and update space safety rules
provisions: Requires the FCC to decide on new satellite licenses within one year
Requires the FCC to decide on license renewals within 180 days
Requires the FCC to decide on minor license changes within 90 days
Lets the FCC extend these deadlines for national security concerns
Requires new rules for space safety and preventing space junk
Requires satellite companies to coordinate with each other to share airwaves

supporters: Supporters say the 1-year deadline for new satellite licenses and 180-day deadline for renewals will help companies launch broadband services faster.
Supporters say requiring satellite companies to coordinate airwave use will reduce conflicts and interference between different services.
Supporters say the new space safety rules will force companies to prevent space junk that could damage other satellites.
critics: Critics say the 1-year deadline for new licenses is too short for the FCC to properly review complex satellite applications.
Critics say rushing license approvals in 90 days for minor changes could miss safety problems that take longer to find.
Critics say the national security extension provision gives the FCC too much power to delay licenses without clear limits.

118-hr-1435.one_liner: Stop states from limiting gas car sales through pollution rules
provisions: Stops states from getting EPA permission for pollution rules that limit gas car sales
Cancels state permissions granted since January 2022 that limit gas car sales
Blocks the EPA from letting states change existing pollution rules to limit more gas cars

supporters: Supporters say this protects car buyers' freedom to choose gas vehicles by stopping states from getting EPA permission for rules that limit gas car sales.
Supporters say this prevents a confusing patchwork of different state rules by blocking states from changing existing pollution standards to limit more gas cars.
Supporters say this fixes government overreach by canceling state permissions granted since January 2022 that limit gas car sales.
critics: Critics say this takes away states' long-standing authority under the Clean Air Act to set stricter pollution standards for cars and trucks.
Critics say canceling state permissions granted since January 2022 will disrupt existing state programs that reduce air pollution and protect public health.
Critics say blocking states from getting EPA permission for pollution rules will prevent communities from addressing local air quality problems.

118-hr-139.one_liner: Roll back federal worker remote work policies to pre-pandemic levels
provisions: Requires federal agencies to return to the remote work rules they had on December 31, 2019
Stops agencies from expanding remote work unless the Office of Personnel Management approves it
Requires the Office of Personnel Management to certify that expanded remote work helps the agency's mission and cuts costs

supporters: Supporters say returning to December 31, 2019 telework policies would restore the in-person oversight and collaboration standards that federal agencies used before pandemic expansions.
Supporters say requiring Office of Personnel Management certification ensures agencies must prove expanded remote work helps their mission and cuts operational costs before implementing new policies.
critics: Critics say forcing agencies back to December 31, 2019 telework policies would eliminate flexible work arrangements that federal employees currently use.
Critics say the Office of Personnel Management certification requirement would create bureaucratic delays when agencies need to adapt their workforce policies quickly.

118-hr-1353.one_liner: Let companies provide 911 calls in areas without cell phone service
provisions: Creates a process for companies to provide 911 calls and emergency alerts in areas without cell service
Companies must prove they can provide service quickly and survive earthquakes and hurricanes
Companies can only use existing cell networks if the current owner agrees in writing
Protects companies from some lawsuits if emergency alerts fail to reach people

supporters: Supporters say this would give 911 service to rural areas that have no cell phone coverage due to lack of towers or power outages.
Supporters say requiring companies to prove their networks can survive earthquakes and hurricanes ensures emergency services work when people need them most.
Supporters say requiring written permission from current spectrum owners protects existing networks from interference.
critics: Critics say the liability protections let companies avoid lawsuits if their emergency alerts fail to reach people during disasters.
Critics say allowing companies to use existing cell networks could interfere with current phone and internet services.
Critics say the approval process through the FCC could be too slow when emergencies happen and people need immediate help.

118-hr-1339.one_liner: Require the FCC to review satellite rules to help farms use precision agriculture technology
provisions: Requires the FCC to review its rules for satellites that provide internet service
The goal is to help farms access technology for precision agriculture
Precision agriculture uses data and technology to reduce environmental impact while farming
The FCC must work with a task force about rural farm internet access

supporters: Supporters say this would help farms access satellite internet technology for precision agriculture that reduces environmental impact while farming
Supporters say the FCC review of satellite rules would improve internet access for rural farms that currently lack good connectivity
Supporters say the task force consultation ensures farmers have input on satellite internet rules
critics: Critics say this adds more regulatory review work for the FCC without providing funding for actual satellite infrastructure
Critics say the required task force consultation could slow down the FCC's review process
Critics say this could delay other FCC priorities while they conduct the satellite rule review

118-hr-140.one_liner: Stop federal employees from censoring speech on social media and other platforms
provisions: Blocks government workers from telling social media companies to remove posts or add warning labels
Makes it illegal for federal employees to censor speech while at work or in uniform
Stops presidential appointees from censoring speech at any time, even off duty
Punishes violations with job discipline and money fines
Applies to removing posts, adding disclaimers, or blocking access to content

supporters: Supporters say this would stop government workers from telling social media companies to remove posts or add warning labels.
Supporters say this protects people who have pending regulatory applications or are part of enforcement actions from being censored.
Supporters say this prevents presidential appointees from censoring speech at any time, even off duty.
critics: Critics say this could stop government from flagging illegal content like terrorist threats to social media platforms.
Critics say this could prevent agencies from working with platforms to address false health information during emergencies.
Critics say the ban on presidential appointees censoring speech could limit government response to national security threats.

118-hr-1567.one_liner: Require agencies to track and report on wildfire prevention work
provisions: Requires the Agriculture and Interior departments to report how many acres they worked on to prevent wildfires each year
Makes agencies create standard procedures for tracking wildfire prevention work
Requires agencies to check if their data is accurate and timely
Makes agencies analyze how well their wildfire prevention work reduces fire risk
Requires the Government Accountability Office to study how well this new reporting system works

supporters: Supporters say this would give Congress and taxpayers clear data on how many acres the Agriculture and Interior departments actually treat for wildfire prevention each year.
Supporters say this would require agencies to verify their data is accurate and analyze whether their wildfire prevention work actually reduces fire risk over time.
Supporters say this would prevent agencies from inflating or falsely reporting their wildfire prevention accomplishments through standardized tracking procedures.
critics: Critics say this would force the Agriculture and Interior departments to spend money on new tracking systems and data reviews instead of actual wildfire prevention work.
Critics say this would create more paperwork and slow down wildfire prevention activities while agencies focus on meeting new reporting requirements.
Critics say this would add bureaucracy without guaranteeing that wildfire prevention work actually improves or that more acres get treated.

118-hr-1530.one_liner: Change VA rules for medical disability exams and contractor communications
provisions: The VA can choose not to publish certain disability exam forms if they think non-VA workers cannot fill them out properly
The VA must report on paying travel costs for veterans going to disability exams anywhere in the world
The VA must work with veteran groups to tell veterans how to contact exam contractors and what personal information to share
Medical exam contractors must send copies of all scheduling messages to the veteran's representative
The VA must report on how to better help government veterans service officers

supporters: Supporters say requiring contractors to send copies of all scheduling messages to veterans' representatives will ensure veterans have proper help during the disability exam process.
Supporters say the VA study on travel reimbursement for disability exams could lead to veterans getting money back for trips to exam facilities anywhere in the world.
Supporters say the outreach program will help veterans understand how to contact exam contractors and what personal information they need to share when called.
critics: Critics say requiring contractors to send copies of all scheduling communications to representatives creates extra administrative work for medical exam companies.
Critics say allowing the VA to withhold disability exam forms from the public reduces transparency when the VA decides non-VA workers cannot fill them out properly.
Critics say the multiple reporting requirements on travel costs and veterans service officer support add bureaucratic tasks without directly helping veterans get benefits.

118-hr-1548.one_liner: Remove paperwork rules from a government office that helps small businesses get funding
provisions: Removes paperwork requirements from a government office that helps small businesses find money to start and grow
This office can now collect information from people without following certain government procedures
The office is part of the SEC, which watches the stock market

supporters: Supporters say this helps the Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation collect information faster to help small businesses find money to start and grow.
Supporters say removing paperwork requirements lets this SEC office work more efficiently when gathering information from small businesses.
critics: Critics say this removes important government procedures that protect people from unnecessary information requests by the SEC office.
Critics say the Paperwork Reduction Act exists to prevent government agencies from collecting information without proper oversight.

118-hr-1606.one_liner: Put the Boots to Business training program for veterans into law
provisions: Makes the Boots to Business Program official
Lets the Small Business Administration run the program
Provides business training to veterans and active military members

supporters: Supporters say this bill gives legal authority to the Boots to Business Program, ensuring veterans have guaranteed access to entrepreneurship training as they transition to civilian life.
Supporters say placing the program under Small Business Administration control provides proper oversight and connects veterans to SBA's existing business resources and loan programs.
Supporters say the training helps veterans and active military members learn specific business skills like writing business plans and understanding finances to start their own companies.
critics: Critics say adding this program to the Small Business Administration's duties increases the agency's workload and costs without clear funding sources.
Critics say the bill creates overlap with existing Department of Veterans Affairs education and job training programs that already serve transitioning veterans.
Critics say government-run business training may not provide the real-world experience veterans need compared to private sector entrepreneurship programs.
