118-hr-159.one_liner: Change how the federal government tests and hires job applicants
provisions: Requires real experts to review job applicants' resumes instead of computers
Bans hiring tests that are only done by computers starting 2 years after this becomes law
Lets agencies create job-specific skill tests where real people judge applicants
Agencies can skip these rules for up to 10% of jobs but must report when they do
Creates online systems for agencies to share hiring tests and qualified applicants
Creates websites with information about federal hiring practices and job requirements

supporters: Supporters say requiring real experts to review resumes instead of computers will help qualified people who get overlooked by automated systems get federal jobs.
Supporters say job-specific skill tests will let applicants show what they can actually do instead of just filling out forms.
Supporters say the online systems for sharing hiring tests and qualified applicants will make the hiring process faster across all federal agencies.
critics: Critics say having real experts review all resumes will cost much more money and make hiring take longer than automated systems.
Critics say the 2-year deadline to stop using computer-only tests is too fast for agencies to train staff and change their systems.
Critics say limiting waivers to only 10% of jobs will not give agencies enough flexibility when they need to hire people quickly.

118-hr-1669.one_liner: Make permanent a program that trains veterans in computer and tech jobs
provisions: Makes permanent a program that trains up to 8,000 veterans per year in computer programming and tech skills
Covers veterans under age 62 who served at least 36 months and were not dishonorably discharged
Pays the same monthly amount as other veteran education benefits
VA works with training companies and pays part of tuition costs
Uses one month of existing GI Bill benefits for each month in this program

supporters: Supporters say this would train up to 8,000 veterans per year in computer programming and data processing skills that lead to high-paying tech jobs.
Supporters say veterans under age 62 who served at least 36 months would get monthly payments equal to Post-9/11 GI Bill amounts while getting this training.
critics: Critics say using one month of existing GI Bill benefits for each month in this program reduces veterans' remaining education money for college degrees.
Critics say the VA paying tuition costs to training companies for up to 8,000 veterans annually adds government spending without requiring job placement guarantees.

118-hr-1715.one_liner: Direct federal agencies to research better weather forecasting using artificial intelligence
provisions: Requires the Energy Department and weather agency to research better weather forecasting using artificial intelligence
Directs the weather agency to test new computer forecasting models against current ones
Lets federal agencies share weather data with universities and other groups
Sets security rules for the research work

supporters: Supporters say using artificial intelligence for weather forecasting could save lives by giving people more accurate warnings about hurricanes and tornadoes.
Supporters say letting universities work with federal weather agencies through data sharing will help scientists create better forecasting tools.
Supporters say testing new computer models against current ones will prove whether the new technology actually works before spending more money on it.
critics: Critics say the bill creates new government programs without setting spending limits or saying how much the research will cost taxpayers.
Critics say allowing federal agencies to share weather data with universities and other groups could create security risks if sensitive information gets leaked.
Critics say the Energy Department and weather agency already do climate research, so this bill duplicates work that is already happening.

118-hr-1615.one_liner: Stop federal regulators from banning gas stoves or making them cost more
provisions: Stops federal regulators from using money to ban gas stoves as dangerous products
Stops federal regulators from using money to create or enforce safety rules that ban gas stoves or make them much more expensive

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects people's freedom to choose gas stoves in their homes by stopping federal regulators from using taxpayer money to ban them as dangerous products.
Supporters say this prevents federal agencies from creating expensive safety rules that would ban gas stoves or make them cost much more for families.
critics: Critics say this bill would stop federal safety regulators from using their funding to protect families from health risks if gas stoves are found to be dangerous.
Critics say this prevents the Consumer Product Safety Commission from creating safety rules about gas stoves even if they find the stoves harm indoor air quality or cause health problems.

118-hr-1727.one_liner: Extend the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park Commission through 2034
provisions: Extends the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park Commission through the year ending September 2034

supporters: Supporters say extending the commission through September 2034 allows continued work on the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park.
Supporters say the 10-year extension provides long-term planning certainty for the commission's activities.
critics: Critics say extending the commission through September 2034 continues federal spending without reviewing whether the commission is still needed.
Critics say the 10-year extension period is too long without requiring progress reports on the commission's work.

118-hr-1640.one_liner: Block energy rules that could make gas stoves unavailable in stores
provisions: Stops the Energy Department from setting energy efficiency rules that would make gas kitchen appliances unavailable in stores
Blocks a February 2023 proposed rule that would set new energy standards for gas and electric stoves and ovens
Prevents future energy efficiency requirements that would eliminate cooking appliances based on fuel type

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects Americans' right to choose gas stoves by stopping the Energy Department from setting rules that would make gas kitchen appliances unavailable in stores.
Supporters say this blocks the February 2023 proposed rule that would set new energy standards for gas stoves and ovens.
Supporters say this prevents future government rules that would eliminate cooking appliances based on what fuel they use.
critics: Critics say this bill blocks energy efficiency updates for kitchen appliances that haven't had new standards in decades.
Critics say this prevents the Energy Department from setting rules that could help consumers save money on energy bills through more efficient appliances.
Critics say this stops the February 2023 rule that would set energy standards for both gas and electric cooking products.

118-hr-185.one_liner: Cancel the rule requiring foreign air travelers to show COVID vaccination proof
provisions: Cancels the CDC rule from April 2022 that requires foreign travelers to show COVID vaccination proof before flying to the US
Blocks any future rules requiring foreign travelers to show COVID vaccination proof for air travel
Stops the government from spending money to enforce vaccination proof requirements for foreign travelers

supporters: Supporters say this would end the CDC rule requiring foreign travelers to show vaccination proof before flying to the US, making travel easier for tourists and business visitors.
Supporters say this would stop the government from spending federal money to enforce vaccination requirements on foreign air travelers.
Supporters say this would prevent future CDC orders from requiring vaccination proof for foreign travelers coming by air.
critics: Critics say this would remove the April 2022 CDC protection that blocks unvaccinated foreign travelers from entering the US by air.
Critics say this would stop the government from enforcing vaccination requirements that help prevent COVID spread from foreign travelers.
Critics say this would end the rule that requires foreign air travelers to be fully vaccinated against COVID-19 before entry.

118-hr-22.one_liner: Stop China from buying oil from US emergency reserves
provisions: Stops the Energy Department from selling oil from US emergency reserves to China
Stops sales of emergency oil to companies controlled by China's government
Makes buyers promise they won't send the oil to China

supporters: Supporters say prohibiting the Energy Department from selling Strategic Petroleum Reserve oil to Chinese Communist Party-controlled entities protects America's emergency supplies.
Supporters say requiring buyers to promise not to export the oil to China ensures the emergency reserves don't end up helping China during a crisis.
critics: Critics say blocking sales to Chinese Communist Party-controlled entities reduces potential buyers for Strategic Petroleum Reserve oil and could lower sale prices.
Critics say the new requirement that buyers promise not to export oil to China adds paperwork that could slow emergency sales when speed matters.

118-hr-21.one_liner: Stop the government from using emergency oil reserves until more federal land is leased for drilling
provisions: Stops the government from releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve
Requires the Energy Department to create a plan to lease more federal land for oil and gas drilling
Keeps the oil release ban until the drilling plan is completed

supporters: Supporters say this would boost domestic oil production by requiring the Energy Department to plan for more drilling on federal lands.
Supporters say this would protect the Strategic Petroleum Reserve for real emergencies instead of allowing releases for political reasons.
Supporters say this would reduce America's dependence on foreign oil by expanding drilling opportunities on government-owned land.
critics: Critics say this would stop the government from releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve during gas price spikes or supply shortages.
Critics say this would force more oil and gas drilling on federal lands, which could harm wildlife and the environment.
Critics say this would tie the Energy Department's hands by linking emergency oil releases to new drilling plans.

118-hr-2.one_liner: Require border wall construction and limit asylum to official entry points
provisions: Requires building a wall along the Mexico border
Stops processing asylum claims from people who enter between official border crossings
Adds more crimes that block someone from getting asylum, like drunk driving causing injury
Requires all employers to use electronic system to check if workers can legally work
Adds penalties for people who stay longer than their visa allows
Gives grants to police for border security work

supporters: Supporters say requiring asylum seekers to enter only at official border crossings will create an orderly process and reduce dangerous illegal crossings between ports of entry.
Supporters say making all employers use the electronic employment verification system will stop businesses from hiring workers without legal status.
Supporters say expanding crimes that block asylum to include drunk driving causing injury will keep dangerous criminals from entering the country.
critics: Critics say stopping asylum processing for people who enter between official crossings will force families fleeing violence to wait in dangerous border areas or return to unsafe conditions.
Critics say requiring all employers to use the electronic verification system will create costly paperwork burdens for small businesses and farms.
Critics say expanding the list of crimes that block asylum will separate families when parents with minor convictions cannot reunite with their children in the US.

118-hr-1734.one_liner: Fund research to detect xylazine and man-made opioids in drugs
provisions: Tells a government science agency to fund research on finding xylazine and man-made opioids in drugs
Funds new technology to quickly test what chemicals are in drugs
Creates guidelines for safely handling and testing these drugs
Helps government agencies, colleges, and companies work together to detect these drugs better

supporters: Supporters say this would help identify xylazine contamination in street drugs, which causes severe skin wounds that do not respond to overdose reversal medication.
Supporters say the near-real time spectrometry technology would let labs quickly test what chemicals are in seized drugs instead of waiting days or weeks for results.
Supporters say bringing together government agencies, colleges, and companies would improve detection capabilities faster than each group working alone.
critics: Critics say this duplicates existing drug testing programs already run by the DEA and CDC laboratories across the country.
Critics say using taxpayer money to fund private sector research on drug detection gives companies free government help to develop products they could sell.
Critics say current gas chromatography and mass spectrometry methods used by forensic labs can already identify xylazine and synthetic opioids without new federal programs.

118-hr-2494.one_liner: Make attacking police officers grounds for deportation
provisions: Makes attacking police officers a reason to deport non-citizens
Applies to any non-citizen who physically attacks a police officer

supporters: Supporters say this bill would protect police officers by making non-citizens who physically attack them face deportation.
Supporters say this bill would create stronger consequences for non-citizens who assault law enforcement officers by making it a deportable offense.
critics: Critics say this bill could lead to deportation for non-citizens who have any physical contact with police officers, even in minor incidents.
Critics say this bill could make non-citizens afraid to report crimes or help police because they might face deportation.

118-hr-2754.one_liner: Name a post office in Laredo, Texas after three service members
provisions: Renames the post office at 2395 East Del Mar Boulevard in Laredo, Texas
Names the building after Lance Corporal David Lee Espinoza
Also honors Lance Corporal Juan Rodrigo Rodriguez and Sergeant Roberto Arizola Jr.

supporters: Supporters say this honors the military service of Lance Corporal David Lee Espinoza, Lance Corporal Juan Rodrigo Rodriguez, and Sergeant Roberto Arizola Jr.
Supporters say renaming the post office at 2395 East Del Mar Boulevard in Laredo gives local people a daily reminder of these veterans.
critics: Critics say Congress should focus on bigger national issues instead of spending time renaming the Laredo post office.
Critics say there are already other ways to honor these three military members without changing federal building names.

118-hr-23.one_liner: Cut IRS funding for tax enforcement
provisions: Cuts IRS funding that was set aside for tax enforcement
Takes back money from the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act that hasn't been spent yet
Reduces funding for Treasury Department tax agencies

supporters: Supporters say this bill would stop the government from spending unused money from the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act on IRS tax enforcement.
Supporters say cutting IRS enforcement funding would protect families and small businesses from more tax audits and investigations.
critics: Critics say reducing IRS enforcement funding would help wealthy people avoid paying taxes they owe.
Critics say taking back this money from the Treasury Department would reduce the government's ability to collect taxes and close the tax gap.

118-hr-26.one_liner: Require doctors to provide medical care to babies born alive during abortions
provisions: Requires doctors to give the same medical care to babies born alive during abortions as other babies born at the same stage
Makes doctors move these babies to a hospital right away
Makes healthcare workers report to police if they see a doctor not following these rules
Sets punishment of up to 5 years in prison and fines for doctors who break these rules
Makes it murder to kill a baby born alive during an abortion
Lets mothers sue doctors who break these rules but protects mothers from being charged with crimes

supporters: Supporters say this would protect babies born alive during abortions by requiring doctors to give them the same medical care as other babies born at the same stage.
Supporters say the requirement to move babies to hospitals right away ensures they get proper medical treatment.
Supporters say the up to 5 years in prison penalty would stop doctors from letting these babies die.
critics: Critics say the 5-year prison sentence would make doctors afraid to provide abortion care even when it's needed.
Critics say forcing healthcare workers to report to police would turn medical situations into criminal cases.
Critics say this law interferes with doctors' medical decisions about care for very sick newborns.

118-hr-2670.one_liner: Fund the military with $886 billion and give troops a 5.2% pay raise for 2024
provisions: Authorizes $886 billion in military spending for the year starting October 2023
Raises military pay by 5.2% for all service members
Funds new weapons systems and military equipment purchases
Pays for military construction projects on bases around the world
Authorizes money for military research and development programs

118-hr-2795.one_liner: Require companies to reveal voting power of executives and major shareholders
provisions: Companies with different types of stock that have different voting rights must reveal more information to shareholders
These companies must tell shareholders how many shares their directors, top executives, and owners with 5% or more of stock control
Companies must also reveal how much voting power these people have when shareholders vote on company directors
This information must be included in materials sent to shareholders before votes

supporters: Supporters say this would help shareholders understand who controls the company when they vote on directors by revealing how much voting power directors, executives, and major owners have
Supporters say shareholders would have access to information about how many shares and voting power each director and executive owns in companies with different classes of stock
Supporters say investors would know which owners control 5% or more of the voting power in companies with multi-class share structures
critics: Critics say this would create additional compliance costs for companies with multi-class share structures that must prepare these new disclosures for shareholder materials
Critics say this could discourage companies from going public if they must reveal more details about their ownership and voting power structure
Critics say this might reduce the appeal of multi-class structures that allow founders and executives to maintain voting control while raising public capital

118-hr-2796.one_liner: Expand a SEC office that helps small businesses raise money
provisions: Requires a SEC office to provide educational materials about raising money to underrepresented small businesses, rural businesses, and businesses hit by natural disasters
Requires this office to host events to promote money-raising options for these same groups
Requires yearly meetings between this office and state securities officials to discuss working together

supporters: Supporters say this would help underrepresented small businesses, rural businesses, and businesses hit by natural disasters learn about ways to raise money through free educational materials and events.
Supporters say the yearly meetings between federal SEC officials and state securities officials would improve coordination and help small businesses get clearer guidance on raising capital.
critics: Critics say expanding the SEC office's duties to provide educational materials and host events would cost taxpayer money for services that private organizations already offer.
Critics say requiring yearly meetings and new educational programs adds government bureaucracy without clear proof these activities would actually help small businesses raise more money.

118-hr-277.one_liner: Require Congress to approve major federal regulations before they take effect
provisions: Requires Congress to approve major federal regulations before they take effect
Defines major regulations as those that cost the economy $100 million or more per year
Includes regulations that raise costs for consumers, businesses, or government agencies
Covers regulations that hurt competition, jobs, investment, productivity, innovation, or US companies' ability to compete with foreign companies
Keeps the current review process for smaller regulations

supporters: Supporters say this would give Congress oversight over regulations that cost the economy $100 million or more per year.
Supporters say this would protect businesses and consumers from regulations that raise their costs without congressional approval.
Supporters say this would help US companies compete with foreign companies by preventing regulations that hurt their ability to compete.
critics: Critics say this would delay important safety and health regulations by requiring congressional approval for rules that cost $100 million or more.
Critics say this would give Congress too much power over expert agency decisions on regulations that affect competition, jobs, and innovation.
Critics say this could block regulations that protect consumers and workers if Congress refuses to approve them.

118-hr-2792.one_liner: Require the SEC to update rules for small businesses every five years
provisions: Requires the SEC to review how it defines small businesses every 5 years
Makes the SEC give Congress recommendations on changing the definition
Tells the SEC to write rules to put these recommendations in place
Covers more small businesses under rules that consider their size

supporters: Supporters say the 5-year review requirement will help more small businesses qualify for regulatory relief by updating the definition of small entity.
Supporters say forcing the SEC to give Congress specific recommendations will reduce unnecessary paperwork and compliance costs for small businesses.
Supporters say expanding the number of entities covered under small business rules will help growing companies that currently face the same regulations as large corporations.
critics: Critics say requiring the SEC to review the small entity definition every 5 years will create uncertainty for businesses about which rules apply to them.
Critics say expanding the definition to cover more entities could weaken investor protections by reducing oversight of larger companies.
Critics say the bill will increase costs for the SEC by requiring regular reviews and new rule-making procedures.

118-hr-2793.one_liner: Let all companies use stock-selling procedures that only newer companies could use
provisions: All companies can now talk to potential investors before officially announcing plans to sell stock
All companies can now submit draft paperwork privately to the SEC before making it public
Expands tools that were previously only available to newer, smaller companies

supporters: Supporters say this gives all companies the same tools that smaller emerging growth companies already have, making the rules fair for everyone.
Supporters say companies can now talk to investors privately before filing paperwork, which saves money if there's no interest.
Supporters say more companies will go public because they can test the market first without spending as much on legal fees.
critics: Critics say large companies don't need these advantages that were created to help smaller companies compete.
Critics say private talks with investors before public announcements mean less transparency for regular investors.
Critics say allowing companies to submit draft registration statements privately to the SEC reduces the information available to investors upfront.

118-hr-2872.one_liner: Change duck stamp rules for waterfowl hunting
provisions: Require waterfowl hunters to carry both electronic and paper hunting stamps
Make states give electronic stamps at purchase and paper stamps after March 10 each year
Electronic stamps expire on June 30

supporters: Supporters say electronic stamps let hunters get permits right away instead of waiting for paper stamps in the mail.
Supporters say requiring both electronic and paper stamps stops hunters from claiming they forgot their permits during checks.
critics: Critics say making states issue both electronic stamps at purchase and paper stamps after March 10 creates extra work for state agencies.
Critics say requiring hunters to carry both electronic and paper stamps makes the process more complicated than just using one type.

118-hr-2812.one_liner: Require the SEC to study costs for small companies going public
provisions: Requires the SEC to study how much small and medium companies pay when they go public
Requires the SEC to report what they find about these costs
Also looks at costs for some other ways companies raise money from investors

supporters: Supporters say the SEC study will give small and medium companies better information about IPO costs before they decide to go public.
Supporters say the report will show policymakers if high costs are stopping companies from going public.
Supporters say studying costs for other ways companies raise money will help the SEC understand the full picture.
critics: Critics say requiring the SEC to do this study wastes taxpayer money on research that private firms already provide.
Critics say small and medium companies need actual cost reductions, not another government study.
Critics say the SEC already knows enough about IPO costs to make needed changes.

118-hr-2797.one_liner: Create a test for people to invest in private investments without meeting wealth requirements
provisions: Creates a free test for investing in certain private investments
People who pass can invest without meeting current wealth requirements
The SEC designs the test for people with financial knowledge
A securities group administers the test

supporters: Supporters say the free test would allow people with financial knowledge to invest in private securities without meeting current income or wealth requirements.
Supporters say this creates equal access to private investment opportunities for people who understand finance but earn less money.
critics: Critics say removing wealth requirements could expose middle-class investors to major losses in risky private securities they cannot afford.
Critics say current income and net worth rules protect people from dangerous private investments that could destroy their savings.

118-hr-2811.one_liner: Suspend the debt limit and cut government spending through 2033
provisions: Stops the government from hitting its debt limit until March 2024 or until debt grows by $1.5 trillion
Cuts government spending each year from 2024 to 2033
Cancels Biden's student loan forgiveness and takes back unspent COVID money
Ends tax credits for solar panels, electric cars, and other clean energy
Requires more adults on Medicaid and food stamps to work or look for work
Requires more oil and gas drilling on federal land and cuts fees companies pay to drill
Makes Congress approve any new government rule that costs more than $100 million per year

supporters: Supporters say this prevents a debt crisis by raising the limit while cutting government spending over 10 years to reduce the deficit.
Supporters say work requirements for Medicaid and SNAP help more adults find jobs instead of staying on government programs.
Supporters say more oil and gas drilling on federal land and lower fees will create jobs and reduce energy costs for families.
critics: Critics say spending cuts over 10 years would hurt programs like education, health research, and safety inspections that families depend on.
Critics say new work requirements would kick millions of adults off Medicaid health insurance and SNAP food assistance.
Critics say ending tax credits for solar panels and electric cars would hurt clean energy jobs and make it harder to fight climate change.

118-hr-288.one_liner: Stop courts from automatically accepting how government agencies interpret laws
provisions: Ends the requirement for courts to accept how agencies interpret laws
Courts must decide legal questions themselves instead of accepting agency answers
Applies when agencies interpret the Constitution, federal laws, and agency rules
Makes it easier for people and businesses to challenge agency decisions in court

supporters: Supporters say courts should decide constitutional and statutory questions themselves instead of accepting agency interpretations.
Supporters say this makes it easier for people and businesses to challenge agency decisions in court by requiring judges to review legal questions without deferring to agencies.
Supporters say agencies should not get special treatment when interpreting federal laws and constitutional provisions.
critics: Critics say courts lack technical expertise when interpreting complex statutory provisions that agencies with specialized knowledge handle daily.
Critics say agencies with years of experience interpreting constitutional and regulatory matters should have input on these legal questions.
Critics say requiring courts to decide all agency rule interpretations without agency input could slow down the legal process.

118-hr-302.one_liner: Create a program to fund students studying energy and computer security
provisions: Creates a program at the Department of Energy
Gives money to graduate students studying energy and computer protection
Gives money to researchers studying energy and computer protection
Students train at government energy labs
Students train at energy companies

supporters: Supporters say this program trains experts to protect power plants and electrical grids from computer attacks by giving money to graduate students studying energy cybersecurity.
Supporters say the hands-on training at government energy labs and energy companies prepares students for real jobs in energy security.
Supporters say this fills critical jobs by funding researchers who study how to protect energy systems from cyber threats.
critics: Critics say the government should not spend taxpayer money funding graduate students and researchers when energy companies can train their own cybersecurity workers.
Critics say this creates another Department of Energy program when existing cybersecurity education already exists at universities.
Critics say sending students to train at government energy labs wastes resources that should go to actual energy production.

118-hr-3091.one_liner: Let federal law enforcement officers buy their retired handguns
provisions: Creates a program for federal law enforcement officers to buy their retired handguns
The General Services Administration runs this program
Officers can only buy handguns that their agency gave them

supporters: Supporters say this program lets federal law enforcement officers buy handguns they already know how to use safely from their years of service.
Supporters say allowing officers to purchase their retired service weapons through the General Services Administration gives them guns they are trained on.
critics: Critics say creating this General Services Administration program puts more handguns into private hands when agencies retire weapons.
Critics say the new program will create administrative costs for the General Services Administration to track and sell retired handguns to officers.

provisions: Funds the Morris K. Udall and Stewart L. Udall Foundation through 2028
Funds the foundation's Environmental Dispute Resolution Fund through 2028
Funds training programs for Native American health care workers through 2028
The foundation helps protect public lands and natural resources
The foundation helps Native tribes govern themselves

supporters: Supporters say this provides federal funding to help Native tribes train health care workers and strengthen self-governance through 2028.
Supporters say the Environmental Dispute Resolution Fund helps solve conflicts over public lands and natural resources without costly court battles.
Supporters say the foundation's programs help protect public lands and give Native Nations tools to govern themselves better.
critics: Critics say this spends federal money on programs that could be handled by states or private groups instead of a federal foundation.
Critics say extending funding through 2028 adds to government spending when budget deficits are already high.
Critics say the federal government shouldn't fund training programs that Native tribes or other organizations could run themselves.

118-hr-3089.one_liner: Make it harder for courts to let the government secretly request people's data from companies
provisions: Makes courts use a higher legal standard before letting the government request customer data without telling the customer
Requires judges to write down specific facts when they allow secret data requests
Forces the Justice Department to report each year how many secret data requests they make and how many courts approve

supporters: Supporters say the higher legal standard will protect customers' privacy by making it harder for the government to secretly request their data without telling them.
Supporters say the requirement for judges to write down specific facts will prevent government abuse of secret data requests.
Supporters say the annual Justice Department reports will create transparency about how often the government makes secret data requests.
critics: Critics say the higher court standard could slow down law enforcement investigations when police need customer data quickly.
Critics say the annual reporting requirement could reveal sensitive law enforcement methods to criminals.
Critics say the new court requirements will create more paperwork and delays for judges handling urgent cases.

118-hr-300.one_liner: Create a public database of government agency settlement agreements
provisions: Creates a public database where government agencies must report their settlement agreements
Covers settlements related to alleged violations of federal law
Lets agencies keep some information private if needed to protect the public interest
Requires agencies to explain why any information is kept private

supporters: Supporters say the public database would let taxpayers see how government agencies spend money on settlement agreements for federal law violations.
Supporters say requiring agencies to explain why settlement information stays private would make government more accountable to citizens.
Supporters say the database would help people track patterns in how agencies break federal laws and pay settlements.
critics: Critics say allowing agencies to keep settlement information private could weaken the database's goal of government transparency.
Critics say the new reporting requirements would create extra paperwork and costs for government agencies.
Critics say making settlement details public could make agencies less willing to settle cases, forcing more expensive court trials.

118-hr-346.one_liner: Create a task force to improve flight safety notices for pilots
provisions: Creates a new FAA task force to review how pilots receive notices about flight safety problems
The task force will study current methods for giving pilots information about airspace issues
Members will recommend better ways to organize and present flight safety notices to pilots
The task force must report their findings and recommendations to Congress

supporters: Supporters say the task force will help pilots get better flight safety information by reviewing how NOTAMs are currently presented to them.
Supporters say improving how flight safety notices are organized could help pilots catch important airspace problems they might miss now.
critics: Critics say creating a new FAA task force will cost taxpayer money when the agency could fix NOTAM problems with existing staff.
Critics say the task force will only study and report to Congress instead of directly fixing how pilots receive flight safety notices.

118-hr-3324.one_liner: Let the Agriculture Department collect marina fees through 2029
provisions: Lets the Agriculture Department collect fees from people using a marina in California's Shasta-Trinity National Forest
Extends this permission through September 2029
Lets the department spend the money it collects from these fees

supporters: Supporters say this lets the Agriculture Department keep collecting fees from marina users in California's Shasta-Trinity National Forest through September 2029.
Supporters say this pays for marina upkeep using money from people who use it instead of all taxpayers.
critics: Critics say this makes people pay fees to use a marina on public land in California's Shasta-Trinity National Forest.
Critics say extending fee collection through September 2029 keeps charging fees without checking if they are still needed.

118-hr-3152.one_liner: Put sanctions on people who help Iran build or move missiles
provisions: Blocks visas and freezes money of people who help Iran get, build, or move missiles covered by international rules
Sanctions adult family members of people who help Iran with missiles
Sanctions people who give major help to or do business with those already sanctioned
Requires reports to Congress about Iran's missile activities and supply chains
The bill's name stands for Fight and Combat Rampant Iranian Missile Exports Act

supporters: Supporters say blocking visas and freezing assets of people who help Iran build or move missiles under international rules will stop Iran from getting weapons technology.
Supporters say sanctioning adult family members of those who help Iran with missiles creates stronger pressure to stop these activities.
Supporters say requiring reports to Congress about Iran's missile supply chains will help lawmakers track the program's growth.
critics: Critics say sanctioning adult family members who may not be involved in missile activities punishes people for their relatives' actions.
Critics say blocking people who do business with those already sanctioned could harm legitimate trade and business relationships.
Critics say the reporting requirements about Iran's supply chains could burden State Department resources without clear benefits.

118-hr-347.one_liner: Require government agencies to estimate inflation effects of executive orders costing over $1 billion
provisions: Requires government agencies that track spending and the economy to estimate inflation effects of executive orders costing $1 billion or more per year
The estimate must classify the inflation impact as none, measurable, or significant but unmeasurable
Does not apply to emergency aid orders or those needed for national security

supporters: Supporters say this would require government agencies to analyze how executive orders costing $1 billion or more per year affect inflation before they take effect.
Supporters say the bill would help Congress and voters understand whether major executive actions will raise prices for families.
Supporters say the exceptions for emergency aid and national security orders ensure the government can still act quickly when needed.
critics: Critics say requiring inflation estimates could delay important executive orders while the Office of Management and Budget and Council of Economic Advisers prepare their analysis.
Critics say the requirement to classify impacts as measurable or unmeasurable may not give useful information to decision makers.
Critics say the $1 billion threshold might miss smaller executive orders that together could still cause inflation.

118-hr-3099.one_liner: Create a new ambassador position to expand Middle East peace agreements
provisions: Creates a new ambassador job at the State Department
The ambassador works to get more countries to make peace with Israel
The ambassador has the same rank as other ambassadors
The ambassador works with other parts of the US government
The Abraham Accords are peace deals between Israel and four Arab countries

supporters: Supporters say creating an ambassador-level position at the State Department shows strong US commitment to expanding peace deals beyond the current four Arab countries in the Abraham Accords.
Supporters say having one Special Envoy coordinate efforts across all US government agencies will make diplomacy more effective than scattered efforts.
Supporters say the ambassador can build on existing success with UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan to bring more Muslim-majority countries into peace deals with Israel.
critics: Critics say creating a new ambassador position adds unnecessary costs when existing State Department diplomats could handle expanding the Abraham Accords.
Critics say pushing more countries to normalize relations with Israel could hurt US relationships with Palestinians and Arab nations that oppose these peace deals.
Critics say the Special Envoy position duplicates work already done by other Middle East diplomats and government agencies.

118-hr-3672.one_liner: Name a Veterans Affairs clinic in Michigan after Pfc. Justin T. Paton
provisions: Names the Veterans Affairs clinic in Indian River, Michigan after Pfc. Justin T. Paton

118-hr-382.one_liner: End the COVID-19 public health emergency
provisions: Ends the COVID-19 public health emergency
This emergency was first declared on January 31, 2020
Takes effect the day the bill becomes law

supporters: Supporters say ending the emergency declared on January 31, 2020 would return government operations to normal after more than six years.
Supporters say the COVID-19 public health emergency is no longer needed and should be terminated immediately when this bill becomes law.
critics: Critics say ending the emergency could cut off federal funding for COVID-19 testing and treatment programs that rely on the January 31, 2020 declaration.
Critics say terminating the emergency on the day this bill becomes law could end important health authorities before alternative plans are ready.

118-hr-3799.one_liner: Turn 2019 health reimbursement rules into law
provisions: Makes existing 2019 government rules into law that let employers pay workers back for health insurance costs instead of offering company health plans
Workers buy their own health insurance that follows Affordable Care Act rules and employers pay them back up to a yearly limit
Money from employers to cover health costs is tax-free for workers
Employers who use this must offer it to all workers in the same job category with the same dollar limits
Workers can use this payment system along with Medicare coverage
Employers must notify workers about the program and verify insurance meets government standards

supporters: Supporters say this gives workers more choice in health insurance by letting them pick their own plans instead of being stuck with one company plan.
Supporters say the tax-free employer payments help workers afford health insurance without the administrative costs that burden small businesses with group plans.
Supporters say workers can keep their insurance when they change jobs since they own their individual plans rather than losing company coverage.
critics: Critics say individual insurance plans cost more than group plans, so workers will get less health coverage for the same employer dollar amount.
Critics say this rule will push employers to drop group health plans and force workers to navigate complex insurance markets on their own.
Critics say requiring the same dollar limits for all workers in the same job category ignores that some workers need more expensive health coverage than others.

118-hr-3564.one_liner: Roll back mortgage fee changes made by federal housing agencies in May 2023
provisions: Brings back the fees that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac charged for mortgages before May 2023
These fees are based on credit scores and down payments
Requires a government report on what the fee changes did
Stops new fee changes until 90 days after the report comes out
Requires agencies to get public input before changing fees in the future
Says future fee changes should be based on risk
Bans fees based on how much debt someone has compared to their income

supporters: Supporters say this brings back the fee structure from before May 2023 that charged fees based on credit scores and down payments.
Supporters say this requires a GAO report on the fee changes and stops new changes for 90 days after the report comes out.
Supporters say this bans agencies from charging fees based on how much debt someone has compared to their income.
critics: Critics say rolling back to the pre-May 2023 fee structure removes changes that agencies made to mortgage pricing.
Critics say the GAO report requirement and 90-day waiting period could delay fee adjustments.
Critics say requiring fees to be risk-based only limits agencies from using other pricing factors.

118-hr-3746.one_liner: Raise the debt limit while cutting government spending and expanding work requirements
provisions: Suspends the federal debt limit until January 2, 2025
Sets spending limits for 2024 and 2025 with automatic cuts if exceeded
Takes back unspent money from COVID-19 programs and the IRS
Ends the pause on federal student loan payments
Requires more adults to work to get food stamps (SNAP)
Requires more adults to work to get cash assistance (TANF)
Speeds up permits for energy projects

supporters: Supporters say the debt limit suspension until January 2025 prevents default while the spending limits for 2024 and 2025 control government spending.
Supporters say the expanded work requirements for SNAP and TANF will encourage more adults to find jobs instead of staying on benefits.
Supporters say taking back unspent COVID-19 money and IRS funds returns unused taxpayer dollars to reduce the deficit.
critics: Critics say the expanded work requirements for SNAP and TANF will cut food stamps and cash assistance for adults who cannot find jobs.
Critics say ending the pause on federal student loan payments will force borrowers to resume payments during tough economic times.
Critics say the spending limits with automatic cuts could harm programs that help families and communities.

118-hr-3941.one_liner: Stop schools from housing non-citizens who don't have legal permission to be here
provisions: Stops public schools and colleges that get federal money from housing non-citizens who don't have legal permission to be in the country
Does not apply during disasters like fires, floods, or tornadoes with official disaster declarations
Covers elementary schools, high schools, and colleges

supporters: Supporters say this keeps public schools and colleges focused on educating students instead of housing non-citizens who don't have legal permission to be in the country.
Supporters say federal education money should go to students and teachers, not to providing shelter for people who entered the country illegally.
Supporters say schools can still help during official disasters like floods and fires, so emergency response is protected.
critics: Critics say this stops public schools and colleges from helping vulnerable non-citizens who need shelter in their communities.
Critics say removing the ability of federally-funded schools to provide housing takes away an important community safety net.
Critics say the disaster exception only covers official declarations and won't help during other emergencies when schools could provide shelter.

118-hr-3981.one_liner: Add reporting rules for schools that take veteran education money
provisions: Schools that take veteran education benefits must report within 30 days when state or federal agencies take action against them
Schools applying for approval of non-accredited courses must also follow these reporting rules
State agencies and the VA must revoke approval for schools that do not report these actions
Veterans who cannot finish courses because the VA removes school approval will not lose their education benefits
The VA must create a database within 180 days to track surveys of schools that take veteran education money

supporters: Supporters say the 30-day reporting rule will help veterans avoid schools that state and federal agencies have taken action against.
Supporters say veterans will keep their education benefits if they cannot finish courses when the VA removes school approval.
Supporters say the new database will help track which schools have problems with their veteran education programs.
critics: Critics say the 30-day reporting deadline is too short for schools to properly notify state agencies and the VA.
Critics say automatic revocation of approval is too harsh and could limit education choices for veterans.
Critics say creating the database within 180 days will cost money and may be rushed.

118-hr-3935.one_liner: Fund the FAA and airports through 2028
provisions: Funds the FAA and National Transportation Safety Board through 2028
Requires the FAA to hire more air traffic controllers
Requires airlines to install voice and video recorders in cockpits
Stops aircraft dispatchers from working from home except during emergencies
Requires airlines to refund passengers with disabilities if their wheelchair cannot fit in the cargo area
Makes airlines seat young children next to adults for free if seats are available next to each other
Creates new rules for flying drones beyond where pilots can see them

supporters: Supporters say hiring more air traffic controllers will make flying safer by reducing delays and preventing accidents.
Supporters say requiring cockpit voice and video recorders will help investigators figure out what went wrong after plane crashes.
Supporters say making airlines refund passengers with disabilities when their wheelchairs cannot fit will protect people who need mobility equipment.
critics: Critics say requiring airlines to install new voice and video recording equipment will cost millions of dollars that could raise ticket prices.
Critics say stopping aircraft dispatchers from working from home will hurt workers who need flexible schedules and increase company costs.
Critics say video recording pilots in cockpits invades their privacy and could distract them from flying safely.

118-hr-400.one_liner: Raise the limit for banks investing in small business funding companies from 5% to 15%
provisions: Raises the limit for banks to invest in small business funding companies from 5% to 15% of their money
Small business funding companies provide loans and investment money to small businesses
Applies to certain types of banking entities

supporters: Supporters say raising the limit from 5% to 15% would let banks put three times more money into small business funding companies.
Supporters say small businesses would get more loans and investment money because banks could invest more in the companies that fund them.
critics: Critics say allowing banks to invest 15% instead of 5% of their money in small business companies increases risk to the banking system.
Critics say banks might lose more money if small business investments fail because they can now put three times more capital at risk.

118-hr-406.one_liner: Give Southeast Asian organization legal protections from lawsuits and taxes
provisions: ASEAN gets protection from certain types of lawsuits in U.S. courts
ASEAN does not pay property taxes on buildings it owns in the U.S.
ASEAN is a group of 10 countries in Southeast Asia including Indonesia, Singapore, and Vietnam

supporters: Supporters say this gives ASEAN the same lawsuit protection that other international organizations already have in the U.S.
Supporters say this helps the U.S. build better ties with the 10 Southeast Asian countries in ASEAN, including Indonesia and Singapore.
critics: Critics say ASEAN will not pay property taxes on buildings it owns in the U.S. while American groups must pay these taxes.
Critics say giving lawsuit protection to ASEAN makes it harder for Americans to take legal action if the organization causes them harm.

118-hr-4366.one_liner: Fund military construction and veterans programs for 2024
provisions: Pays for building new military bases and facilities in 2024
Pays for VA offices that handle veterans disability and school benefits
Pays for VA hospitals and medical care for veterans
Pays for upkeep of veterans cemeteries
Pays for building and fixing homes for military families

supporters: Supporters say this bill ensures veterans get medical care through VA hospitals and disability benefits they earned through service.
Supporters say military families need safe housing and the bill funds construction and repairs for Army, Navy, and Air Force family homes.
Supporters say the military construction funding for all branches keeps bases ready to defend the country.
critics: Critics say the military construction funding for new Army, Navy, and Air Force facilities often exceeds original budgets, costing taxpayers more than planned.
Critics say the bill spreads funding across too many different agencies like the American Battle Monuments Commission instead of focusing on core veteran and military needs.

provisions: Gives money to border security to guard the U.S. borders
Gives money to immigration enforcement to find and deport people who entered the country illegally
Gives money to airport security workers who check passengers and bags
Gives money to the Coast Guard to patrol U.S. waters
Gives money to the Secret Service to protect the President and other government officials
Gives money to FEMA to respond to hurricanes, floods, and other disasters
Gives money to the agency that protects government computer systems
Sets rules on how the agencies can spend the money

supporters: Supporters say this funding helps U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents stop illegal border crossings and drug smuggling at ports of entry.
Supporters say Transportation Security Administration funding keeps airports safe by screening passengers and bags for weapons and explosives.
Supporters say FEMA funding helps communities rebuild after hurricanes, floods, and wildfires destroy homes and businesses.
critics: Critics say too much money goes to Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations instead of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services processing legal immigration cases.
Critics say border security agencies get more funding than the Federal Emergency Management Agency that helps disaster victims.
Critics say this money could instead fund the Department of Education or Department of Health and Human Services programs that help families.

provisions: Gives money to pay military salaries for 2024
Provides funds to buy weapons and military equipment
Pays for military research and testing programs
Funds military health care programs
Gives money to intelligence agencies
Pays for destroying old chemical weapons

supporters: Supporters say this bill ensures military service members receive their salaries and health care benefits in 2024.
Supporters say funding for weapons and equipment keeps the military ready to defend the country.
Supporters say money for intelligence agencies helps protect national security.
critics: Critics say the billions spent on weapons and military equipment could go to schools and health care instead.
Critics say funding military research and testing programs wastes taxpayer money.
Critics say giving more money to intelligence agencies increases government surveillance.

118-hr-443.one_liner: Require Labor Department workers to get training on finding human trafficking
provisions: Requires the Department of Labor to train its workers on human trafficking
Training covers how to spot signs of trafficking
Training covers how to help law enforcement with trafficking cases

supporters: Supporters say training Department of Labor workers to spot trafficking signs would help rescue victims during workplace inspections.
Supporters say teaching Department of Labor staff how to assist law enforcement would give police more trained eyes to identify trafficking cases.
critics: Critics say requiring Department of Labor to train all its workers on trafficking detection creates new costs without specifying funding.
Critics say this expands Department of Labor duties beyond workplace safety into law enforcement work.

118-hr-4368.one_liner: Fund food assistance programs, farm support, and food safety for 2024
provisions: Funds food assistance programs like SNAP that help families buy groceries
Pays for food safety inspections at meat plants and other food facilities
Funds rural housing loans and business development programs
Provides crop insurance payments to farmers
Pays for international food aid to other countries
Funds agricultural research and farm statistics

supporters: Supporters say SNAP food assistance programs help families buy groceries when they cannot afford food.
Supporters say food safety inspections at meat plants protect people from getting sick from unsafe food.
Supporters say crop insurance payments help farmers stay in business when bad weather destroys their crops.
critics: Critics say SNAP food assistance programs are expensive and cost taxpayers billions of dollars each year.
Critics say this bill spends taxpayer money on international food aid to other countries instead of helping Americans.
Critics say crop insurance payments give taxpayer money to farmers who should buy their own insurance.

118-hr-497.one_liner: Cancel a rule requiring healthcare workers to get COVID-19 vaccines
provisions: Cancels a 2021 rule that said healthcare workers must get COVID-19 vaccines
The rule applied to hospitals and clinics that take Medicare and Medicaid payments
Stops the government from making similar vaccine rules in the future
Healthcare facilities can now take Medicare and Medicaid payments without making staff get vaccinated

supporters: Supporters say this protects healthcare workers' freedom to choose about COVID-19 vaccines without losing jobs at hospitals and clinics that take Medicare and Medicaid payments.
Supporters say healthcare facilities can keep their Medicare and Medicaid funding even if staff are not vaccinated against COVID-19.
Supporters say this stops the government from making similar vaccine rules for healthcare workers in the future.
critics: Critics say unvaccinated healthcare workers could spread COVID-19 to patients in hospitals and clinics that take Medicare and Medicaid payments.
Critics say elderly and sick patients who use Medicare and Medicaid could face higher risk of getting COVID-19 from unvaccinated staff.
Critics say this removes a safety rule that protected vulnerable patients from COVID-19 in healthcare settings.

118-hr-4470.one_liner: Continue a chemical plant security program through September 2025
provisions: Keeps a Department of Homeland Security program running through September 2025
The program sets security rules for chemical plants
Without this bill, the program would stop operating

supporters: Supporters say this bill keeps the Department of Homeland Security's security program for chemical plants running through September 2025.
Supporters say the program protects communities near chemical facilities from terrorist attacks.
Supporters say without this bill, chemical plants would lose federal security rules.
critics: Critics say the program forces chemical companies to follow federal security rules that cost them money.
Critics say extending the program through September 2025 continues federal control over private chemical facilities.

118-hr-485.one_liner: Stop federal health programs from using disability-based pricing
provisions: Blocks federal health programs from using a pricing method that treats disabled lives as worth less
Applies to Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health plans, and other federally funded programs
Affects decisions about treatment coverage and payment amounts

supporters: Supporters say this bill would stop Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee health plans from using quality-adjusted life years that discount the value of disabled people's lives.
Supporters say this would protect disabled patients from having their treatment coverage and payment amounts decided by measures that treat their lives as worth less.
critics: Critics say removing quality-adjusted life years from Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee health programs could increase costs without a tool to measure treatment effectiveness.
Critics say federal health programs need this pricing method to make fair coverage and reimbursement decisions with limited budgets.

118-hr-467.one_liner: Make all fentanyl-related substances illegal under federal drug laws
provisions: Classifies all fentanyl-related substances as illegal drugs with the same penalties as heroin
Creates a new registration process for researchers studying these substances with government funding
Allows researchers to use one registration for multiple related study sites
Lets researchers make small amounts of these substances for studies without separate manufacturing permits

supporters: Supporters say placing all fentanyl-related substances in Schedule I gives law enforcement the same penalties to use against fentanyl dealers as heroin dealers.
Supporters say the new registration process for government-funded research will help scientists study these substances faster.
Supporters say allowing one registration for multiple research sites will reduce paperwork for scientists.
critics: Critics say classifying all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I could block medical research into potential treatments.
Critics say the broad classification may criminalize substances that have not been proven dangerous.
Critics say researchers will still face barriers studying these substances even with the new registration process.

118-hr-4665.one_liner: Fund State Department foreign programs and international aid for 2024
provisions: Provides money for State Department operations in other countries
Funds foreign aid programs through USAID
Pays for international security assistance to other nations
Supports Peace Corps volunteers and U.S. embassies abroad
Funds programs that promote democracy and human rights overseas

supporters: Supporters say this funds State Department operations needed to protect Americans abroad and run U.S. embassies in other countries.
Supporters say this provides foreign aid through USAID that helps respond to humanitarian crises and promotes stability in key regions.
Supporters say this supports Peace Corps volunteers and democracy programs that build relationships with other nations and advance American values overseas.
critics: Critics say this spends taxpayer money on foreign programs when domestic infrastructure and social services need more funding.
Critics say this sends international security assistance to countries that may not always support American interests or use the aid effectively.
Critics say this funds democracy and human rights programs that other nations may view as unwanted interference in their internal affairs.

118-hr-500.one_liner: Let investment companies delay withdrawals when they suspect elder financial abuse
provisions: Lets investment companies delay withdrawals for up to 15 days if they think someone 65 or older is being financially exploited
Lets them delay another 10 days if they confirm exploitation is happening
Also applies to adults 18 or older who cannot protect themselves
Companies must keep the money in a bank account during delays
Requires the SEC to make recommendations about stopping financial exploitation of older adults

supporters: Supporters say this bill would protect adults 65 and older from scammers who try to steal their retirement savings by giving investment companies 15 days to investigate suspicious withdrawals.
Supporters say the additional 10-day delay gives companies time to work with authorities to stop financial theft before victims lose their money.
Supporters say this bill helps adults 18 and older who cannot protect themselves from being tricked into giving away their investments.
critics: Critics say the 15-day delay keeps people from accessing their own money when they need it for emergencies or bills.
Critics say investment companies could misuse these rules to block legitimate withdrawals from customers for up to 25 days total.
Critics say adults 65 and older should have the right to withdraw their own money without companies deciding if they are being exploited.

118-hr-5110.one_liner: Let schools use federal education funds to buy weapons for archery and shooting sports training
provisions: Lets schools use federal education money to buy weapons for teaching archery, hunting, and shooting sports
Changes a rule that currently stops schools from using these funds to buy weapons or train students to use them
Creates an exception only for archery, hunting, and shooting sports classes

supporters: Supporters say this lets schools use federal education money to teach students archery, hunting, and shooting sports skills.
Supporters say this gives schools the ability to offer outdoor education programs that were blocked by current federal funding rules.
critics: Critics say this allows schools to spend federal education money on weapons that are currently banned from school purchases.
Critics say this changes federal safety rules that prevent schools from using education funds to buy weapons or train students to use them.

118-hr-5.one_liner: Give parents rights to review school curriculums and meet with teachers
provisions: Parents can review what their children learn in school
Parents can meet with their child's teachers at least twice each school year
Parents can see school budgets and how money is spent
Parents can review lists of books in school libraries
Schools must post what they teach online for parents to see
Schools cannot sell student information to make money
Schools must tell parents about violence at their child's school

supporters: Supporters say this gives parents the right to see what their children learn by requiring schools to post all curriculum online and allow parents to review teaching materials.
Supporters say this ensures parents stay connected to their child's education by requiring teachers to meet with parents at least twice each school year.
Supporters say this protects student privacy by stopping schools from selling student information to companies for money.
critics: Critics say requiring schools to post all curriculum online and provide extensive documentation to parents will create extra work and costs for already busy school staff.
Critics say allowing parents to review library book lists could lead to book removal when parents object to certain materials.
Critics say requiring teachers to meet with parents twice per year for every student could take time away from classroom instruction and planning.

118-hr-538.one_liner: Require companies to tell customers when smart devices have cameras or microphones
provisions: Companies must tell customers when smart devices have cameras or microphones
Does not cover phones, laptops, and other devices where people normally expect cameras
Applies to smart home devices like connected appliances and other products

supporters: Supporters say this helps consumers know when smart home appliances have cameras or microphones that could record them.
Supporters say the disclosure requirement protects privacy by telling people about recording features in devices like smart TVs and connected appliances.
critics: Critics say the disclosure requirements add new rules and costs for companies making internet-connected devices.
Critics say consumers can already find information about cameras and microphones in product manuals and descriptions.

provisions: Extends wildlife conservation programs through the year 2028
Continues the Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program
Continues money for protecting African elephants, Asian elephants, rhinoceroses, tigers, great apes, and marine turtles
Changes how several wildlife conservation programs work

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects African elephants, Asian elephants, rhinoceroses, tigers, great apes, and marine turtles through 2028.
Supporters say this continues the Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program that helps private landowners protect animal habitats.
Supporters say these conservation programs prevent endangered species from going extinct.
critics: Critics say extending these wildlife programs through 2028 costs taxpayers money that should go to other priorities.
Critics say the changes to how conservation programs work could make them work worse or cost more.
Critics say this spends money on protecting animals in other countries like African elephants instead of helping Americans.

118-hr-5585.one_liner: Make it a federal crime to flee from Border Patrol officers near the border
provisions: Makes it a federal crime to drive away from Border Patrol officers within 100 miles of the US border
Sets prison sentences for people who commit this crime
Requires longer prison sentences if someone gets badly hurt or dies during the chase
Permanently bans non-citizens from getting legal status if they commit this crime while in the US illegally

supporters: Supporters say this would protect Border Patrol officers from dangerous car chases in the 100-mile border zone where they work.
Supporters say the required longer prison sentences for cases with death or serious injury would stop people from putting officers and others at risk.
Supporters say the permanent ban on getting legal status would deter people in the US illegally from running from Border Patrol.
critics: Critics say the 100-mile border zone covers nearly 200 million Americans who live far from the actual border.
Critics say the required minimum prison sentences take away judges' power to look at each case differently.
Critics say the permanent ban on ever getting legal status is too harsh and ruins people's chances for life.

118-hr-5528.one_liner: Require a study of government buying rules for security risks
provisions: Tells the Office of Management and Budget to study how government agencies buy things
The study checks if rules about buying the cheapest option create security problems
The office must report what they find to Congress

supporters: Supporters say the Office of Management and Budget study will identify when lowest price procurement rules create national security risks.
Supporters say the report to Congress will help lawmakers understand if cheap foreign equipment threatens government security.
critics: Critics say requiring the Office of Management and Budget to evaluate all agency procurement activities adds unnecessary bureaucracy.
Critics say the study could be used to justify abandoning lowest price rules and waste taxpayer money on expensive contracts.

118-hr-5856.one_liner: Continue funding programs that fight human trafficking around the world
provisions: Continues funding for programs that fight human trafficking in other countries
Requires all U.S. aid projects to include anti-trafficking work
Adds organ trafficking to the government's yearly trafficking report

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing international anti-trafficking programs will continue funding that helps rescue victims in other countries.
Supporters say requiring all U.S. foreign aid projects to include anti-trafficking strategies will catch more traffickers.
Supporters say adding organ trafficking information to the annual Trafficking in Persons Report will help governments track this crime.
critics: Critics say mandating anti-trafficking work in all foreign aid projects will increase costs and slow down other assistance programs.
Critics say requiring organ trafficking data in the yearly report will create more work for government agencies.

118-hr-5862.one_liner: Give customs agents more authority to reorganize customs revenue jobs and staffing
provisions: Lets Customs and Border Protection add duties to existing customs workers
Lets CBP create new job types and pay grades for customs revenue workers
Lets CBP reduce staffing in some customs areas if it will not go below optimal levels
Adds national account managers and international trade analysts to jobs that cannot be cut easily

118-hr-5860.one_liner: Fund the federal government through November 17, 2023
provisions: Funds federal agencies at the same spending levels as 2023 through November 17, 2023
Prevents a government shutdown that would otherwise start October 1, 2023
Provides emergency funding for disaster relief through FEMA
Extends the National Flood Insurance Program through November 17, 2023
Extends airport improvement grants and FAA programs through December 31, 2023
Extends funding for community health centers and diabetes programs through November 17, 2023

118-hr-663.one_liner: Fund programs preventing child abuse in Native American communities through 2028
provisions: Continues funding programs that prevent child abuse in Native American families through 2028
Lets tribes use grant money to pay for child protective services and other family help
Expands a national center that trains people working with Native American children
Creates model agreements between tribes and states to handle child abuse cases

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects Native American children by continuing funding for abuse prevention programs through 2028
Supporters say tribes can now use grant money to pay for child protective services instead of just treatment programs
Supporters say the expanded national center will train more people who work with Native American children in urban areas
critics: Critics say this bill costs taxpayers money to fund these programs for five more years through 2028
Critics say expanding the national center adds more government workers and bureaucracy
Critics say the model agreements between tribes and states could create confusion about which government handles child abuse cases

118-hr-589.one_liner: Require sanctions on Iran's Supreme Leader and President for human rights abuses
provisions: Freezes money and property of Iran's Supreme Leader and President in the United States
Stops Iran's top leaders from getting permission to enter the United States
Requires the President to check every few months if sanctions should apply to Iranian officials
Targets Iranian groups that help with human rights abuses or terrorism

supporters: Supporters say freezing the Supreme Leader and President's money in the United States will stop Iran's top officials from using American banks to fund oppression.
Supporters say blocking visas for Iran's leaders will prevent them from traveling to the US while they abuse their own people.
Supporters say targeting Iranian groups that help with human rights abuses will cut off support for violence against protesters.
critics: Critics say blocking Iran's President from entering the United States could hurt talks to solve nuclear and other problems.
Critics say freezing Iranian leaders' property won't change how Iran treats protesters since most of their money is kept in other countries.
Critics say requiring the President to check sanctions every few months creates too much work without clear benefits.

118-hr-6126.one_liner: Fund military aid and defense systems for Israel
provisions: Replaces military equipment that was given to Israel
Pays back the Defense Department for training and services given to Israel
Buys Iron Dome and David's Sling defense systems for Israel
Develops Iron Beam defense system for Israel
Funds State Department security programs
Gives the President more power to transfer military equipment to Israel
Takes back unspent money from the IRS

118-hr-662.one_liner: Give states block grants to help farmers with 2022 disaster losses
provisions: Lets the Department of Agriculture give block grants to states and territories
Uses existing funding to help farmers who lost crops or livestock in 2022
Covers losses from droughts, wildfires, hurricanes, floods, and other natural disasters
Only applies to disasters that happened in calendar year 2022

supporters: Supporters say this would help farmers and ranchers who lost crops and livestock during the droughts, wildfires, hurricanes, and other natural disasters that hit in 2022.
Supporters say block grants let states decide how to distribute the aid to farmers who need it most in their area.
Supporters say this uses existing Department of Agriculture funding instead of requiring new taxpayer money.
critics: Critics say limiting aid to only 2022 disasters leaves out farmers who suffered losses from natural disasters in 2021, 2023, and other years.
Critics say block grants could lead to unequal distribution of aid, with some states getting more help per affected farmer than others.
Critics say this sets a precedent of using federal money to bail out farmers for weather-related losses that are part of normal farming risks.

118-hr-6363.one_liner: Fund the federal government through early 2024 to prevent shutdown
provisions: Funds most federal agencies through February 2, 2024 at 2023 spending levels
Funds farm, energy, veterans, and transportation agencies through January 19, 2024
Extends farm programs that were set to expire
Extends public health programs and the U.S. Parole Commission
Prevents government shutdown that would start November 17, 2023

supporters: Supporters say this prevents a government shutdown that would start November 17, 2023 by funding federal agencies through February 2024.
Supporters say this extends farm programs and public health programs that were set to expire, keeping essential services running.
Supporters say this maintains funding for veterans affairs, transportation, and agriculture agencies through January 19, 2024 at 2023 levels.
critics: Critics say this only provides temporary funding through February 2024 instead of full-year budget certainty for federal agencies.
Critics say maintaining 2023 spending levels fails to account for inflation affecting government operations.
Critics say extending programs temporarily instead of long-term reauthorization creates ongoing uncertainty.

118-hr-6914.one_liner: Require colleges to provide pregnancy information to students
provisions: Requires colleges that receive federal student aid to give students information about pregnancy rights and resources
Colleges must list places that help pregnant students carry their baby to term and care for the baby after birth
Colleges must explain what support they offer pregnant students and new parents
Colleges must tell students how to report pregnancy discrimination

118-hr-6678.one_liner: Make Social Security fraud grounds for deportation and blocking entry for non-citizens
provisions: Makes creating fake IDs without permission grounds for deporting non-citizens
Makes lying on Social Security disability applications grounds for deporting non-citizens
Blocks non-citizens from entering the U.S. if convicted of these Social Security fraud crimes
Applies to people convicted of the crimes or who admit to doing them

118-hr-6679.one_liner: Block Hamas members and October 7 attackers from US immigration benefits
provisions: Blocks Hamas members from entering the United States
