critics: Critics say this removes protection for southern prairie chickens that scientists listed as endangered.
Critics say this cancels November 2022 protections when prairie chicken populations are declining.

118-sres-417.one_liner: Expresses Senate support for Israel against Hamas
provisions: States the Senate stands with Israel as it defends itself
Says Israel has the right to defend itself
Calls on all countries to condemn Hamas' war on Israel
Says the US remains committed to Israel's security
Supports emergency military supplies and other help for Israel
Calls on the US to lead efforts to cut off Hamas funding from Iran and other sources
Says this does not declare war or authorize US military force

supporters: Supporters say this resolution reaffirms Israel's right to defend itself and shows US commitment to a key ally's security.
Supporters say calling on all countries to condemn Hamas' war on Israel builds international pressure against terrorism.
Supporters say supporting emergency military supplies helps Israel protect itself while the resolution clearly states it does not authorize US military force.
critics: Critics say the resolution's one-sided support for Israel could make the conflict worse by not addressing both sides.
Critics say supporting emergency military supplies and aid could increase violence and civilian deaths.
Critics say calling on the US to lead efforts to cut off Hamas funding from Iran could pull America deeper into the conflict.

119-hconres-61.one_liner: Remove U.S. troops from fighting terrorist groups in the Western Hemisphere
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. troops out of fights with terrorist groups in the Western Hemisphere
Does not apply if Congress has passed a law allowing the military action
Covers any group the President has labeled a terrorist organization
Applies to military operations in North, Central, and South America

supporters: Supporters say this bill would force the President to get Congress approval before fighting any terrorist group he has labeled in North, Central, and South America.
Supporters say this would stop military operations against presidentially designated terrorist organizations in the Western Hemisphere unless Congress passes a law allowing the fights.
critics: Critics say this could end ongoing U.S. military operations against terrorist groups across the Western Hemisphere.
Critics say this would slow down the President's response to threats from terrorist organizations the President has designated in the Americas.

119-hconres-38.one_liner: Stop U.S. military action against Iran without Congress approval
provisions: Tells the President to end all military action against Iran unless Congress declares war or approves the use of force
Lets the U.S. defend itself if Iran attacks first
Uses the War Powers Resolution to force the President to remove troops

supporters: Supporters say this would make the President follow the Constitution by getting Congress to declare war or approve force before military action against Iran.
Supporters say the War Powers Resolution requires congressional approval for hostilities, and this bill would end unauthorized military action against the Iranian government.
Supporters say the bill protects the right to self-defense if Iran attacks the United States first.
critics: Critics say forcing the removal of U.S. forces could limit the President's ability to respond quickly to Iranian threats against American troops or allies.
Critics say the self-defense exception might not cover protecting U.S. bases or allies from Iranian attacks.
Critics say this could weaken deterrence against Iran by restricting military options unless Congress approves them first.

119-hconres-64.one_liner: Remove U.S. military forces from Venezuela unless Congress declares war or authorizes force
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. military forces out of Venezuela
Only applies if Congress has not declared war on Venezuela
Only applies if Congress has not given permission for military action there

supporters: Supporters say this bill would make Congress vote before the U.S. goes to war with Venezuela, as the Constitution requires.
Supporters say this would stop the President from using military force in Venezuela without getting permission from Congress first.
Supporters say this would pull U.S. forces out of Venezuela unless Congress votes to declare war or authorize military action there.
critics: Critics say this bill would tie the President's hands if Venezuela threatens U.S. citizens or allies in South America.
Critics say this could help Venezuela's government by forcing the U.S. to remove military pressure.
Critics say this would require the President to pull forces out even if they are protecting American interests in the region.

118-sres-504.one_liner: Request information from the State Department about Israel's human rights practices
provisions: Asks the State Department to provide Congress with information about Israel's human rights practices
Requests information about steps the US has taken to promote human rights in Israel's activities in Gaza and the West Bank
Asks for an assessment of whether Israel follows international human rights law
Requests information about whether Israel will use US security assistance in armed conflicts in Gaza and the West Bank

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would give Congress the information it needs to oversee how Israel uses US security assistance in Gaza and the West Bank.
Supporters say the State Department assessment of Israel's compliance with international human rights law would help ensure US aid follows existing human rights standards.
critics: Critics say this resolution creates reporting requirements about Israel's human rights practices that other US allies do not have.
Critics say the State Department already provides Congress with information about human rights practices through existing reports.

119-hjres-130.one_liner: Cancel a rule that stopped coal leasing in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office
provisions: Cancels a Bureau of Land Management rule from November 2024
The rule stopped all future coal leasing in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office
Brings back coal leasing under the 2015 land use plan
Makes federal coal in this Wyoming area available for companies to lease again

supporters: Supporters say this bill brings back coal leasing in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office that was stopped by the November 2024 Bureau of Land Management rule.
Supporters say restoring the 2015 land use plan will create coal mining jobs and revenue for Wyoming communities.
critics: Critics say this bill ignores the court ruling that required the Bureau of Land Management to study climate impacts before allowing coal leasing in the Buffalo Field Office.
Critics say canceling the 2024 rule removes protections that made federal coal unavailable for future leasing in this Wyoming area.

119-hjres-140.one_liner: Allow mineral and geothermal leasing on 225,504 acres in Minnesota
provisions: Cancels a 2023 rule that stopped companies from leasing forest land for mining
Affects 225,504 acres in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, Minnesota
Lets companies lease this land to look for minerals and geothermal energy
Removes protections that were supposed to last 20 years
Includes areas near the Boundary Waters wilderness

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2023 rule would create mining jobs in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties where 225,504 acres would be open for mineral leasing.
Supporters say allowing companies to lease this land for mineral exploration would boost the local economy and provide domestic sources of critical minerals.
Supporters say the 20-year mining ban hurts local communities that depend on resource extraction for jobs and tax revenue.
critics: Critics say removing protections from 225,504 acres near the Boundary Waters wilderness would threaten clean water in the Rainy River Watershed.
Critics say canceling the 2023 rule would break promises to protect the 1854 Ceded Territory of the Lake Superior Chippewa from mining damage.
Critics say mineral leasing in these three Minnesota counties would harm tourism that depends on clean lakes and forests.

119-hconres-68.one_liner: Remove U.S. troops from Venezuela unless Congress votes to keep them there
provisions: Orders the President to remove U.S. troops from Venezuela
Troops can stay only if Congress declares war against Venezuela or votes to authorize military action there

supporters: Supporters say this would make the President remove U.S. troops from Venezuela unless Congress votes to authorize the mission.
Supporters say this follows the Constitution by requiring Congress approval before keeping military forces in another country.
critics: Critics say forcing removal of U.S. troops from Venezuela could hurt American security interests in the region.
Critics say this could end important military partnerships or intelligence work that protects Americans.

119-hjres-131.one_liner: Cancel a rule that limited oil drilling to 400,000 acres in an Alaska wildlife refuge
provisions: Cancels a December 2024 rule from the Bureau of Land Management
The rule limited oil and gas drilling to 400,000 acres in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
Opens up all 1.6 million acres in the refuge for oil and gas drilling
Removes protections from 1.2 million acres that were off-limits to drilling

supporters: Supporters say this would make an additional 1.2 million acres in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge available for oil and gas drilling.
Supporters say removing the limit of 400,000 acres would increase domestic oil production.
Supporters say the 2024 rule blocked access to areas with the highest potential for finding oil.
critics: Critics say this would remove protections from 1.2 million acres in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
Critics say opening all 1.6 million acres to drilling could harm caribou and other wildlife in the refuge.
Critics say this overturns rules designed to protect and conserve resources in the wildlife refuge.

119-hjres-117.one_liner: End the national emergency declared on July 30, 2025
provisions: Ends the national emergency that the President declared on July 30, 2025
Stops any special powers the President got from the emergency declaration
Returns government operations to normal rules

supporters: Supporters say this bill would end the July 30, 2025 national emergency declaration and return the government to normal operating rules.
Supporters say the special presidential powers granted by the July 30, 2025 emergency should be stopped and regular procedures restored.
critics: Critics say ending the July 30, 2025 national emergency could remove needed presidential authorities that are still required.
Critics say this bill would force government operations back to normal rules before the situation that prompted the July 30, 2025 declaration is fully resolved.

119-hr-1005.one_liner: Stop public schools from taking money from China's government
provisions: Public schools cannot take money from China's government or the Chinese Communist Party
Public schools cannot sign contracts with China's government or the Chinese Communist Party
Schools that break these rules lose their federal funding
Schools must tell the Education Department about any foreign funding

supporters: Supporters say blocking public schools from taking Chinese government money protects students from foreign influence.
Supporters say requiring schools to tell the Education Department about foreign funding gives parents and officials important information.
Supporters say schools that follow the ban on Chinese government contracts will keep getting federal education funds.
critics: Critics say schools could lose all their federal education funding if they accidentally sign a contract with someone connected to the Chinese government.
Critics say the requirement to report all foreign funding to the Education Department creates extra work for school staff.
Critics say the ban on contracts with Chinese government groups could end useful student exchange programs.

119-hr-1049.one_liner: Require schools to tell parents about foreign money and influence in their schools
provisions: Schools must tell parents they have the right to ask about foreign money in their schools
Parents can request to see any teaching materials bought with foreign government money
Parents can request to know how many school workers are paid with foreign government money
Parents can request information about contracts or funding from foreign countries
Schools must post notice of these parent rights on their websites
Schools that don't comply lose federal education funding

supporters: Supporters say parents have the right to know if foreign governments are paying school workers or funding teaching materials used in their children's classrooms.
Supporters say schools should post public notices about these parent rights on their websites so families can request information about foreign funding.
Supporters say this bill ensures transparency when foreign countries have contracts or funding agreements with local schools.
critics: Critics say schools will face administrative costs to track foreign funding sources and respond to parent requests for information about contracts and staff compensation.
Critics say the requirement to notify parents about foreign influence could discourage schools from participating in existing international education programs and partnerships.
Critics say schools risk losing all federal education funding if they fail to properly post notices or respond to parent requests about foreign involvement.

119-hr-1047.one_liner: Speed up connections for reliable power plants to the electric grid
provisions: Requires federal energy regulators to create new rules for connecting power plants to the electric grid
Lets reliable power plants that can turn on when needed skip ahead in the waiting list
Allows power companies to request their reliable plants get moved up in line
Gives regulators 60 days to approve or reject these requests

supporters: Supporters say this would help reliable power plants that can turn on when needed connect to the electric grid faster by allowing them to skip ahead in the waiting list.
Supporters say the 60-day deadline for federal regulators to approve or reject these requests would speed up decisions for power companies.
critics: Critics say this would give dispatchable power plants preferential treatment in the interconnection queue over renewable energy projects.
Critics say allowing power companies to request their plants get moved up in line could delay other energy projects already waiting for grid connections.

119-hjres-142.one_liner: Cancel DC's tax law to keep federal tax cuts
provisions: Cancels a DC tax law passed in December 2025
Keeps tips exempt from DC income tax for tipped workers
Keeps the higher standard tax deduction for all DC taxpayers
Blocks DC from restoring its child tax credit for families
Keeps business tax benefits for commercial property

supporters: Supporters say this keeps tips exempt from DC income tax for restaurant workers and other tipped employees.
Supporters say this preserves the higher standard tax deduction that reduces taxes for all DC taxpayers.
Supporters say this maintains business tax benefits for commercial property owners in DC.
critics: Critics say this blocks DC from restoring its child tax credit that would help families with children.
Critics say this prevents DC from making its own tax decisions and forces the city to keep federal tax changes.
Critics say this reduces tax revenue that DC needs to fund local services.

provisions: AI summary temporarily unavailable
119-hjres-72.one_liner: Relating to a national emergency by the President on February 1, 2025.

supporters: Supporters say this bill provides Congress with necessary oversight of the February 1st emergency declaration to ensure proper checks and balances.
Supporters say this legislation clarifies the scope and duration of emergency powers used since February 1st to prevent government overreach.
critics: Critics say this bill undermines the President's ability to respond quickly to the ongoing emergency situation declared on February 1st.
Critics say the legislation creates unnecessary bureaucratic delays when swift executive action is needed to address the national emergency.

119-hr-131.one_liner: Cut costs for Colorado communities paying for a water pipeline project
provisions: Removes interest payments that Colorado communities owe for the Arkansas Valley Conduit water pipeline
Extends the repayment time to 100 years
Pipeline brings water from Pueblo Reservoir to communities in Arkansas River Valley

supporters: Supporters say removing interest payments will help Colorado communities in the Arkansas River Valley afford water from the Pueblo Reservoir pipeline.
Supporters say the 100-year repayment period will make monthly payments more manageable for these communities.
critics: Critics say removing interest payments will force taxpayers to subsidize the Arkansas Valley Conduit construction costs.
Critics say the 100-year repayment period means the Bureau of Reclamation will wait much longer to recover project costs.

119-hr-1608.one_liner: Require DHS to write a report on preventing car and truck attacks
provisions: Requires DHS to write a report about preventing people from using cars and trucks in terrorist attacks
Report must list what threats exist now and what new threats might come
Report must identify places that could be targets like airports and government buildings
Report must explain how DHS works with police to prevent vehicle attacks
Report must suggest new technology to detect and stop vehicle attacks
DHS must give Congress a classified version and post a summary online
DHS must present the findings to Congress in a briefing

supporters: Supporters say the threat assessment requirement would help identify current and emerging vehicle attack threats that DHS may not be tracking.
Supporters say identifying vulnerable locations like airports and government buildings would help protect places where many people gather.
Supporters say the coordination requirements with police agencies would improve information sharing to prevent vehicle attacks.
critics: Critics say the reporting requirement adds paperwork burden to DHS when the agency could use those resources for actual security work.
Critics say the classified report structure limits public oversight since only the summary goes online while Congress gets the full details.
Critics say the bill may duplicate existing DHS assessments of critical infrastructure sites like airports that already have security reviews.

119-hr-1069.one_liner: Block federal funding to schools with Chinese government partnerships
provisions: Blocks federal money to elementary and high schools that partner with Chinese government groups
Cuts funding to schools with Confucius Institutes or Chinese-funded learning centers
Stops funding to schools that get Chinese teaching materials, staff, or money
Lets schools ask for an exception if they prove their Chinese partnership helps America
Requires the Education Department to notify schools about these new rules

supporters: Supporters say cutting federal funding to schools with Confucius Institutes protects students from Chinese government influence in American classrooms.
Supporters say blocking federal money to schools that get Chinese teaching materials and staff prevents foreign control of elementary and high school education.
Supporters say requiring schools to prove their Chinese partnerships help America before getting waivers ensures taxpayer money only supports programs that benefit the United States.
critics: Critics say removing federal funding from schools with Chinese-funded learning centers will eliminate language programs that help thousands of students learn Mandarin.
Critics say the waiver requirement forces schools to choose between losing federal education money and ending partnerships that provide free teaching resources and staff.
Critics say blocking funding to schools that receive Chinese teaching materials will hurt rural schools that depend on these programs for foreign language classes.

119-hr-1366.one_liner: Allow mining waste disposal on federal land without proving minerals exist
provisions: Lets mining companies dispose of waste on federal land even if the land has no valuable minerals
Overturns a 2022 court ruling that limited where mining companies could dispose of waste
Creates a fund to clean up old abandoned mines
Requires fees from mining companies that go into the cleanup fund
Lets mining companies claim as many waste disposal sites as they need

supporters: Supporters say this fixes the legal uncertainty created by the 2022 Rosemont court ruling that blocked mining projects from moving forward.
Supporters say the bill creates a fund paid for by mining company fees to clean up old abandoned mines across the country.
Supporters say mining companies need flexibility to dispose of waste rock and this allows them to claim as many disposal sites as their operations require.
critics: Critics say this lets mining companies dump waste on federal lands even when those lands contain no valuable minerals worth mining.
Critics say the bill overturns court protections that prevented mining companies from using federal land solely for waste disposal.
Critics say mining companies can now claim unlimited waste disposal sites on public land under their approved operations.

119-hr-1531.one_liner: Require federal agencies to exclude China from international financial groups if China threatens Taiwan
provisions: Requires Treasury, Federal Reserve, and SEC to exclude China from six international financial organizations if the President says China threatens Taiwan
Covers organizations like the Group of Twenty and Bank for International Settlements
President can waive this requirement if it serves US national interest

supporters: Supporters say this bill gives the US a way to pressure China by removing them from six important financial groups like the Group of Twenty and Bank for International Settlements when China threatens Taiwan's security or economic system.
Supporters say the President can waive these exclusion rules if keeping China in these organizations serves US national interests, which gives flexibility to avoid hurting America.
Supporters say requiring the Treasury, Federal Reserve, and SEC to take action creates real consequences when China threatens Taiwan instead of just empty warnings.
critics: Critics say excluding China from six major financial organizations like the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision could damage US relationships with other member countries who want to keep working with China.
Critics say this bill gives the President too much power to decide when China threatens Taiwan, which could lead to excluding China from important financial groups over minor disagreements.
Critics say removing China from organizations that help oversee global banking and securities could make the world's financial system less stable and harder to manage.

119-hr-1676.one_liner: Set deadlines for federal approval of state wildlife conservation plans
provisions: Gives the federal government 180 days to approve state wildlife conservation plans
Automatically approves state wildlife plans if the federal government misses the deadline
Requires the federal government to set aside grant money for states when it misses deadlines

supporters: Supporters say the 180-day deadline would speed up approval of state wildlife plans that now sit in federal offices for months or years.
Supporters say automatic approval prevents federal delays from stopping important conservation work that protects local wildlife.
Supporters say states would get their grant money faster when federal agencies miss deadlines instead of waiting indefinitely for approvals.
critics: Critics say automatic approval after 180 days could allow weak conservation plans to pass without proper federal review of whether they meet wildlife protection standards.
Critics say removing federal oversight could let states waste grant money on poorly planned programs that fail to protect endangered species.
Critics say the 180-day deadline is too short for federal experts to properly check if state plans follow conservation science and legal requirements.

119-hr-2189.one_liner: Remove certain TASERs and similar devices from federal gun regulations
provisions: Removes TASERs and similar non-lethal weapons from federal gun laws
Only covers devices that fire projectiles slower than 500 feet per second
Devices cannot be easily changed to shoot regular bullets
The ATF must decide within 90 days if a device qualifies when manufacturers ask

supporters: Supporters say removing TASERs and similar devices from federal gun laws will help police departments get non-lethal tools faster without gun regulation paperwork.
Supporters say the 90-day ATF decision timeline will speed up approval for new de-escalation devices that could save lives.
Supporters say the 500 feet per second speed limit and ban on regular ammunition ensures these devices stay safe and non-lethal.
critics: Critics say removing federal oversight of TASER-type devices could lead to misuse by police without proper safety checks.
Critics say the definition of less-than-lethal devices is too broad and manufacturers could exploit loopholes to avoid gun regulations.
Critics say taking these weapons out of gun control laws could put more dangerous devices on the market without enough safety testing.

119-hr-2262.one_liner: Stop counting voluntary training as paid work time
provisions: Changes federal rules about what counts as work hours
Voluntary training outside regular work hours does not count as paid time
Workers can skip training without it affecting their job
Training cannot include actual work tasks

supporters: Supporters say this helps workers get job training without forcing employers to pay overtime for voluntary programs outside regular work hours.
Supporters say workers are protected because they can skip training without it affecting their job status or working conditions.
Supporters say this clarifies federal rules so employers can offer professional development without wage costs for voluntary training.
critics: Critics say workers may feel pressured to attend unpaid training even though it is called voluntary.
Critics say this reduces worker pay by excluding training time from hours worked under federal labor law.
Critics say employers could use voluntary training programs to get around paying overtime wages.

119-hr-1949.one_liner: Remove government restrictions on natural gas exports to other countries
provisions: Removes the requirement for a government agency to approve natural gas sales to other countries
Cancels rules about free trade agreements for natural gas exports
Gives FERC, a federal agency that regulates energy, control over approving exports and shipping facilities
FERC must decide that exports help the public

supporters: Supporters say giving FERC exclusive authority over LNG facilities would speed up approval by having one agency instead of multiple agencies review projects.
Supporters say removing the DOE approval requirement would allow natural gas companies to export more quickly and boost domestic production.
Supporters say more LNG exports would create jobs in the natural gas industry and help the US sell energy to other countries.
critics: Critics say removing DOE oversight could weaken environmental and safety reviews of LNG export facilities.
Critics say more natural gas exports could raise prices for American families by sending domestic gas overseas.
Critics say FERC may not fully consider climate impacts when deciding if exports help the public interest.
