119-hr-261.one_liner: Remove Commerce Department permit rules for undersea cables in marine sanctuaries
provisions: Stops the Commerce Department from requiring permits for undersea cable work in marine sanctuaries
If another government agency already approved the cable work, Commerce cannot ask for more permits
Covers installing, fixing, and removing undersea internet cables
Lets NOAA work with other agencies when cable work might damage marine sanctuary areas

supporters: Supporters say this bill cuts red tape by stopping the Commerce Department from requiring extra permits when other federal or state agencies have already approved undersea cable work.
Supporters say this speeds up installation of undersea internet cables that provide internet service to communities.
Supporters say the bill still allows NOAA to work with other agencies when cable work might damage marine sanctuary areas.
critics: Critics say removing Commerce Department permit requirements weakens protection of national marine sanctuaries from cable installation damage.
Critics say other agencies that approve cable work may not have the same expertise about marine sanctuary protection that the Commerce Department has.
Critics say this bill allows undersea cable companies to bypass Commerce Department review even when their work could harm sensitive marine areas.

119-hr-2550.one_liner: Cancel an Executive Order that removed union rights from some federal agencies
provisions: Cancels an Executive Order from March 27, 2025 that removed union rights from some federal agencies
Brings back the right for federal workers at those agencies to form unions and bargain for pay and benefits
Keeps existing union contracts in place through their original end dates

supporters: Supporters say this restores union rights for federal workers that were removed by the March 27, 2025 Executive Order.
Supporters say federal employees at affected agencies should be able to bargain for better pay and working conditions like other workers.
Supporters say keeping existing union contracts in place protects deals workers already made with their agencies.
critics: Critics say this blocks the president's ability to manage federal agencies without union interference.
Critics say union contracts at federal agencies could cost taxpayers more money through higher wages and benefits.
Critics say some federal agencies work better when managers can make quick decisions without union rules.

119-hr-2659.one_liner: Create a government task force to fight Chinese cyber attacks
provisions: Creates a government task force to fight Chinese hackers
Task force coordinates agencies like the FBI and Department of Defense
Agencies must share information about cyber attacks with the task force
Task force reports to Congress once a year for 6 years about cyber threats
First report due within 18 months

supporters: Supporters say this task force would help CISA coordinate the FBI, Department of Defense, and other agencies that currently fight Chinese hackers separately.
Supporters say requiring agencies to share cyber attack information with the task force would help stop Chinese hackers faster.
critics: Critics say creating another government task force without clear funding would add bureaucracy without stopping cyber attacks.
Critics say waiting 18 months for the first report is too slow when Chinese hackers attack government systems every day.

119-hr-2270.one_liner: Stop counting employer-paid childcare and eldercare when calculating overtime pay
provisions: Currently, the value of employer-paid childcare and eldercare counts when calculating overtime pay rates
Removes childcare and eldercare benefits from overtime pay calculations
Makes it cheaper for employers to offer these benefits since they won't increase overtime costs
Affects workers who get overtime pay when working more than 40 hours per week

supporters: Supporters say removing childcare and eldercare benefits from overtime calculations would encourage more employers to offer these benefits since they won't increase overtime costs.
Supporters say this change would help working parents and caregivers access employer-provided childcare and eldercare services that many companies currently don't offer.
Supporters say the bill removes a barrier that prevents employers from providing family-friendly benefits.
critics: Critics say workers who receive employer-paid childcare and eldercare will see their overtime pay rates reduced when these benefits are excluded from the calculation.
Critics say the bill cuts worker compensation by removing the value of these benefits from the 1.5 times regular rate formula for overtime hours.
Critics say this shifts costs from employers to workers by reducing total pay for those working more than 40 hours per week.

119-hr-2312.one_liner: Change who can be paid the lower $2.13 tipped worker wage
provisions: Removes the $30 per month tip requirement that currently applies to tipped workers
Removes job duty requirements when deciding if someone counts as a tipped worker
Lets employers set work periods to measure if tips plus wages meet the $7.25 minimum wage
Allows more workers to be paid $2.13 per hour instead of $7.25 per hour as long as tips make up the difference

supporters: Supporters say this would remove the $30 per month tip requirement that prevents some workers from being classified as tipped employees.
Supporters say this would remove job duty requirements that limit which workers can be paid the tipped minimum wage of $2.13 per hour.
Supporters say this gives employers flexibility to set work periods for calculating if tips plus wages meet the $7.25 minimum wage.
critics: Critics say this allows more workers to be paid $2.13 per hour instead of $7.25 per hour as long as tips make up the difference.
Critics say removing the $30 monthly tip requirement eliminates a protection that ensures workers actually receive tips.
Critics say letting employers set their own work periods gives them too much control over how wages are calculated.

119-hr-3015.one_liner: Recreate a government council that advises on coal industry matters
provisions: Recreates the National Coal Council under the Department of Energy
The council will give advice about coal and the coal industry
The council will follow the same rules it had on November 19, 2021
Removes the rule that required the council to get a new charter every two years
The original council was created in 1984

supporters: Supporters say recreating the National Coal Council under the Department of Energy will restore expert advice on coal and coal industry matters.
Supporters say removing the Federal Advisory Committee Act requirement for two-year charter renewals will let the council work without paperwork delays.
Supporters say using the charter rules from November 19, 2021 brings back the proven system that worked from 1984 until the council ended.
critics: Critics say recreating the National Coal Council under the Department of Energy duplicates work that existing advisory committees could handle.
Critics say removing the Federal Advisory Committee Act requirement for two-year charter reviews reduces government oversight of the council.
Critics say establishing the council with the November 19, 2021 charter rules creates unnecessary bureaucracy within the Department of Energy.

119-hr-2988.one_liner: Require retirement plan managers to focus on financial returns when investing workers' money
provisions: Retirement plan managers must make investment choices based mainly on how much money the investment will make
Plan managers can consider other factors only when two investments have the same expected returns
Plan managers cannot treat some advisors or service providers differently than others when hiring them
Plan managers must vote company shares only in ways that help workers and retirees make more money
Plan managers must send notices to workers in certain retirement plans about their investment choices

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects workers' retirement money by requiring plan managers to choose investments based on how much money they will make, not political causes.
Supporters say the rule that plan managers cannot treat some advisors differently than others when hiring them prevents discrimination and ensures the best people get hired.
Supporters say requiring plan managers to vote company shares only in ways that help workers and retirees make more money ensures retirement funds grow instead of being used for political purposes.
critics: Critics say the restriction that plan managers can consider other factors only when two investments have the same expected returns could prevent them from avoiding companies with climate risks that might lose money over time.

Critics say limiting when plan managers can consider non-pecuniary factors could hurt long-term investment performance by blocking consideration of environmental and social risks that affect company profits.
Critics say the requirement that investment choices be based mainly on financial returns ignores that environmental and governance problems at companies often lead to financial losses for investors.

119-hr-2721.one_liner: Give headstones to veterans who died before November 1990
provisions: Creates a 2-year program to give headstones or burial markers to veterans who died on or before November 1, 1990
Only covers veterans who were not dishonorably discharged from the military
Veterans or their families must request the headstone
Updates the VA website to show the new rules for who can get headstones

supporters: Supporters say this program fixes the eligibility gap for veterans who died before November 1, 1990 and allows their families to request headstones.
Supporters say this honors veterans who served but were excluded by the previous November 1, 1990 cutoff date for burial markers.
critics: Critics say the program could be expensive since it covers veterans who died over multiple decades before 1990.
Critics say the 2-year pilot timeline may not be enough time to serve all families of pre-1990 veterans who request headstones.

119-hr-2683.one_liner: Control foreign remote access to sensitive US technology through the internet
provisions: Makes the same rules that apply to shipping sensitive technology overseas also apply to remote internet access
Requires permits for foreign people to access US technology that could be used for military purposes
Lets the Commerce Department fine people for accessing this technology without permission
Applies to internet and cloud access from locations outside the US

supporters: Supporters say this closes a security gap where foreign people could access US technology with military uses through the internet without any permits or oversight.
Supporters say it gives the Commerce Department the power to issue licenses and fine people who break the rules for remote access to sensitive items.
Supporters say this prevents foreign countries from getting around export controls by accessing dual-use technology through cloud services instead of buying it directly.
critics: Critics say US tech companies will lose business because foreign customers will need permits to access their cloud services and internet platforms.
Critics say the broad definition of remote access through internet and cloud computing will create costly compliance burdens for American businesses.
Critics say requiring licenses for foreign access to technology could slow down international business and hurt US competitiveness.

119-hr-2965.one_liner: Limit costs from new rules on small businesses to zero each year
provisions: Requires the Small Business Administration to keep total costs from federal rules on small businesses at zero or below each year
Includes costs from new rules and changes to existing rules
Requires any new rule that costs small businesses money to be balanced by reducing costs from other rules

supporters: Supporters say this would require the Small Business Administration to ensure federal rules add zero net costs to small businesses each year
Supporters say this would force agencies to reduce costs from existing rules whenever they create new rules that cost small businesses money
Supporters say this would prevent the annual small business regulatory budget from growing above zero
critics: Critics say this would prevent agencies from creating new rules that cost small businesses unless they first eliminate equal costs from other federal rules
Critics say this zero-cost requirement would force the Small Business Administration to make agencies remove existing rules to allow new ones
Critics say this would limit agencies from addressing new problems if those solutions add any costs to the small business regulatory budget

119-hr-3109.one_liner: Require a study on US oil refineries and how to expand them
provisions: Requires the Energy Department to order a study on US oil refineries
The study must look at how refineries help US energy security
The study must find ways to expand refinery capacity
The study must identify government actions that reduced refinery capacity
The study must recommend how to increase refinery capacity

supporters: Supporters say this study will help the US become more energy independent by finding ways to expand domestic oil refinery capacity.
Supporters say the report will identify specific government actions that have reduced refinery capacity, helping remove barriers to domestic energy production.
critics: Critics say this study wastes taxpayer money on research designed to expand fossil fuel infrastructure when the country should focus on clean energy.
Critics say requiring the Energy Department to find ways to increase refinery capacity goes against climate goals to reduce oil use.

119-hr-3123.one_liner: Let families collect veterans' pensions that were approved but not paid before death
provisions: Creates rules for the VA to pay pensions to families when the veteran died before getting paid
Gives the money to the veteran's spouse first, then children, then parents who depended on the veteran, then the estate
Families must file paperwork within one year of the veteran's death to get the money
If no one applies within a year, the money goes to the veteran's estate unless it would go to the state

supporters: Supporters say this ensures families get pensions that veterans earned but died before the VA paid them.
Supporters say the priority system - spouse first, then children, then dependent parents - makes clear who gets the money.
Supporters say requiring families to file within one year gives them time to apply while stopping money from going to the state.
critics: Critics say the VA will spend more money tracking down families and processing these new benefit claims.
Critics say the one-year deadline is too short for families who may not know the veteran had a pending pension.
Critics say this adds more paperwork to an already slow VA system.

119-hr-3187.one_liner: Give one acre of Forest Service land to Perry County Arkansas for public use
provisions: Gives about one acre of Forest Service land to Perry County Arkansas
The county must use the land for public purposes like education and youth programs
If the county stops using the land for public purposes the Forest Service can take it back
The county must pay all costs including surveys and environmental studies
A survey will determine the exact size of the land

supporters: Supporters say this gives Perry County one acre to build education and youth facilities without costing federal taxpayers since the county pays all survey and environmental study costs.
Supporters say this helps local students and youth programs by providing land for public facilities in Perry County.
Supporters say the reversion clause protects federal interests because if Perry County stops using the land for public purposes, the Forest Service can take it back.
critics: Critics say this gives away one acre of federal land that belongs to all Americans to benefit only Perry County residents.
Critics say Perry County taxpayers will have to pay for surveys and environmental studies which could cost thousands of dollars.
Critics say the Forest Service loses control of one acre that could be used for forest conservation or public recreation.

119-hr-3062.one_liner: Create a new approval process for oil, gas and electric lines crossing US borders
provisions: Requires companies to get permits from federal agencies before building oil pipelines, gas pipelines, or electric lines across US borders with Canada and Mexico
Sets deadlines for government agencies to approve or deny these permit requests
Requires Congress to vote before the President can cancel existing permits for cross-border energy projects
Replaces the current system where the President makes these decisions through executive orders

supporters: Supporters say this creates deadlines for government agencies to approve or deny permit requests, which gives energy companies more certainty about project timelines.
Supporters say requiring Congress to vote before the President can cancel existing permits protects investments in cross-border energy projects.
Supporters say this replaces the current executive order system with a standardized permit process through federal agencies like FERC and DOE.
critics: Critics say requiring Congress to vote before the President can cancel existing permits could make it harder to stop oil and gas pipelines that communities oppose.
Critics say this takes decision-making power away from the President and gives it to federal agencies and Congress, which could slow responses to changing energy needs.
Critics say this creates new permit requirements for companies building energy infrastructure across borders with Canada and Mexico, which adds regulatory steps.

119-hr-3383.one_liner: Remove SEC limits on how much investment funds can put into private funds
provisions: Stops the SEC from limiting how much closed-end investment funds can put into private funds
Stops the SEC from blocking the sale of shares from these investment funds
Makes the same changes for business development companies

supporters: Supporters say removing SEC limits on closed-end funds investing in private funds will give more money to startups and small businesses.
Supporters say stopping the SEC from blocking sales of these fund shares gives investors more choices to grow their money.
Supporters say this helps business development companies raise more capital for small businesses that need funding.
critics: Critics say removing SEC limits exposes closed-end fund investors to riskier private investments that could lose their money.
Critics say stopping the SEC from limiting these fund sales removes important protections for ordinary investors.
Critics say this allows funds to put investor money into less regulated private investments without proper oversight.

119-hr-3400.one_liner: Let VA doctors work in US territories for up to one year
provisions: Lets VA doctors work in places like Puerto Rico and Guam for up to one year
These doctors treat veterans at VA hospitals in these places
VA pays these doctors extra money as bonuses
The doctors work with local doctors when needed to help veterans

supporters: Supporters say this would help veterans living in Puerto Rico, Guam, and other US territories get better access to VA doctors at their local hospitals.
Supporters say the bonuses paid to traveling doctors would help recruit physicians willing to work in these remote areas where veterans currently have limited care options.
Supporters say requiring these doctors to work with local providers would improve care quality and coordination for the estimated veterans living in these territories.
critics: Critics say the relocation and retention bonuses for traveling physicians would cost taxpayers extra money without specifying how much the program would spend.
Critics say sending VA doctors to territories for up to one year could leave mainland VA hospitals short-staffed when they already struggle to serve veterans.
Critics say the one-year limit on assignments means veterans in territories may lose their doctors frequently and not get steady long-term care.

119-hr-3492.one_liner: Make gender-affirming medical care for minors a federal crime
provisions: Makes it a federal crime to give hormones or do surgeries on minors to change their sex
Sets punishment of up to 10 years in prison and fines for doctors who provide this care
Creates exceptions for children born with both male and female body parts or hormone problems
Protects minors from being arrested for receiving this care
Expands rules against female genital cutting to include more people who help or allow it
Protects people who had female genital cutting from being arrested

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects children from irreversible surgeries and hormone treatments that change their bodies before they are old enough to make these decisions.
Supporters say the 10-year prison sentence will stop doctors from performing these procedures on minors.
Supporters say the bill includes exceptions for children born with both male and female body parts, showing it targets only gender-change procedures.
critics: Critics say this bill makes medical care between families, doctors, and transgender youth into a federal crime punishable by 10 years in prison.
Critics say the threat of prison time will make doctors afraid to help transgender minors, even when families want this care.
Critics say this removes medical decisions from families and doctors and puts the federal government in control of healthcare choices.

119-hr-3486.one_liner: Increase prison sentences for non-citizens who enter illegally and commit crimes
provisions: Makes non-citizens who enter the US illegally and later get convicted of a serious crime serve at least 5 years in prison
Raises the maximum prison time for entering illegally multiple times from 2 years to 5 years
Raises the maximum prison time for non-citizens who were removed and try to enter again from 2 years to 10 years
Makes non-citizens with past serious crime convictions who try to enter again serve at least 10 years in prison
Sets up to 10 years in prison for non-citizens who were removed 3 or more times and try to enter again

supporters: Supporters say the 5-year mandatory minimum for non-citizens who enter illegally and later commit felonies will keep dangerous criminals in prison longer to protect communities.
Supporters say increasing maximum penalties from 2 to 5 years for repeated illegal entry will stop people from trying to cross the border multiple times.
Supporters say the 10-year mandatory minimum for those with past felony convictions who try to re-enter will prevent the most dangerous criminals from returning to the US.
critics: Critics say the mandatory minimum sentences of 5 and 10 years will cost taxpayers millions more in prison costs each year.
Critics say increasing penalties from 2 to 10 years for people who were removed and try to re-enter will separate families for much longer periods.
Critics say the mandatory minimums prevent judges from considering individual cases when someone with a past felony conviction tries to re-enter.

119-hr-3425.one_liner: Improve oversight and tracking of federal security guards at federal buildings
provisions: Requires the Federal Protective Service to create new testing and training rules for security guards within one year
Orders quarterly reviews of secret test results to find ways to improve security
Makes security guards take extra training if they fail secret tests
Requires the Federal Protective Service to upgrade systems that track security guard schedules within 180 days
Creates procedures to notify federal building workers when security guards are missing
Requires yearly reports to Congress on these security improvements

supporters: Supporters say the quarterly reviews of secret test results will help identify security gaps at federal buildings before they become problems.
Supporters say the new tracking system requirements will ensure federal workers know when security guards are absent from their posts.
Supporters say mandatory extra training for guards who fail secret tests will improve protection for the thousands of federal employees working in these buildings.
critics: Critics say the new testing protocols and quarterly reviews will create costly administrative burdens for the Federal Protective Service without clear funding sources.
Critics say the 180-day deadline to upgrade tracking systems is too short and may force rushed technology purchases.
Critics say requiring yearly Congressional reports for three years adds unnecessary paperwork that diverts resources from actual security work.

119-hr-3424.one_liner: Require GSA to expand office space sharing among federal agencies
provisions: GSA must work with agencies to find problems with shared office arrangements
GSA must create rules to expand office space sharing
GSA must find ways special-purpose rooms can help with sharing
GSA must set goals to measure if shared office arrangements work
GSA must report to Congress within 6 months

supporters: Supporters say this would save taxpayer money by having GSA work with agencies to share office space instead of renting separate federal buildings.
Supporters say requiring GSA to create rules for expanding space sharing would reduce waste in federal leasing costs.
Supporters say the 6-month Congressional briefing requirement would ensure agencies actually follow through on shared-space arrangements.
critics: Critics say requiring GSA to collaborate with all tenant agencies and develop new criteria would create more bureaucratic meetings and paperwork.
Critics say shared office arrangements could hurt agency productivity when workers from different federal departments use the same special-purpose rooms.
Critics say the costs of GSA staff time to establish measurable objectives and identify shared-space concerns could exceed any savings from office sharing.

119-hr-3628.one_liner: Require state regulators to consider rules for 10-year electricity planning
provisions: Requires state regulators to consider making electric companies plan for reliable power over 10 years
Focuses on power plants that can run continuously for at least 30 days
Applies only to electric companies that use long-term planning methods
Defines reliable power plants as those with 30 days of fuel and ability to work during bad weather

supporters: Supporters say this would help prevent blackouts by encouraging state regulators to require electric companies to plan for power plants that can run for 30 days straight.
Supporters say the 10-year planning requirement would ensure electric companies prepare for reliable power when severe weather hits.
Supporters say this focuses on power plants that provide important grid services like frequency and voltage support during emergencies.
critics: Critics say this could increase electricity costs because the 30-day fuel storage requirement would force expensive investments in backup fuel.
Critics say the bill favors fossil fuel plants that can store 30 days of fuel over renewable energy sources that depend on weather.
Critics say this creates unnecessary regulatory requirements for state authorities overseeing electric companies that already use long-term planning.

119-hr-3638.one_liner: Require the Energy Department to study electricity supply chains and report to Congress
provisions: Requires the Energy Department to study how America gets the parts needed to make and move electricity
The department must report what they find to Congress
The first report is due within one year after this becomes law
The study must look for weak spots in getting electricity equipment
The department must find what stops America from processing more minerals used in electricity
The report must suggest ways to fix problems and strengthen supply chains

supporters: Supporters say the required assessment of electricity supply chain vulnerabilities would help identify weak spots before they become major problems
Supporters say the study of barriers to processing critical minerals in America would help reduce dependence on foreign countries for electricity equipment
critics: Critics say requiring the Energy Department to conduct these periodic studies and reports would cost taxpayers money for more government bureaucracy
Critics say the one-year deadline for the first report may force rushed analysis of complex supply chain issues

119-hr-3616.one_liner: Require yearly power grid checks and federal approval before rules that could hurt electricity supply
provisions: Requires yearly checks on whether the electric grid has enough power to stay reliable
If power supply looks too low, the grid watchdog must notify federal energy regulators
Federal agencies must submit proposed rules affecting power plants to energy regulators for review
Energy regulators can recommend changes to proposed federal rules
Federal agencies cannot finish new rules until energy regulators say the rules will not hurt power supply

supporters: Supporters say this prevents blackouts by requiring yearly checks on whether the electric grid has enough power to stay reliable.
Supporters say this gives energy regulators power to recommend changes to federal rules that could hurt power supply before those rules are finished.
Supporters say this creates an early warning system that notifies energy regulators when the electric grid does not have enough power generation.
critics: Critics say this slows down environmental rules by forcing federal agencies to submit proposed rules affecting power plants to energy regulators for review.
Critics say this gives energy regulators too much power by letting them block federal rules until they approve them.
Critics say the yearly reliability assessments could add costs and bureaucracy to electric grid oversight.

119-hr-3632.one_liner: Let more groups ask federal regulators to keep power plants open for reliable electricity
provisions: Lets electricity companies join state regulators in asking federal officials to keep power plants from closing
Allows federal regulators to order power plants to stay open for up to 5 years if closing them would hurt electricity service
Requires power plant owners to give 5 years notice before closing units except in emergencies
Exempts actions taken to follow federal orders from environmental laws
Requires federal regulators to set payment rates and decide who pays for plants ordered to stay open

supporters: Supporters say this would prevent blackouts by letting federal regulators order power plants to stay open for up to 5 years when closing them would hurt electricity service.
Supporters say the 5-year notice requirement gives grid operators time to find replacement power sources before plants close.
Supporters say allowing transmission organizations to file complaints gives the people who run the electrical grid a voice in keeping it stable.
critics: Critics say the exemption from environmental laws lets power plants ignore pollution rules when following federal orders to stay open.
Critics say forcing plants to stay open for up to 5 years could raise electricity costs for consumers who must pay for the required compensation.
Critics say this could keep dirty coal and gas plants running longer instead of replacing them with cleaner energy sources.

119-hr-3617.one_liner: Require the Energy Department to secure America's energy resource supply chains
provisions: Requires the Energy Department to study which energy resources America needs most
Orders ongoing checks of supply systems to find weak spots that could cause shortages
Directs studies of how much America relies on importing energy materials from other countries
Requires the Energy Department to create plans to strengthen domestic energy supplies
Orders work on backup materials and better ways to reuse energy resources

supporters: Supporters say the required studies of import reliance and domestic supply plans would help America become less dependent on foreign countries for critical energy materials.
Supporters say the ongoing supply chain assessments would help spot weak spots before they cause energy shortages that hurt families and businesses.
Supporters say the research on recycling and reuse technology would help stretch existing energy materials further and reduce waste.
critics: Critics say this creates more government studies and assessments without providing actual money to fix the supply problems it finds.
Critics say the Energy Department already tracks energy resources and requiring these ongoing assessments adds duplicate work that wastes taxpayer money.
Critics say the bill gives the Energy Department new duties to study adversarial nations and supply chains but no clear authority to take action on the results.

119-hr-4058.one_liner: Require FEMA to help groups get grants for terrorism protection
provisions: Requires FEMA to help groups apply for grants that protect communities from terrorist attacks
Requires FEMA to survey grant recipients every year
Requires FEMA to report how they use feedback from grant recipients
Requires FEMA and a government watchdog agency to report to Congress on how FEMA follows these new rules

supporters: Supporters say this would help local governments and organizations better access grants that protect communities from terrorist attacks by requiring FEMA to provide ongoing technical assistance.
Supporters say the annual surveys of grant recipients would ensure FEMA gets regular feedback to improve these security programs.
Supporters say requiring FEMA to report to Congress on how they use stakeholder feedback would create accountability for these homeland security grant programs.
critics: Critics say this would force FEMA to hire additional staff to conduct annual surveys and provide ongoing technical assistance, increasing administrative costs.
Critics say the required annual surveys would create new paperwork burdens for local governments and organizations that receive these grants.
Critics say the reporting requirements duplicate existing oversight since FEMA already reports to Congress on grant programs.

119-hr-3838.one_liner: Fund the military and set defense policies for the year starting October 2025
provisions: Pays for Department of Defense programs and activities for the year starting October 2025
Sets how many troops can serve in active duty and reserves
Pays for buying and upgrading military equipment like aircraft
Sets military pay rates and healthcare rules
Funds military research and development projects
Sets rules for defense contracts with private companies
Funds nuclear security programs and nuclear facility safety

supporters: Supporters say the military pay rate increases and updated healthcare rules will help the military recruit and keep experienced service members.
Supporters say funding for aircraft upgrades and new military equipment will give troops better tools to complete their missions.
Supporters say the nuclear security program funding will protect nuclear facilities from safety risks and security threats.
critics: Critics say the defense contract rules with private companies could limit competition and increase costs for taxpayers.
Critics say the troop strength levels authorized for active duty and reserves exceed what military leaders have requested for current missions.
Critics say the research and development project funding lacks specific timelines and measurable goals for delivering new military capabilities.

119-hr-3898.one_liner: Remove Clean Water Act protections from waste treatment systems and several water types
provisions: Removes Clean Water Act protections from waste treatment systems
Removes protections from water that only flows during rain
Removes protections from farmland that used to be wetlands
Removes protections from underground water
Lets the Army Corps of Engineers exclude other water areas from protection

supporters: Supporters say this removes Clean Water Act rules from farmland that used to be wetlands, helping farmers avoid costly permits.
Supporters say this stops the government from regulating temporary water that only flows during rain storms.
Supporters say this gives the Army Corps of Engineers more power to decide which water areas actually need federal protection.
critics: Critics say this removes Clean Water Act protections from underground water sources that supply drinking water to communities.
Critics say this allows waste treatment systems to operate without Clean Water Act oversight, risking pollution.
Critics say this removes federal protection from converted farmland that used to be important wetlands.

119-hr-4090.one_liner: Speed up mining for metals and minerals on federal lands
provisions: Tells Interior to find mining projects on federal lands that can be approved right away and speed them up
Tells Interior to find federal land good for mining metals and minerals
Tells Interior to cancel or change rules that make mining harder
Tells Interior to recommend law changes to expand U.S. metal and mineral production
Tells Interior to review state and local laws that block mining projects
Tells Interior to report on how much money the U.S. spends importing metals and minerals

supporters: Supporters say this bill would reduce America's dependence on foreign countries for critical metals and minerals by speeding up mining projects on federal lands.
Supporters say the requirement for Interior to cancel rules that burden mining projects would cut red tape and create jobs in mining communities.
Supporters say having Interior recommend law changes to expand U.S. mineral production would strengthen national security by securing domestic supply chains.
critics: Critics say directing Interior to expedite mining projects on federal lands could skip important environmental reviews that protect wildlife and water sources.
Critics say requiring Interior to review state and local laws that block mining projects overrides communities' right to control development in their areas.
Critics say prioritizing land identification for mining could open protected areas like national forests to industrial development.

119-hr-3668.one_liner: Speed up environmental reviews for natural gas pipeline projects
provisions: Makes the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) the single agency in charge of environmental reviews for natural gas pipelines and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals
Other agencies must follow FERC's rules instead of doing their own separate reviews
FERC cannot wait more than 90 days to approve or deny a project after the environmental review is finished
Pipeline companies no longer need water quality permits from states
Agencies must accept data collected by drones or satellites from pipeline companies

supporters: Supporters say this speeds up pipeline approvals by making FERC the only lead agency instead of having multiple agencies do separate reviews.
Supporters say the 90-day deadline prevents energy projects from getting stuck in endless delays.
Supporters say requiring agencies to accept drone and satellite data makes reviews faster and more efficient.
critics: Critics say removing state water quality permits takes away states' ability to protect their local water sources.
Critics say having only FERC lead environmental reviews instead of multiple agencies could miss important environmental problems.
Critics say the 90-day deadline forces FERC to rush decisions about projects that affect communities for decades.

119-hr-4405.one_liner: Require the Justice Department to publish all records about Jeffrey Epstein's case
provisions: Makes the Justice Department publish all records about Jeffrey Epstein's investigation and prosecution
Includes records about Ghislaine Maxwell, flight logs, and travel records
Must publish names of government officials connected to the case
Can hide victim personal information and details that would hurt other federal investigations
Must report to Congress within 15 days about what records were released and what was hidden

supporters: Supporters say this would make public the names of government officials connected to the Epstein case so people can see who was involved.
Supporters say publishing flight logs and travel records would show the public who traveled with Epstein.
Supporters say requiring DOJ to report to Congress within 15 days would ensure the government releases information quickly.
critics: Critics say publishing names of people referenced in Epstein records could damage reputations of those who were not charged with crimes.
Critics say releasing investigative materials could interfere with active federal investigations that DOJ is still working on.
Critics say the bill could expose private details about people mentioned in records despite protections for victims.

119-hr-4371.one_liner: Add requirements for placing immigrant children without parents
provisions: Requires officials to consider if a child might run away, hurt themselves, or hurt others when deciding where to place them
Requires children 13 and older with gang tattoos or gang arrests to be placed in secure facilities
Requires collecting names, birth dates, Social Security numbers, and background checks for all adults in homes of potential caregivers
Stops placing children with caregivers who are in the US illegally

supporters: Supporters say requiring background checks for all adults in potential homes protects children from being placed with people who have criminal records.
Supporters say placing children 13 and older with gang tattoos or gang arrests in secure facilities keeps other children and the community safe.
Supporters say stopping placement with people who are in the US illegally ensures children go to homes with legal caregivers.
critics: Critics say stopping placement with people who are in the US illegally will separate children from family members who could care for them.
Critics say requiring children 13 and older with gang markings to go to secure facilities puts more children in detention instead of homes.
Critics say collecting Social Security numbers and immigration status from all adults in homes will scare away potential caregivers.

119-hr-4305.one_liner: Keep running a hotline for small businesses to report problems with federal rules
provisions: Requires the Small Business Administration to keep running the Red Tape Hotline
The hotline lets small businesses report problems with federal rules that are hard to follow
The office must report yearly to the Small Business Administration and Congress about complaints received

supporters: Supporters say this bill helps small businesses by keeping the Red Tape Hotline open so they can report problems with federal rules that are hard to follow.
Supporters say the yearly reports to Congress and the Small Business Administration will show lawmakers which federal rules cause the most problems for small businesses.
Supporters say maintaining the hotline gives small business owners a voice when federal agencies create rules that hurt their operations.
critics: Critics say the bill requires spending taxpayer money to keep running the hotline and produce yearly reports without guaranteeing any federal rules will actually be removed.
Critics say the resources used for the hotline and annual reporting could be better spent on direct programs that help small businesses grow.
Critics say the bill creates more bureaucracy by requiring yearly reports instead of focusing on cutting the actual regulations that burden small businesses.

119-hr-4593.one_liner: Change how the government defines showerheads for water rules
provisions: Sets a new government definition for showerheads used in water rules
Uses a definition created by an engineering group instead of the old government definition
Requires the Department of Energy to update its showerhead rules to use the new definition

supporters: Supporters say this gives the Department of Energy clear legal authority to use the American Society of Mechanical Engineers definition for showerheads in federal regulations.
Supporters say this implements Executive Order 14264 from April 2025 that already directed the Department of Energy to change its showerhead definition.
critics: Critics say this replaces the government's water efficiency definition with one created by an engineering industry group.
Critics say this could weaken federal water efficiency regulations by changing how showerheads are defined and measured.

119-hr-4423.one_liner: Continue blocking World Bank funding to Burma
provisions: Tells the U.S. person at the World Bank to keep blocking loans and funding to Burma
Makes an exception if the Treasury Department says blocking the money hurts America
Continues blocking that started after Burma's military took power in 2021

supporters: Supporters say this keeps pressure on Burma's military government by making the U.S. World Bank director vote to continue the funding pause that started after the 2021 coup.
Supporters say this prevents American money from flowing through the World Bank to Burma's military regime that took power by force.
Supporters say the Treasury Department can still change course if blocking the money hurts U.S. national interests.
critics: Critics say this hurts ordinary people in Burma who need World Bank loans for schools, hospitals, and other basic services.
Critics say this reduces America's influence by forcing the U.S. World Bank director to vote the same way every time instead of negotiating.
Critics say the bill continues the funding pause without setting clear goals for when Burma could get World Bank money again.

119-hr-4922.one_liner: Block DC from changing criminal sentences and tighten youth crime rules
provisions: Stops DC from changing any criminal sentence that exists when this bill becomes law
Changes the age limit for youth offenders from 24 years old to 18 years old
Removes judges' ability to give youth offenders sentences lighter than the required minimum
Requires DC's Attorney General to post youth crime data online every month

supporters: Supporters say this prevents DC from weakening existing criminal sentences and keeps punishment consistent across cases.
Supporters say changing the youth offender age from 24 to 18 means adults over 18 face full adult sentences instead of lighter youth penalties.
Supporters say removing judges' ability to give sentences below the required minimum ensures violent offenders serve appropriate prison time.
critics: Critics say this removes DC's local control over its own criminal justice system and blocks needed sentencing reforms.
Critics say changing the youth offender age from 24 to 18 cuts off rehabilitation programs for thousands of young adults who could benefit from treatment.
Critics say removing judges' discretion to reduce minimum sentences eliminates flexibility needed for individual cases and circumstances.

119-hr-4776.one_liner: Reduce environmental reviews required for federal projects
provisions: Makes fewer government projects need environmental reviews
Stops agencies from requiring environmental reviews just because a project gets federal money
Lets projects skip environmental reviews if they already had reviews under other environmental laws
Requires agencies to only look at direct effects of a project, not possible future or indirect effects
Limits how people can challenge environmental review decisions in court

supporters: Supporters say this would speed up approval for infrastructure projects like roads and bridges by eliminating duplicate environmental reviews when projects have already been reviewed under other federal or state environmental laws.
Supporters say the bill would reduce construction delays by requiring agencies to focus only on direct project effects rather than speculative future impacts.
Supporters say limiting court challenges would prevent activist groups from using lawsuits to block needed energy and transportation projects.
critics: Critics say restricting environmental reviews to only direct effects would ignore important impacts like air pollution that spreads to nearby communities or effects on wildlife migration patterns.
Critics say allowing projects to skip environmental reviews based on other agency reviews could let harmful projects proceed without proper analysis of environmental risks.
Critics say limiting judicial review would reduce the public's ability to challenge government decisions that could damage local environments and communities.

119-hr-498.one_liner: Stop Medicaid from paying for treatments that change gender for people under 18
provisions: Stops Medicaid from paying for treatments that change someone's body to match a different gender for people under 18
Includes surgeries, implants, and hormone treatments
Still allows payment for treatments that fix genetic disorders, early puberty, or chromosome problems
Still allows payment for treatments that reverse previous gender change treatments
Still allows payment for treatments needed to prevent death or serious harm to the body

supporters: Supporters say this protects children under 18 from surgeries, implants, and hormone treatments by stopping Medicaid funding for gender transition procedures.
Supporters say the bill maintains Medicaid payment for treatments for genetic disorders, early puberty, and chromosome problems while blocking funding for gender transition procedures.
Supporters say this saves taxpayer money while still covering treatments needed to prevent death or serious harm to the body.
critics: Critics say this denies Medicaid coverage for hormone treatments and surgeries that transgender youth under 18 need, creating financial barriers to care.
Critics say the ban discriminates against transgender minors who depend on Medicaid by blocking coverage for these specific procedures.
Critics say this interferes with medical decisions between doctors, parents, and patients by limiting which treatments Medicaid will cover for people under 18.

119-hr-4626.one_liner: Change how the government sets energy efficiency rules for home appliances
provisions: Lets the Energy Department change appliance efficiency rules when needed instead of by set deadlines
Lets companies ask to cancel efficiency rules if they make appliances cost more or become hard to buy
Changes how the government decides if efficiency rules are worth the cost
Requires the Energy Department to report meetings with groups tied to China or that oppose certain energy sources
Stops new efficiency rules for electric transformers
Allows new efficiency rules for clothes washers and dishwashers

supporters: Supporters say this lets companies petition to cancel efficiency rules that make appliances cost more or become hard to buy for consumers.
Supporters say changing from set deadlines to when-needed timing gives the Energy Department more flexibility to set proper standards.
Supporters say the new criteria for economic justification will ensure efficiency rules don't price out consumers from buying appliances.
critics: Critics say letting companies petition to cancel efficiency rules could weaken standards that help reduce energy use in homes.
Critics say the disclosure requirements single out groups with ties to China or that oppose certain energy sources.
Critics say stopping new efficiency rules for electric transformers could prevent energy savings in the power grid.

119-hr-4758.one_liner: Cancel federal programs that help people make homes more energy efficient
provisions: Cancels rebates that help low and moderate income households switch to electric home equipment
Cancels grants that train contractors to do energy efficiency work
Cancels federal help for states to adopt certain building energy codes
Takes back any unused money from these programs

supporters: Supporters say this saves taxpayer money by ending rebate programs that pay for electric home equipment.
Supporters say this gives homeowners more freedom to choose their energy sources without federal programs pushing them toward electric equipment.
Supporters say this cuts federal spending on programs that tell states what building energy codes to adopt.
critics: Critics say this takes away rebates that help low and moderate income households afford electric heat pumps and other equipment.
Critics say this eliminates grants that train contractors to do energy efficiency work, which could cost jobs in that field.
Critics say this stops federal help for states to adopt building energy codes that could lower energy bills for homeowners.

119-hr-504.one_liner: Expand the Miccosukee Reserved Area to include Osceola Camp in Everglades National Park
provisions: Adds Osceola Camp to the Miccosukee Reserved Area in Florida
Osceola Camp is currently part of Everglades National Park
Requires the Department of the Interior to protect buildings in Osceola Camp from flooding
The Department must work with the Miccosukee Tribe on flood protection

supporters: Supporters say adding Osceola Camp to the Miccosukee Reserved Area returns traditional tribal lands to the Miccosukee Tribe.

118-hr-2799.one_liner: Loosen rules for companies selling stock and let more people invest in private companies

critics: Critics say the $250,000 exemption removes important protections that help investors know what they're buying.
Critics say raising the revenue limit to $1.5 billion lets very large companies avoid disclosure rules meant to protect shareholders.
Critics say increasing fund investor limits from 250 to 600 people makes it harder for regulators to track who is investing.

118-hr-6544.one_liner: Speed up permits and cut fees for nuclear power plants

Supporters say the government buying power from nuclear plants for many years will help companies get loans to build new reactors.
critics: Critics say cutting permit fees means taxpayers subsidize nuclear power companies instead of the companies paying their own costs.
Critics say requiring faster environmental reviews for nuclear plant applications could skip important safety studies.

118-hr-3843.one_liner: Continue grants to states for dental health workers in areas with shortages

critics: Critics say continuing these state grants through 2028 will cost taxpayers money that could be used elsewhere.

D.C. must provide enough parking for any new buildings

supporters: Supporters say this gives D.C. the RFK Stadium campus for free to build a new stadium or develop homes and stores that create jobs.

critics: Critics say giving D.C. valuable federal land for no cost wastes taxpayer money that could benefit all Americans.
Critics say commercial development near National Park Service lands could damage those protected areas despite the bill's safety rules.

118-hr-5375.one_liner: Create a working group with Japan, Australia, and India

supporters: Supporters say creating a working group with Japan, Australia, and India would help the US prepare for the next pandemic by sharing information and resources with key allies.

Supporters say increasing trade and business ties with Japan, Australia, and India would create jobs for American workers and open new markets.
critics: Critics say requiring the State Department to create another working group and strategy report adds more paperwork without clear benefits.

118-hr-533.one_liner: Define Tibet more broadly for U.S. policy and direct efforts to counter Chinese disinformation

critics: Critics say expanding the U.S. definition of Tibet to include areas in four Chinese provinces could harm diplomatic relations with China.
Critics say directing a U.S. office to counter Chinese statements about Tibet interferes in China's internal affairs.

118-hr-7176.one_liner: Remove rules that limit natural gas exports and imports

supporters: Supporters say this streamlines approval by putting FERC in charge of both export permits and terminal construction instead of splitting authority between the Energy Department and FERC.

critics: Critics say moving export approval from the Energy Department to FERC could weaken oversight of how much natural gas leaves the country.

118-hr-7511.one_liner: Require detention of non-citizens arrested for theft and let states sue over immigration

supporters: Supporters say this keeps communities safe by requiring the government to detain non-citizens who are here illegally and have been arrested for break-ins, theft, or shoplifting.

critics: Critics say this violates due process by requiring detention of people who have only been arrested, not convicted, for crimes like shoplifting.

118-hr-7102.one_liner: Create an office in the Small Business Administration for Native American businesses

118-hres-1052.one_liner: Set House rules for voting on two bills

118-hres-1061.one_liner: Adopt the Senate version of a government funding bill for 2024
